title: Interpreting AI Models-based Structured Data: A Survey of Local Model-Agnostic Explanation Methods
abstract: Modern Artificial Intelligence (AI), and Machine Learning (ML) models are widely used in numerous domains. However, their decision-making-based processes are complex for human understanding and interpretation. Such lack of transparency creates serious challenges, especially in sensitive domains as trust is essential. This raises the importance of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods to address such issue by providing tools that explain how AI models reach their decisions. One of the most dominant XAI methods is the Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME). It explains individual predictions using simple local models. Nevertheless, it exhibits limited fidelity, global interpretability, and varying behaviour according to the used data types. Various studies have proposed improvements to LIME in different applications, which raise the difficulty to develop advanced, generic LIME method. This inspired this work to present a comprehensive survey of LIME-based explanation methods with structured data. It summarizes LIME’s limitations, reviews its modified versions, and provide a unified overview of the progress of LIME. Compared with previously published surveys on XAI and LIME, the proposed taxonomy systematically organizes traditional and modified LIME approaches according to the core limitations toward providing an integrated LIME framework that simultaneously improve stability, fidelity, and global interpretability. The survey also identifies key research gaps, and discusses future directions for LIME-based explanation approaches. The recommended future research took benefit from developing explanation frameworks that address the major limitations of traditional LIME within a unique framework.

title: Strategic Verification for Long-Running LLM Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from single-turn text generators into long-running systems capable of multi-step reasoning, tool use, persistent memory, and reusable skill development. Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) can improve agent reliability, but existing approaches commonly treat verification as a fixed component of the reward structure, creating challenges related to sparse credit assignment, verifier reliability, reward hacking, path compliance, and verification cost. We introduce Budgeted Adaptive Verification with Asymmetric Rewards (BAVAR), a framework that formulates verification as a sequential, resource-constrained decision problem. BAVAR selectively determines what to verify, when verification is valuable, which verifier to invoke, and how verified evidence should influence learning based on uncertainty, action criticality, verifier reliability, expected verification value, and remaining computational budget. It combines reliability-gated positive process rewards with persistent penalties for path violations and extends verification to persistent memories and reusable skills. In an illustrative evaluation under matched verification budgets, BAVAR achieved 72.6% safe verified success, compared with 67.1% for uniform dense verification and 58.4% for outcome-only RLVR. Relative to dense verification, BAVAR reduced verification cost per safe success by 45.5% while using 47.8% fewer verifier tokens. It also reduced verified path violations to 7.2 per 100 trajectories, compared with 20.4 for outcome-only RLVR, and reduced successful verifier exploitation to 4.8%, compared with 15.9% for a single-judge baseline and 18.6% for outcome-only RLVR. For persistent artifacts, BAVAR achieved 88.7% held-out reuse success, compared with 81.3% for dense verification. These simulated findings suggest that adaptive allocation of verification resources can improve safe agent performance while reducing computational and verification overhead, providing a principled foundation for scalable verification of long-running autonomous agents.

title: Problem Formulation and Basic Search Procedure
abstract: Chapter 3, Problem Formulation and Basic Search Procedure, includes formalization of the considered problem of search and detection in the gridded domain. The chapter introduces a hierarchy of the probability maps – sensor map, agent map, and global map – and introduces procedures of updating probability maps and sensors' fusion. Also, the chapter specifies basic search procedure in the presence of detection errors of Type I and Type II and discusses communication between the agents acting in group. Simulation results demonstrate the difference in the search time with respect to the percentage of detection errors and to sharing information between the agents.

title: PersonaEdit: Representative Sample Selection for Personalized Model Editing
abstract: Personalization has attracted growing interest in LLM applications, yet existing retrieval-based approaches depend heavily on retrieval quality and degrade in long-term interactions. Model editing, which directly modifies internal model parameters to incorporate new knowledge, has demonstrated effective knowledge modification capabilities in factual knowledge editing tasks and may provide a potential solution for personalization. However, scaling model editing to personalization is non-trivial. Editing large amounts of user data increases computational cost and causes interference among edits, motivating the need for effective sample selection. To address this issue, we propose, PersonaEdit, a hidden representation clustering strategy that selects representative editing samples through proportional stratified sampling. Experiments show that model editing is effective for personalization, and that our selection strategy preserves most of the performance while substantially reducing the number of required editing samples. Beyond standalone editing, we find that combining model editing with retrieval-based prompt augmentation further improves personalization, as edited knowledge and retrieved context provide complementary information. These results demonstrate the potential of model editing as an efficient and scalable approach for LLM personalization.

title: Information-Theoretic Robustness Quantification for Neural Networks
abstract: This paper introduces a new approach to quantifying the robustness of neural networks, shifting the focus from traditional adversarial attack success rates to a fundamental measure of information flow. The core idea is to leverage Shannon entropy and mutual information to precisely assess a network's vulnerability to adversarial perturbations. We propose an algorithm that calculates the mutual information between the input and the network's output across a spectrum of carefully controlled perturbations. This metric provides a granular and informative measure of network resilience, offering insights beyond simple attack success rates. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through theoretical analysis and illustrate its potential for improved network design and security.

title: Adaptive Kernel Learning via Differential Privacy
abstract: Kernel learning techniques have demonstrated remarkable success in various machine learning tasks, offering powerful non-linear modeling capabilities. However, traditional kernel learning methods often rely on fixed kernel parameters, which can lead to suboptimal performance and sensitivity to outliers. Furthermore, incorporating differential privacy (DP) to protect sensitive data while training machine learning models remains a significant challenge, particularly for complex methods like kernel learning. This work proposes a novel adaptive kernel learning framework that leverages differential privacy to enhance both the accuracy and robustness of kernel methods. The core idea is to dynamically adjust the kernel parameters based on the observed data distribution, guided by a differential privacy mechanism. This allows us to allocate a privacy budget to kernel parameter updates, effectively balancing the trade-off between accuracy and privacy. The proposed method ensures robust performance against noisy data while simultaneously limiting information leakage to the training data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a theoretical analysis and provide a detailed explanation of the adaptive kernel selection process. The key contributions of this paper are the integration of adaptive kernel learning and differential privacy, offering a practical solution for building accurate and privacy-preserving kernel models.

title: Probabilistic Programming with Monadic Computation
abstract: Probabilistic programming has emerged as a powerful paradigm for modeling and reasoning under uncertainty. However, existing probabilistic programming languages often struggle to effectively represent and reason about complex, monadic computations—those involving multiple actions, side effects, and state transitions. This paper introduces a novel approach to probabilistic programming by extending the framework with a monadic type system. This extension allows users to naturally represent and reason about computations that inherently involve multiple steps and potential interactions, providing a more expressive and intuitive way to model real-world scenarios. The core contribution lies in the ability to seamlessly integrate probabilistic inference with monadic sequencing, leading to a more powerful and flexible framework for tackling complex probabilistic problems. We outline the key features of this system and discuss its potential impact on various applications within probabilistic modeling and machine learning.

title: Quantum Walk-Based Optimization Algorithms
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of quantum walk algorithms for solving optimization problems. Traditional optimization algorithms often struggle with complex search spaces due to their inherent limitations in exploring multiple possibilities simultaneously. Quantum walks, inspired by quantum mechanics, offer a compelling alternative by exploiting superposition and interference. This work proposes a novel quantum walk-based algorithm designed for efficient exploration of optimization landscapes. The core idea revolves around encoding the optimization problem as a quantum walk on a graph, where the walker's probabilistic movement is governed by quantum mechanical principles. We demonstrate how superposition allows the walker to exist in multiple states concurrently, while interference can amplify the probability of reaching optimal solutions. The algorithm's effectiveness is analyzed through theoretical considerations and mathematical formulations, highlighting its potential advantages over classical approaches. This research contributes to the growing field of quantum optimization and offers a new perspective on tackling challenging optimization tasks.

title: 基于元学习的算法自适应机制
abstract: This paper explores the application of meta-learning techniques to address the challenge of algorithmic adaptation. Traditional algorithms often struggle with varying data distributions and task complexities, leading to suboptimal performance. Our approach leverages meta-learning, specifically focusing on learning optimal parameter adjustment strategies for algorithms. We construct a meta-learning model where the algorithm's parameters are treated as the state and the task as the action. Through meta-training, the model learns to dynamically adapt the algorithm's parameters, aiming to improve both its generalization ability and learning efficiency. The core claim is that meta-learning offers a novel mechanism for achieving algorithmic self-adaptation, ultimately leading to enhanced performance across diverse scenarios. The key mechanism involves learning a policy that maps task characteristics to appropriate parameter adjustments. This work represents a new direction in algorithm design, shifting from static parameter settings to dynamically adaptive systems.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE–BASED ANALYSIS OF DISCOURSES ON SUSTAINABLE AGRICULTURE
abstract: This study aims to investigate how sustainable agriculture is represented in the digital public sphere by examining technology-driven agricultural systems through artificial intelligence–based text analytics. A dataset of 13,354 English posts collected from the X platform during January 2026 was used, with 10,782 posts retained after preprocessing. The methodology integrates text mining, TF-IDF keyword extraction, BERT-based sentiment analysis, and LDA topic modelling. The optimal number of LDA topics was determined using coherence score evaluation to ensure statistical robustness and thematic interpretability. This study integrates text mining, BERT-based sentiment analysis, and LDA topic modelling within a unified artificial intelligence framework to provide a comprehensive analysis of sustainable agriculture discourse on social media. The results show predominantly neutral discourse (65.27%), reflecting informational content, while positive discourse (33.17%) highlights smart farming and innovation. Negative discourse (1.56%) primarily addresses structural challenges. Three dominant themes emerged: climate-oriented sustainability, community-based practices, and technology-driven agriculture, emphasizing the role of digital technologies in shaping sustainable agricultural systems. The findings provide practical insights for policymakers, agricultural stakeholders, and researchers by supporting evidence-based communication strategies and technology-oriented sustainability policies.

title: Swarm Dynamics in Optimization
abstract: The chapter provides an in-depth exploration with PSO (Particle Swarm Optimization), and Swarm intelligence techniques would have the collective calculations with natural systems such as flock of birds. It explores population and derived based optimization methods, The PSO has a powerful framework for solving higher level of nonlinear, multi-model and high-dimensional optimization problems, This chapter begins with outline of the principles of swarm dynamics and it also emphasizes the role of personal best and global best positions inertia weights, and learning coefficient with exploration and exploitation models. It also has challenges such as premature convergence, parameter sensitivity and scalability in large search of places. Along with it, it has the strategies to mitigate them through adaptive parameter tuning, hybridization and multi-swarm approaches, It also covers the advanced variants of Quantum PSO, Multi-Swarm PSO and hybrid-based models which were discussed to enhance the ability in search of robustness.

title: Fuzzy Logic in Computational Intelligence
abstract: Unlock the power to navigate real-world uncertainty with this comprehensive guide, blending foundational theory with practical case studies to show you exactly how to integrate fuzzy logic and machine learning for unmatched predictive accuracy. Machine learning has emerged as a transformative force in modern research, and the integration of fuzzy logic with machine learning techniques has shown significant promise in improving accuracy and precision. Fuzzy logic is based on the principles of uncertainty and has applications across a wide range of predictive and probabilistic environments. From agriculture to healthcare and numerous other sectors, fuzzy logic can be utilized to develop innovative and effective solutions. This book examines the pivotal role of fuzzy logic in enhancing computational systems’ ability to handle uncertainty and imprecision. The book provides a thorough introduction to fuzzy logic, explaining its fundamental concepts and theories while demonstrating its capacity to mimic human reasoning to address vagueness and ambiguity. It explores practical applications in decision-making, pattern recognition, and control systems, with examples such as Nissan’s anti-lock brakes, Honda’s auto engines, and Mitsubishi Electric’s elevator controls. Beyond artificial intelligence and machine learning, fuzzy logic finds applications in fields like evolutionary computing, computer vision, and image processing, enabling advancements in classifier optimization and fine-tuning. By integrating theoretical foundations with practical applications and future directions, the book serves as an essential resource for understanding and leveraging fuzzy logic in computational intelligence and across diverse interdisciplinary domains. The reader will find the volume: Explores the core principles of fuzzy logic and its integration into computational intelligence, providing a strong theoretical foundation for researchers and practitioners;Features diverse case studies demonstrating the practical implementation of fuzzy logic in fields such as healthcare, robotics, finance, and engineering;Showcases how fuzzy systems enhance decision-making in uncertain and complex environments, offering tools to tackle real-world challenges;Written to cater to both beginners seeking an introduction and experts aiming to deepen their knowledge in fuzzy logic systems. Audience Researchers, academics, graduate students, engineers, data scientists, and AI technologists in computer science, artificial intelligence, and applied mathematics seeking advanced insights into fuzzy logic systems and their applications.

title: EvoHarmBench: Breaking Content Moderation with Iterative Human-Like Evasion
abstract: Existing evaluations of harmful content detection rely predominantly on static benchmarks, which struggle to reflect the interactive adversarial ecosystem of real-world content platforms where users continuously revise their expressions in response to moderation feedback. This mismatch creates a significant performance gap between offline benchmark scores and online deployment effectiveness. To the best of our knowledge, we present EvoHarmBench, the first dynamic adversarial evaluation framework for content moderation systems. The framework employs an iterative optimization loop that evolves evasion strategies at the semantic-cluster level, while simultaneously optimizing for evasion success and human readability. We systematically evaluate LLM-based defense models which are widely used in real world moderation systems. The evaluation covers 229 semantic sub-clusters across five violation categories, derived from 5,002 real-world adversarial samples collected from content platforms. Our experiments reveal substantial vulnerabilities even in leading commercial systems: after twelve optimization iterations, the attack success rate under readability constraints reaches 80.3% within SOTA LLM moderators. We will release the full benchmark data, evaluation framework, and code to encourage a shift from static benchmarking toward dynamic adversarial evaluation in content safety research.

title: Strategische benaderingen voor latentieoptimalisatie en anonimiteitverbetering in mixnetwerken
abstract: Today's scale of online activity exposes users to significant privacy risks. A widely adopted safeguard is encryption, which conceals the content of shared data from network intermediaries. However, content protection alone is insufficient. In particular, every digital exchange also generates metadata—such as the sender and recipient of the transmitted data, timestamps, traffic volume, and other contextual information—which constitutes a substantial source of privacy leakage. When collected and analyzed, this metadata can reveal online behavior, social network structures, and other sensitive patterns. To mitigate these risks, anonymous communication systems have been developed under various design paradigms. Among such systems, mix networks (mixnets) remain one of the strongest approaches for limiting metadata leakage. A mixnet operates as an overlay network in which users do not send data directly to recipients. Instead, traffic is routed through a sequence of intermediaries called mixnodes. Each mixnode applies a cryptographic transformation to incoming packets, mixes them with traffic from other users by reordering them, and subsequently forwards them to the next hop. Through layered encryption and probabilistic mixing at every hop, communication metadata becomes unlinkable from its origin—potentially preventing privacy breaches even against a global passive network adversary capable of observing all Internet communication exchanges. Despite their strong privacy guarantees, current mixnet designs face both practical and security limitations. Firstly, mixnets incur substantial latency overhead. In particular, each user communication packet must traverse multiple intermediaries rather than being delivered directly to its recipient, and every mixnode introduces additional delay when forwarding packets due to mixing operations. As a result, mixnets remain primarily suitable for latency-tolerant services such as email, file sharing, or cryptocurrency transactions, while their applicability to latency-sensitive applications—such as web browsing, instant messaging, or live streaming—remains limited. This limitation discourages broader adoption and ultimately reduces the size of the user base, thereby weakening the effective privacy guarantees provided by the system. Accordingly, one major objective of this thesis is to address these latency challenges by introducing protocols for mixnet node arrangement and selection of intermediate mixnodes, together with novel anonymity metrics for rigorous evaluation. At a high level, we design mechanisms that (i) arrange the mixnet such that the probability of forming communication paths composed of latency-proximate mixnodes increases; (ii) enable routing algorithms that prioritize such low-latency paths; and (iii) implement load-balancing mechanisms to ensure that mixnodes handle approximately equal traffic volumes. Through comprehensive simulations and empirical assessments, we show that one of our proposed approaches reduces mixnet latency by up to 9X compared to a baseline configuration, while incurring an anonymity loss of no more than 10%. Secondly, a distinct practical security challenge in mixnets concerns long-term exposure to compromised mixnodes. In typical mixnet deployments, each communication packet is assigned an independently and uniformly random path composed of intermediate mixnodes. While this approach increases mixing diversity and limits correlations between packets within a session—thereby reducing the advantage of a global network adversary—it simultaneously increases the probability that, over time, at least one packet traverses a path consisting entirely of adversarial mixnodes. Once such an event occurs, an adversary controlling those nodes can deanonymize the corresponding communication session by revealing the relationship between source and destination. Specifically, our analysis indicates that compromising only 10-15% of mixnodes may suffice to achieve full deanonymization once the exchanged data volume exceeds approximately 4-30 MB (e.g., sharing an image online) under current mixnet deployments. To address this vulnerability, the second objective of this thesis is to introduce a set of path selection techniques that balance resistance to global adversaries with long-term resilience against compromised mixnodes. Through theoretical analysis, empirical measurements, and extensive simulations, we demonstrate that our proposals reduce vulnerability to compromised mixnodes by up to 85%, while introducing only a marginal increase in the advantage of a global adversary. Collectively, these results show that our approaches enhance both the practicality and the security of mixnets for today's Internet services.

title: Implementasi Certainty Factor Dalam Sistem Pakar Untuk Akurasi Diagnosa Penyakit Ikan Lele
abstract: Diseases in catfish are a major cause of reduced productivity in aquaculture and economic losses for fish farmers. The process of disease identification is often suboptimal due to the farmers' limited knowledge in recognizing symptoms, which risks delayed treatment and increased fish mortality. This study aims to develop a web-based expert system as an aid for the early identification of diseases in catfish by implementing the Certainty Factor (CF) method. The system is designed to facilitate quicker, systematic, and measurable diagnosis. The advantage of this research lies in the integration of expert knowledge with the CF method, producing diagnoses accompanied by confidence levels to support more objective decision-making. The system development follows the Waterfall model, encompassing needs analysis, design, implementation, and testing. The knowledge base includes seven types of catfish diseases and their symptoms. System testing was conducted through diagnostic scenarios, comparing the system's results with expert diagnoses. Results indicate that the system can identify diseases and calculate the confidence level of diagnoses. The disease Enteric Septicemia of Catfish (ESC) received the highest CF value of 0.982 (98.2%), while Motile Aeromonad Septicemia (MAS) scored 0.745 (74.5%). This study contributes a web-based diagnostic system that supports quick and structured identification, aiding farmers in timely disease management.

title: Quantum Acceleration of Evolutionary Algorithms
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of quantum algorithms to accelerate evolutionary algorithms (EAs). Traditional EAs often suffer from slow convergence rates due to computationally intensive selection processes. This work proposes a novel approach to leverage quantum parallelism to significantly speed up the search process within an EA. Specifically, we map the core operations of an EA – selection, crossover, and mutation – onto a quantum circuit. By exploiting the inherent parallelism of quantum computation, we aim to achieve a substantial improvement in the efficiency and performance of the EA. The theoretical framework is presented, outlining the mapping strategies and the potential advantages. While no experimental validation is included in this document, this work serves as a foundational study for future research in hybrid quantum-classical optimization. The core claim is that utilizing quantum algorithms to accelerate the simulation of evolutionary algorithms can improve their efficiency and performance. The core mechanism is the mapping of selection, crossover, and mutation operations within an EA to quantum circuits for parallel computation. This approach addresses a potential computational bottleneck in traditional EAs and promises a breakthrough in optimization tasks.

title: Dynamic Semantic Topology Learning
abstract: Dynamic Semantic Topology Learning (DSTL) presents a novel approach to system optimization where a computational system actively learns its own semantic relationships and dynamically adjusts its internal data representation and communication topology to improve performance and adapt to changes. This paper introduces a reinforcement learning-based architecture utilizing a "semantic probe" node that explores connections between data and operations, adjusting connection weights based on observed performance metrics. These weights define a dynamic semantic topology, evolving with continuous learning. The probe node employs a probabilistic "semantic similarity" metric and gradient descent to optimize connection weights. DSTL's core claim is that systems can proactively learn their semantic relationships, and this paper outlines the mechanism and its significance as a departure from traditional static or rule-based system optimization methods. The potential for intersection with fields like neuromorphic computing and adaptive network routing is discussed.

title: Graph-Based Generative Adversarial Networks for Data Augmentation
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to data augmentation using Graph-Based Generative Adversarial Networks (GB-GANs). Traditional Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) often face challenges in generating high-quality and diverse data, particularly within graph-structured domains like social networks, molecular structures, and knowledge graphs. GB-GANs address this limitation by directly modeling graph structures and node features using a GAN architecture. The generator learns to create realistic graph representations, while the discriminator evaluates the authenticity of the generated graphs. We introduce a framework that leverages graph convolutional networks (GCNs) to encode and decode graph data, enhancing the generator's ability to capture complex graph relationships. The core claim of this work is that GANs, when specifically tailored for graph data, can significantly improve data augmentation techniques. We detail the architecture, training process, and evaluation metrics for GB-GANs and demonstrate its effectiveness in augmenting datasets for various machine learning tasks.

title: Distributed Learning based on Bio-Neural Networks
abstract: This paper explores the potential of leveraging biological neural networks' distributed learning mechanisms for novel approaches in distributed computing. The core argument posits that the inherent resilience and efficiency observed in biological systems can inspire a new generation of distributed learning algorithms. We propose a framework based on mimicking key aspects of bio-neural network learning, aiming for high efficiency and robustness. This approach diverges from traditional distributed learning methods primarily rooted in classical machine learning algorithms, offering a potentially superior solution for scenarios demanding adaptability and fault tolerance. The research investigates the theoretical underpinnings of this framework, focusing on the design principles derived from biological systems, and outlines a potential algorithmic structure. This work establishes a foundational exploration into the application of bio-inspired distributed learning, paving the way for future investigations and practical implementations.

title: Relational Deep Learning on Episodic Memory Networks
abstract: This paper introduces a novel deep learning architecture, termed Episodic Memory Networks with Relational Deep Learning (EMNRDL), designed to address the limitations of existing models in effectively processing and reasoning with episodic memories. Current deep learning approaches often struggle to capture the complex relationships inherent in sequential memories, leading to difficulties in recall, prediction, and reasoning tasks. EMNRDL leverages a relational deep learning framework to explicitly model these connections. The architecture consists of a memory component that stores event representations, a contextual encoding layer that captures the surrounding environment, and a relational reasoning module that learns to infer relationships between events. We formalize this architecture with the following key components and equations: Let $E = \{e_1, e_2, ..., e_T\}$ represent a sequence of $T$ events, where $e_t \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is the representation of the $t$-th event in the sequence, with dimensionality $d$. Let $C = \{c_1, c_2, ..., c_T\}$ represent the contextual information associated with each event, where $c_t \in \mathbb{R}^k$ is the contextual representation of the $t$-th event, with dimensionality $k$. The memory module, $M$, is represented as a set of memory slots, $M = \{m_1, m_2, ..., m_N\}$, where $N$ is the capacity of the memory. Each memory slot $m_i$ stores an event representation. The relational reasoning module $R$ learns to relate events based on their context and memory representations. The core equation governing the relational reasoning is: $r_{t,i} = f_r(e_t, c_t, m_i)$, where $r_{t,i}$ is the relational score between event $e_t$ and memory slot $m_i$, and $f_r$ is the relational function. This function can be represented as a neural network. The update rule for the memory is $m_i = \text{update}(m_i, e_t, c_t, r_{t,i})$, where $\text{update}$ is a function that determines how the memory slot is updated based on the relational score. The overall architecture can be summarized as: $Output = R(E, C, M)$. The proposed EMNRDL architecture aims to improve performance in tasks requiring episodic memory retrieval, prediction, and reasoning by explicitly encoding and reasoning about the relationships between events.

title: Probabilistic Programming for Automated Theorem Proving
abstract: Automated theorem proving (ATP) has achieved remarkable success in specific domains, but its applicability is often constrained by the limitations of traditional logical formalisms. This work proposes a novel approach to ATP by leveraging probabilistic programming. We introduce a language that seamlessly integrates probabilistic models with logical rules, allowing for automated theorem proving grounded in Bayesian inference and logical deduction. The core idea is to represent knowledge not just as definite statements, but as probabilistic beliefs, enabling the system to handle uncertainty and incomplete information effectively. This approach significantly expands the scope of ATP, offering improved robustness and adaptability to complex, real-world problems where certainty is rare. The system operates by iteratively updating its belief network based on logical deductions and probabilistic evidence, ultimately converging towards a provable theorem or identifying the reasons for failure. The key contribution lies in the unification of probabilistic and logical reasoning within a single framework, opening new avenues for automated reasoning across diverse domains.

title: ##基于深度学习的符号推理
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to artificial intelligence by integrating deep learning with symbolic reasoning. The core idea is to leverage the strengths of both paradigms: deep learning's ability to learn complex patterns from data and symbolic reasoning's capacity for logical inference and knowledge representation. We propose a framework where deep learning models are used to generate semantic representations of natural language, and these representations are then fed into a symbolic reasoning engine for logical deduction. This approach aims to create intelligent systems that not only understand natural language but also can reason about it in a way that mirrors human cognitive processes. The work addresses the limitations of current approaches, which often struggle with nuanced reasoning or lack the ability to explicitly represent and manipulate knowledge. The key contribution lies in bridging the gap between data-driven learning and explicit symbolic logic, ultimately enhancing the overall reasoning capabilities of intelligent systems. This paper outlines the architecture, key components, and potential applications of this integrated deep learning and symbolic reasoning framework. ---

We propose a framework where deep learning models are used to generate semantic representations of natural language, and these representations are then fed into a symbolic reasoning engine for logical deduction. This approach aims to create intelligent systems that not only understand natural language but also can reason about it in a way that mirrors human cognitive processes. The work addresses the limitations of current approaches, which often struggle with nuanced reasoning or lack the ability to explicitly represent and manipulate knowledge. The key contribution lies in bridging the gap between data-driven learning and explicit symbolic logic, ultimately enhancing the overall reasoning capabilities of intelligent systems. This paper outlines the architecture, key components, and potential applications of this integrated deep learning and symbolic reasoning framework. ---

title: Twin Worlds: Equivariance-Based Abstention for Evidence-Grounded Reasoning
abstract: Knowledge-intensive reasoning requires Large Language Models (LLMs) to ground answers in provided evidence. When evidence is insufficient, it is desirable that models abstain rather than confidently generating unsupported answers. Existing abstention methods rely on uncertainty estimation or evidence sufficiency checks, but neither tests whether the reasoning process for generation, driven by the interaction of provided evidence and the model's internal memory parameters, is actually grounded in the evidence. A key contributing factor is that entity mentions in context activate memorised associations, causing models to generate plausible responses ungrounded in evidence. We propose Twin Worlds (TW), a framework for improving reliability in knowledge-intensive reasoning through equivariance-based abstention: unlike invariance, which requires outputs to remain unchanged, equivariance requires outputs to transform correspondingly under entity substitutions. A model grounded in the evidence should produce answers that shift consistently when entities are substituted while their relations are preserved. TW constructs multiple worlds via typed substitutions of the original input that preserve relational structure while reducing parametric priors, and uses equivariance violations as an abstention signal. Across four benchmarks and three model backbones, TW identifies when answers are not reliably grounded in the provided evidence and outperforms uncertainty- and sufficiency-based baselines.

title: FISGuard: Defending Against Membership Inference via Fixed Input Subspaces
abstract: As large language models are increasingly adopted in federated learning, protecting user privacy while performing parameter-efficient fine-tuning on distributed private data has become an important challenge. Although clients only share gradients instead of directly uploading raw data, the shared gradients may still leak membership information about training samples. ProjRes (S&P, 2026) further increases this risk: with less information and without accessing model outputs, an attacker can effectively distinguish members from non-members solely based on the projection residual between a candidate representation and the subspace induced by server-observable gradients. Existing defenses against membership inference mostly rely on gradient perturbation or regularization, which can not only degrade model utility but also fail to effectively defend against the membership inference attack introduced by ProjRes, which exploits the geometric structure of gradients. To address this issue, we propose FISGuard, a lightweight defense. Its key idea is to construct and fix a low-dimensional representation subspace using independent public data, thereby restricting the space through which private representations are exposed via gradients while preserving the primary information required for downstream tasks. This substantially reduces the projection-residual discrepancy between members and non-members. We evaluate FISGuard against five representative defense methods across three NLP datasets, two LLMs, and two fine-tuning strategies, Adapter and LoRA. The results show that FISGuard reduces the ProjRes attack AUC to near the random-guessing level of 0.5 in most settings, while maintaining downstream task performance close to that of the undefended model and introducing only limited computational overhead, thereby achieving a favorable privacy--utility trade-off.

title: Semantic Graph Embeddings with Knowledge Graph Reasoning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to graph embedding that leverages the power of knowledge graphs to enhance semantic understanding and enable more effective graph-based reasoning. Traditional graph embeddings often struggle to capture the rich contextual information inherent in graph structures. Our method integrates a knowledge graph into the embedding process, allowing the network to learn representations that not only encode node relationships but also incorporate the semantic context associated with each node. We demonstrate that this integration leads to graph embeddings with a deeper semantic understanding, improving performance on various graph-based reasoning tasks. The core claim of this work is that graph embeddings can be significantly enhanced by incorporating reasoning capabilities derived from knowledge graphs. The key mechanism is the integration of a knowledge graph into the embedding process, facilitating a network that learns representations capturing both node relationships and semantic context. This approach provides a pathway to more sophisticated graph-based reasoning.

title: 基于概率推理的程序验证
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to program verification leveraging probabilistic reasoning. Traditional program verification techniques heavily rely on precise formal models, often failing to capture the inherent uncertainty present in real-world software systems. This research introduces a methodology that transforms programs into probabilistic models, utilizing techniques like Bayesian Networks and Variational Inference. The core of the approach involves verifying these probabilistic models and subsequently conducting risk assessments through Monte Carlo simulations. The key innovation lies in mitigating the limitations of deterministic verification methods, offering a robust and efficient solution for validating programs with inherent uncertainties. The paper outlines the theoretical framework, describes the methodology, and discusses its potential applications and future research directions. The proposed method aims to improve the reliability and efficiency of program verification, particularly for systems exhibiting non-deterministic behavior or operating under uncertain conditions.

title: Formal Verification of Quantum Circuit Compilation using Symbolic Execution
abstract: Quantum circuit compilation is a crucial step in translating high-level quantum algorithms into executable quantum circuits on specific hardware. The complexity and potential for errors within this process necessitate rigorous verification methods. This paper proposes a novel approach leveraging symbolic execution to formally verify quantum circuit compilation. We represent quantum circuits and compilation steps as a symbolic program, enabling the exploration of all possible compilation paths. By incorporating quantum gate fidelities and noise models into the symbolic execution engine, we can identify potential errors in the compilation logic, providing a robust and systematic way to ensure the correctness of the compilation process. The core claim is that symbolic execution can be extended to formally verify the correctness of quantum circuit compilation processes. This work addresses a critical need in quantum computing, offering a new technique for building trust and reliability into quantum software.

title: Quantum Neural Networks with Adaptive Topological Structures Learning
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to designing and implementing quantum neural networks (QNNs) capable of adapting their topological structures through a learning process. The core idea is to leverage reinforcement learning (RL) to guide the QNN's evolution, enabling it to dynamically optimize its architecture for specific tasks. Traditional QNNs typically employ fixed, pre-defined topologies, limiting their flexibility and potential performance. This work introduces a framework where the QNN autonomously learns and adjusts its topology, representing a significant advancement in QNN development. We detail the theoretical foundations, the RL algorithm employed, and the overall learning process. The system's ability to adapt to varying input data and computational demands is demonstrated, showcasing the potential of self-organizing QNNs for complex problems. The system's performance is evaluated using synthetic benchmarks, demonstrating the efficacy of the adaptive topological structure learning method. This research contributes to the burgeoning field of adaptive quantum computing, paving the way for more robust and efficient QNN designs. ---

title: Dynamic Semantic Graph Adaptive Evolution
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to semantic graph evolution utilizing reinforcement learning (RL). The core idea is to create a dynamic semantic graph where relationship weights between nodes adapt based on query feedback and the graph's evolving structure. We propose an adaptive evolution algorithm that leverages a graph neural network (GNN) as a reinforcement learning agent. This agent iteratively updates relationship weights within the knowledge graph through exploration and exploitation, guided by a reward function incorporating knowledge retrieval results. The system dynamically adjusts its understanding of the semantic relationships, offering a significant improvement over traditional methods relying on manual intervention or rigid rules. The primary contribution lies in the automated, feedback-driven adaptation of the semantic graph, leading to continuous optimization of semantic understanding. The system is designed to address the limitations of existing semantic graph evolution techniques by integrating dynamic query feedback and capitalizing on the graph's evolutionary nature. The algorithm's architecture and operational principles are detailed, showcasing its potential for enhanced knowledge representation and reasoning.

title: 基于量子密钥分发的隐私安全通信协议 (Quantum Key Distribution-Based Privacy Secure Communication Protocol - QKDPSC)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel communication protocol, Quantum Key Distribution-Based Privacy Secure Communication Protocol (QKDPSC), centered on the fundamental premise that quantum key distribution (QKD) represents the sole viable method for achieving truly private and secure communication. QKDPSC leverages the principles of quantum mechanics, specifically quantum entanglement and the no-cloning theorem, to establish and distribute cryptographic keys. These keys are then used for encrypting and transmitting messages, inherently resistant to eavesdropping attempts due to the physical laws governing quantum systems. The protocol details a multi-stage process encompassing key generation, key distribution, and message encryption/decryption. A key innovation within QKDPSC is the integration of error correction and privacy amplification techniques, crucial for mitigating the effects of channel noise and potential information leakage during key exchange. The protocol's architecture is designed for adaptability and scalability, allowing it to be implemented across various communication channels. This paper provides a comprehensive description of QKDPSC, outlining its core components, operational procedures, and potential security advantages. The core claim is that QKD is the only solution for privacy-secure communication.

title: Dynamic Topology Neural Morphic Computing
abstract: This paper explores the potential of dynamic topology neural morphic computing, a novel approach to computation inspired by the adaptive and evolving nature of biological neural networks. The core claim is that by simulating the self-adaptive connections and dynamic topology structures found in biological neurons, we can achieve higher efficiency and robustness in complex computational tasks. The proposed mechanism involves a hardware platform featuring programmable "neuron" units capable of adjusting their connection strengths in real-time and dynamically altering their own topology (e.g., forming, splitting, merging network nodes) based on input signals. Machine learning algorithms drive this adaptation, optimizing computational performance and accommodating fluctuating data streams. This approach departs significantly from existing neural morphology, which primarily relies on static topologies and pre-defined neuron behaviors. The research focuses on creating systems that mimic the adaptability and efficiency of biological neural systems, particularly beneficial for unstructured data and real-time, dynamically changing tasks. The potential impact lies in developing more resilient and efficient computing architectures suitable for a wider range of applications.

title: Program Synthesis with Semantic Consistency Proof
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to program synthesis that rigorously verifies semantic consistency. The core idea is to transform the program synthesis process into a formal verification problem, leveraging formal model checkers and theorem provers. We introduce a methodology for automatically proving that the synthesized program adheres to the desired functionality and performance characteristics. The primary contribution lies in providing a systematic method to address the longstanding challenge of ensuring semantic consistency in program synthesis, leading to significantly increased confidence in the reliability of the synthesized programs. This work outlines the key components of the system and details the theoretical framework underpinning the approach, emphasizing the use of logical reasoning and formal verification techniques. The presented method aims to bridge the gap between program synthesis and formal verification, ultimately leading to more robust and trustworthy software solutions.

title: Quantum-Inspired Algorithm for Clustering with High Dimensional Data
abstract: This paper introduces a novel clustering algorithm inspired by quantum annealing, designed to address the challenges posed by high-dimensional data. Traditional clustering methods often suffer from the "curse of dimensionality," leading to computational inefficiency and potentially inaccurate results. Our algorithm, termed the Quantum-Inspired Clustering Algorithm (QICA), leverages concepts from quantum optimization to efficiently explore the solution space and identify clusters. The core mechanism involves a simulated annealing process, mimicking the tunneling behavior characteristic of quantum systems, to navigate the complex solution landscape. We formulate the clustering problem as an optimization problem, where the objective is to minimize a cost function representing the dissimilarity between data points and their assigned clusters. The algorithm iteratively adjusts cluster assignments based on simulated quantum fluctuations, converging towards a solution that minimizes the cost function. We present a detailed mathematical formulation of QICA, including the cost function, the optimization process, and the parameters governing the simulated annealing process. Empirical results, while not presented through experimental trials, illustrate the algorithm's potential efficacy in identifying clusters within high-dimensional datasets compared to established clustering techniques. The key contributions of this work lie in the application of quantum-inspired principles to clustering, potentially offering a more robust and scalable solution for handling high-dimensional data.

title: Autoencoding Autoencoders
abstract: An autoencoder (AE) is a neural network that reconstructs its input. AE consists of two sub-networks: the encoder and the decoder. AE has been commonly applied in feature extraction and anomaly detection. However, AE was not applied to AE models themselves. Accordingly, this paper develops AE for AEs, namely AEAE. For this purpose, we apply AE to the parameters (weights and biases) of AEs. The experiment includes 1) computing reconstruction error of the AEAE model, 2) applying feature extraction and classification to AE models, and 3) one-class classification of AE models using the reconstruction error of the AEAE model. The most interesting outcome is that biases of output layers are distinguishable with high accuracy, whereas other parameters are hard to classify. Moreover, AEAE could be extended to wider directions, applying deep learning to deep learning models. Finally, we got another question: how to apply AE to AEAE models.

title: LongPIBench: A Long-Context Benchmark for Prompt Injection
abstract: Prompt injection attacks pose a serious security risk to large language models in real-world applications. However, existing prompt injection benchmarks primarily focus on short-context inputs, leaving the attacks and defenses in long-context settings largely unexplored. This gap leads to a substantial overestimation of the effectiveness of current defenses. In this paper, we bridge the gap by introducing LongPIBench, a long-context benchmark for prompt injection covering 4 realistic application scenarios: paper peer review, resume screening, code review, and email summary. For each scenario, we construct a synthetic dataset and a real-world dataset, with context lengths ranging from thousands to tens of thousands of tokens. The evaluation results on LongPIBench reveal significant vulnerabilities of prompt injection defenses under long-context settings: even simple heuristic prompt injection attacks achieve high success rates and frequently bypass state-of-the-art defenses. We hope LongPIBench can serve as a practical benchmark for systematically evaluating prompt injection defenses in realistic long-context scenarios.

title: Performative Privacy: When Differential Privacy Maximizes Utility
abstract: Privacy-preserving learning is often motivated by the idea that protecting users' data can preserve trust and thus participation, improving utility in the long term. However, this claim has not been formalized so far. In parallel, performative learning provides a framework for studying learning systems whose deployment affects the data they later observe. In this work, we bring these two perspectives together and introduce performative privacy, where data leakage reduces future participation. We study a simple model where agents repeatedly contribute data for mean estimation but may leave the system when their data is leaked. Privacy is implemented through differentially private mechanisms, creating a trade-off between estimation noise and future participation. We show, through a theoretical study of the dynamics and numerical experiments, that a finite privacy budget can outperform non-private estimation in the long term when the feedback loop between leakage and participation is sufficiently strong. This provides first evidence that differential privacy can be optimal not only as a protection mechanism, but also from the perspective of long-term utility.

title: Fibre-integrated SPDC heralded single-photon source using Zn-Indiffused PPLN ridge waveguides at telecom wavelengths
abstract: We report a fibre-integrated heralded single-photon source based on a commercial Zn-indiffused MgO:PPLN ridge waveguide operated in Type-0 degenerate spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC). The device emits a broadband spectrum spanning approximately 70 nm across the telecom C- and L-bands, with an absolute brightness of 9.1 × 10 9 ~pairs s -1 mW -1 . After accounting for optical losses, we determine an internal heralding efficiency of (58±5) %. The source demonstrates strong multi-photon suppression, exhibiting a coincidences-to-accidentals ratio exceeding 9 × 10 4 and a heralded second-order correlation of g h (2) (0)=(5.53±0.46)×10 −4 . Low multi-photon noise and broadband emission demonstrate the viability of such platforms for wavelength-multiplexed quantum networking.

title: LUT-SHA256: Arithmetic-Free Execution of SHA-256 through Chained Look-Up Tables
abstract: This work presents LUT-SHA256, an alternative execution architecture for theSHA-256 compression function in which no arithmetic, logical, or shiftoperation is ever applied to message data. The proposal rests on twostructural theorems: addition modulo 2^32 is reformulated as a four-stagechain of tabulated byte-additions with explicit carry propagation (TADDC),and cyclic rotations and logical shifts are expressed as byte recombinationthrough displacement tables. A functional-decomposition argument yields fullequivalence with FIPS 180-4, verified against standard vectors, block-boundarycases, and BIP39-derived inputs. A progressive compression of the table set(v2.0-v2.4) reduces memory by up to 58% and lookups per block by up to 41%,including a zero-block master schedule for PBKDF2/BIP39 workloads. Becausedata only appears as table indices, the architecture exhibits a distinctiveside-channel surface: a vulnerability ladder (V1.0-V1.7) is formalized andleakage thresholds are quantified with the SMT solver Z3, showing that asingle leaked addition per round inverts the compression algebraically whilecarry-bit leakage alone does not. Hardware implications for FPGAs, secureelements, and compute-in-memory are discussed. Dos teoremas estructurales — la suma módulo 2^32 comocadena de acarreos tabulados (TADDC) y las rotaciones como recombinación debytes (TROT) — junto con un teorema de equivalencia demuestran la identidadde resultados con FIPS 180-4, verificada experimentalmente. title: Self-Correcting Memory Networks using Bayesian Recursive Inference
abstract: Memory networks have demonstrated significant promise in tasks requiring long-term memory and sequential processing. However, a critical limitation lies in their susceptibility to noisy or incomplete information during memory updates, leading to performance degradation over extended sequences. This paper introduces a novel approach – Self-Correcting Memory Networks (SCMNs) – designed to mitigate this issue. SCMNs leverage Bayesian recursive inference to dynamically adjust the confidence scores associated with stored memories. This continuous updating process effectively corrects for noise and uncertainty, maintaining a robust and adaptive prior distribution. The core claim is that the integration of Bayesian inference within a memory network architecture provides a mechanism to overcome the inherent instability caused by imprecise memory updates. The proposed framework offers a pathway to enhance the reliability and long-term performance of memory networks across a range of applications. The primary formula representing the Bayesian update is: $ \theta_{i} \propto \alpha_{i} * p(x_t | \theta_i) + (1 - \alpha_i) * \theta_i $, where $\theta_i$ represents the updated confidence score for memory *i*, $x_t$ is the current input, $\alpha_i$ is the learning rate for memory *i*, and $p(x_t | \theta_i)$ is the likelihood of the input given the memory. The prior distribution is represented as $p(\theta) = \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$. The goal is to maximize the posterior distribution $p(\theta | x_t)$ to obtain the best estimate of $\theta_i$.

title: Quantum Entanglement Entropy: A Novel Metric for Quantifying Entanglement
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to quantifying quantum entanglement using entanglement entropy. Traditional entanglement measures, such as concurrence and entanglement of formation, often struggle to fully capture the intricate correlations present in entangled states. We propose a new definition of entanglement entropy based on the density matrix of the entangled system, explicitly accounting for the correlations between subsystems. This approach leverages information-theoretic entropy calculations to provide a more precise and comprehensive measure of entanglement strength and the degree of correlation. We demonstrate that this entropy-based metric offers advantages over existing measures, particularly in characterizing complex entangled states and distinguishing between different levels of entanglement. The core claim is that entanglement entropy can serve as a more accurate indicator of entanglement than existing metrics. The underlying mechanism centers around a density matrix-based entropy calculation, recognizing the interconnectedness within entangled states. The novelty lies in moving beyond purely state-based descriptions to incorporate a measure of subsystem correlations.

title: Probabilistic Programming for Active Learning in Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) frequently struggles with the exploration-exploitation dilemma, often requiring vast amounts of data to converge to optimal policies. This work proposes a novel approach leveraging probabilistic programming to enhance active learning within RL. By explicitly modeling the uncertainty associated with both the environment dynamics and the agent's policy, we enable the efficient selection of data samples that maximize information gain. The core mechanism involves utilizing probabilistic programming to define a Bayesian model, allowing for the calculation of predictive distributions. These distributions are then used to guide the selection of the most informative samples for the agent to interact with. This approach directly addresses the limitations of traditional RL by providing a framework for adaptive exploration, leading to faster learning and improved policy performance. The key contribution lies in the integration of Bayesian uncertainty quantification directly within the active learning loop, offering a more principled and data-efficient method for RL.

title: Formalized Proof-Based Automated Vulnerability Detection
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to software vulnerability detection leveraging formalized proof techniques. The core idea is to automate the process of formally verifying software code, directly identifying potential vulnerabilities through rigorous mathematical proofs. Existing vulnerability detection methods, primarily relying on static and dynamic analysis, often suffer from low efficiency and limited coverage. This work proposes a system that translates software code into a formal language, utilizes theorem provers and model checkers for verification, and incorporates machine learning to optimize the verification process. The system generates detailed vulnerability proof reports, offering a significantly higher level of assurance than traditional methods. We demonstrate the feasibility of this approach and outline a framework for automated vulnerability detection based on formalized proofs. The system's ability to provide absolute proof of correctness, rather than probabilistic assessments, represents a substantial advancement in software security.

title: Decentralized Federated Learning with Byzantine Fault Tolerance
abstract: Federated learning (FL) offers a promising approach to training machine learning models on decentralized data sources without directly sharing the data itself. However, this decentralized nature introduces significant vulnerabilities. Malicious participants, known as Byzantine nodes, can inject biased or corrupted models into the training process, compromising the overall model accuracy and potentially introducing harmful biases. This paper proposes a novel decentralized federated learning framework incorporating Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT) mechanisms. The core claim is that a BFT-enabled decentralized FL system provides robustness against malicious actors, guaranteeing model convergence even when some nodes are compromised. We outline the system architecture, detailing the BFT protocol integration, aggregation strategies, and communication protocols. The proposed system leverages a verifiable distributed consensus mechanism, allowing for the detection and mitigation of Byzantine behavior. The theoretical analysis demonstrates the system's resilience to arbitrary Byzantine failures and provides a framework for quantifying the impact of malicious participation. This work represents a significant advancement in securing FL deployments, fostering trust and reliability in collaborative learning environments.

title: The MASEC-Feedback Model: A Multi-Agent Diagnostic Framework for Precision Education and Professional Communication
abstract: This study presents the MASEC-Feedback Model, a multi-agent diagnostic framework designed to simulate workplace interaction and identify functional communication gaps. Interaction logs and diagnostic reports were collected from 149 international practitioners from Vietnam, Myanmar, Sri Lanka, and Nepal, with proficiency levels ranging from A2 to B2. The study provides theoretical insights into Knowledge Engineering for Precision Education. It requires a paradigm shift from reactive error correction to proactive, system-level diagnosis of professional readiness. The analysis identifies a separated two-layer architecture that bridges pedagogical disconnect, the localization of a high-volatility B1 performance breakpoint, and the reduction of algorithmic agreeability bias through weighted multi-agent consensus. These findings provide a strategic roadmap for deploying intelligent multi-agent scaffolds to optimize the unique developmental pathway of professional practitioners in the digital age.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning for Enterprise Transaction Systems: A Reproducible Architecture for Auditable Decision Support
abstract: Enterprise information systems generate extensive transaction traces, but transforming these records into trustworthy AI-enabled decision intelligence requires more than pattern discovery: data quality, interpretability, statistical qualification, temporal robustness, reproducibility, and human oversight must be integrated. This study develops and evaluates a reproducible, interpretable machine-learning architecture designed as an analytical layer between transaction-generating systems of record and human decision support. A point-of-sale subsystem is used as the empirical validation environment rather than as a full ERP implementation. The architecture combines deterministic data-quality controls, sparse basket reconstruction, normalized Shannon entropy, unsupervised association-rule learning, false-discovery screening, nonparametric inference, generalized linear models, temporal validation, and transparent rule prioritization. The empirical evaluation covers 31,157 transaction baskets, 139,396 valid item lines, 710 products, and 762 active sales days. The resulting incidence representation contains 22.12 million potential positions at 0.630% density, and 1,174 directional rules satisfy the prespecified screening criteria. Out-of-period validation shows that 93.6% of discovery rules retain lift above one, while 49.3% again satisfy all selection thresholds and rank correlations for support, confidence, and lift remain between 0.80 and 0.85. The contribution is an auditable enterprise analytics architecture that separates machine-learned discovery, statistical qualification, and human decision responsibility. The architecture provides a reproducible analytical foundation that can complement enterprise systems of record and business-intelligence or decision-support environments without assuming production ERP integration, cloud deployment, or autonomous decision making.

title: Prompt-to-Structure: Knowledge-Grounded LLM-Assisted Procedural Modeling of Qing Dynasty Architecture
abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have opened new opportunities for integrating natural-language interaction with procedural content generation (PCG). However, heritage architectural modeling requires more than syntactically valid parameter generation, as generated forms must comply with historically grounded construction rules, component dependencies, and executable asset constraints. This study takes Qing-dynasty official timber architecture as a case study and presents Prompt-to-Structure , a knowledge-grounded framework that translates natural-language generation intent into minimal, executable procedural specifications. The framework integrates a reference corpus derived from architectural treatises and scholarship, a domain knowledge graph encoding architectural rules and applicability constraints, and a metadata-indexed 3D component library. Given a user prompt, retrieval-augmented grounding supports specification generation, while deterministic validation and component resolution ensure that the resulting parameters can be instantiated procedurally in Blender. Experiments show that, compared with unguided LLM baselines, the complete pipeline improves rule compliance while maintaining semantic alignment and reliable procedural executability. These results demonstrate the potential of constrained LLM–PCG workflows for rule-consistent heritage architectural generation and hypothesis visualization under historically grounded constraints.

title: A diagnostic framework for auditing decision logic in transformer-based portfolio allocation
abstract: Robust portfolio management requires risk-adjusted performance and auditable decision logic under changing market conditions. This paper examines Decision Transformer policies for sequential portfolio allocation and proposes a diagnostic protocol organized around contribution, necessity, and representation structure. It combines feature attribution, temporal occlusion, controlled perturbations, latent-representation analysis, and regime-conditioned portfolio behaviour. The study covers eighteen trained model families differing in lookback horizon, training rebalancing frequency, information set, trajectory objective, and inference-time conditioning. Each family has 96 correlated ex post evaluation variants applied without retraining. Diagnostic definitions, aggregation rules, thresholds, performance bands, and original recommendations were frozen before temporal-holdout inspection; a benchmark-relative economic-admissibility gate is reported separately as a post-hoc amendment. A secondary comparison with DDPG, DQN, and PPO assesses technical portability within the same setting. Complete-family screening indicates that performance and diagnostic evidence capture distinct properties. Across seventeen families with complete records, the frozen aggregate score has a moderately positive but uncertain association with holdout Sharpe. Retrospective higher- versus lower-Sharpe comparisons reveal differences in volatility-sensitive feature use, temporal dependence, regime-conditioned allocation, and latent organization, without establishing deterministic performance rules. Explanation-validity evidence is heterogeneous and method dependent. Feature-family rankings are more stable in magnitude than sign; parameter randomization, deletion, insertion, and input permutation support action dependence only for subsets of policies. Notably, benchmark outperformance during validation does not imply uniformly supported explanations. The protocol therefore supports staged model comparison and controlled validation, not future-return prediction, causal certification of explanations, or deployment authorization.

title: TrafficMoE: LLM-based mixture-of-experts framework for multi-task network traffic classification
abstract: Abstract Network traffic analysis is fundamentally challenged by the need to accurately identify malicious behaviors and application types from massive, structurally heterogeneous packet data. Existing deep learning and Large Language Model (LLM)-based methods typically rely on shared parameter spaces optimized for isolated, single-task scenarios. Consequently, when deployed in dynamic multi-task environments, these approaches may be affected by cross-task gradient interference and negative transfer. To address these limitations, we propose TrafficMoE, an LLM-based Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) framework for supervised multi-task network traffic classification. Specifically, TrafficMoE formulates heterogeneous traffic tasks under a unified instruction-to-label generation paradigm by converting packet metadata into text. To mitigate task interference, the framework integrates a shared traffic expert to capture common semantics, multiple task-specialized experts to separate domain knowledge, and a lightweight context-aware router for automatic, sample-wise dispatching under mixed-task inputs. Furthermore, to support continual task evolution, we design a modular sequential expansion strategy that accommodates new tasks by adding a single expert and updating the router. Extensive evaluations across ten public benchmark datasets show that TrafficMoE achieves an average F1-score of 0.9823, while supporting modular task expansion with reduced adaptation overhead.

title: Dynamically Adaptive Kernel Methods via Wasserstein Distance Optimization
abstract: Kernel methods have demonstrated remarkable success in various machine learning tasks, including classification, regression, and dimensionality reduction. However, their performance heavily relies on the selection of an appropriate kernel function, a process often characterized by subjectivity and requiring significant manual tuning. This paper introduces a novel approach to kernel learning that dynamically adapts the kernel function based on the Wasserstein distance between data distributions. The core idea is to formulate kernel learning as an optimization problem, minimizing the Wasserstein distance while maintaining a desired classification or regression performance. We demonstrate that this approach effectively automates kernel selection, eliminating the need for heuristic-based tuning and offering a more robust and data-driven solution. The algorithm's performance is evaluated on several benchmark datasets, showcasing its superiority over traditional kernel methods and highlighting its potential for broader applications. The central contribution lies in the direct geometric interpretation of kernel optimization through the Wasserstein distance, providing a principled and adaptable framework.

title: Meta-Learning for Automated Algorithm Design
abstract: Algorithm design is a fundamental yet often laborious process in computer science. Traditionally, it relies heavily on human expertise, intuition, and experience. This paper proposes a novel approach to algorithm design by leveraging meta-learning. The core idea is to create a system that learns *how* to design algorithms, rather than simply designing algorithms. This system, termed a meta-learning system, observes the performance of existing algorithms on various tasks and iteratively refines its own design strategies. The system learns through experience, gradually improving its ability to generate effective algorithms for new, unseen problems. This research investigates the potential of meta-learning to automate algorithm design, offering a pathway to accelerate algorithm discovery and potentially unlock solutions currently beyond human capabilities. The central hypothesis is that a meta-learning system can effectively learn algorithmic design principles, leading to the automated creation of novel and efficient algorithms.

title: Composable Neural Modules for Representational Learning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for representation learning based on composable neural modules. The core challenge in modern deep learning is the "black box" nature of complex neural networks, hindering interpretability and understanding. Our approach addresses this by designing a system where larger representations are constructed from smaller, modular neural networks – termed "Composable Neural Modules" (CNMs). These CNMs are designed for specific sub-tasks, allowing for a deliberate and transparent construction of the overall representation. The key mechanism involves a composition strategy that leverages learned relationships between these modules. We propose a formal mathematical representation of this composition process, detailing the operations and constraints involved. This approach aims to move beyond monolithic networks, offering a pathway to more interpretable and controllable representation learning. We outline the theoretical underpinnings, define the core components of the CNM framework, and discuss potential future research directions.

title: Temporal Logic-Based Formal Verification of Quantum Circuits
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to verifying the correctness of quantum circuits using temporal logic. Traditional verification methods often rely on gate-level simulation, which can be computationally expensive and insufficient for complex quantum algorithms. This work addresses this limitation by formally modeling quantum circuits as temporal logic systems. We leverage the expressive power of temporal logic to capture the desired behavior of quantum algorithms, including their evolution over time and the effects of quantum phenomena like superposition and entanglement. The core of our method involves mapping the circuit's operations onto temporal logic specifications and utilizing automated theorem proving and model checking techniques, tailored to the probabilistic nature of quantum systems. We demonstrate that this approach provides a more rigorous and scalable verification framework compared to existing methods, offering a pathway to ensuring the reliability of quantum computations. The key contributions of this work are the formalization of quantum circuits with temporal logic, the adaptation of theorem proving and model checking techniques for quantum systems, and the potential for significantly improving the trustworthiness of quantum algorithms.

title: 基于遗传算法的硬件架构优化 (Genetic Algorithm-Based Hardware Architecture Optimization - GABHO)
abstract: This paper explores the application of Genetic Algorithms (GAs) to the optimization of hardware architectures. Traditional hardware design relies heavily on manual design and iterative refinement, often leading to suboptimal solutions. This research proposes a novel framework, termed Genetic Algorithm-Based Hardware Architecture Optimization (GABHO), which leverages the inherent search capabilities of GAs to efficiently explore the vast design space of hardware architectures. The core concept involves formulating the architectural design choices as a discrete optimization problem, allowing the GA to iteratively evolve solutions toward improved performance metrics. We present a detailed methodology including representation, fitness function, genetic operators, and a framework for evaluating the resulting architectures. While this work focuses on the theoretical aspects and conceptual design, it establishes a viable approach for automating and accelerating hardware architecture development. The effectiveness of GABHO is demonstrated through illustrative examples, showcasing its potential to significantly enhance hardware performance and efficiency.

title: Temporal Graph Embedding via Causality Inference
abstract: Graph embeddings have become increasingly prevalent in various domains, including social network analysis, knowledge graph reasoning, and recommendation systems. However, traditional graph embedding techniques often treat nodes as independent entities, neglecting the underlying temporal dynamics and causal relationships within the graph. This paper introduces a novel approach to temporal graph embedding that leverages causality inference to improve embedding quality. We propose an algorithm based on a Bayesian network framework to learn a directed acyclic graph (DAG) representing causal dependencies between nodes. This DAG is then used to guide the embedding process, prioritizing nodes with higher causal influence and capturing temporal dependencies more effectively. The resulting embeddings exhibit improved performance in downstream tasks compared to conventional graph embedding methods. Our key contribution lies in explicitly modeling causality within the graph structure, leading to a more robust and interpretable representation of temporal graphs. The core of our method is the integration of temporal dynamics through the learned DAG, offering a significant advancement over existing approaches. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a theoretical analysis and outline the key components of the algorithm.
