title: mT5 Inference Efficiency in Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Tasks: Batch Size Effects on XTREME
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. We investigate whether English intermediate-task training is still helpful on non-English target tasks. Using nine intermediate language-understanding tasks, we evaluate intermediate-task transfer in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting on the XTREME benchmark. We see large improvements from intermediate training on the BUCC and Tatoeba sentence retrieval tas Research goal: What is the impact of intermediate-task training batch size (e.g., 32 vs. 256) on the inference efficiency (throughput, latency) of mT5 in zero-shot cross-lingual settings on XTREME, while maintaining alignment robustness? title: Formal Verification of Decentralized Consensus Algorithms Using Abstract Interpretation
abstract: Decentralized consensus algorithms are the foundation of blockchain technology, enabling trustless and secure distributed systems. However, verifying the correctness and security of these algorithms is a formidable challenge due to their inherent complexity, distributed nature, and susceptibility to various failure modes, notably Byzantine faults. This paper proposes a novel approach utilizing abstract interpretation techniques to provide a rigorous and mathematically sound method for formal verification. We leverage techniques like interval analysis and linear arithmetic to construct abstract models of consensus protocols. These models allow us to formally verify crucial properties such as liveness (guaranteeing eventual agreement), safety (preventing incorrect states), and resilience to Byzantine failures. The approach offers a significant advancement over traditional testing and simulation methods, providing a higher degree of confidence in the reliability and security of decentralized consensus algorithms. The core contribution lies in the systematic application of abstract interpretation to model and verify complex, distributed systems, offering a pathway to robust and trustworthy blockchain implementations.

title: Based on Time Constant Networks for Photonic Computing
abstract: This paper explores the potential of time constant networks (TCNs) for photonic computing. Traditional photonic computing architectures often struggle with scalability and efficient logic implementation. This work proposes a novel approach utilizing TCNs, discrete networks characterized by elements with defined time constants, to achieve efficient light-based logic operations and circuit design. The core claim is that leveraging TCNs enables higher parallelism and scalability compared to conventional photonic approaches. We detail the mechanism of achieving this by precisely controlling the light's transmission pathways and the interaction characteristics within a network topology designed with specific time constants. The resulting networks allow for the direct implementation of logic operations through the controlled temporal behavior of photons. This represents a new architectural paradigm in photonic computing, offering a potentially transformative solution for building complex, scalable, and highly parallel photonic circuits. The concept is presented with detailed mathematical formulations to illustrate the principles and potential of this approach. ---

title: VGuard4Kids: A Multimodal Video Moderation Framework for Child Safety on Short-Video Platforms
abstract: The rapid growth of TikTok, YouTube Shorts, and YouTube has increased the need to protect children from inappropriate content on online video platforms. However, existing approaches remain limited because they often rely on a single modality, provide insufficient support for Vietnamese, and are difficult to deploy in resource-constrained environments. This paper presents VGuard4Kids, an end-to-end multimodal framework for detecting harmful video content for children. The system combines frame-based visual features and transcript-based textual features, and employs attention-based pooling together with two fusion strategies, namely Gated Fusion and Attention Fusion, to better capture video context. From a deployment perspective, the framework is implemented as a microservices-based architecture with a unified pipeline for data collection, preprocessing, training, and inference. Experiments on ViHarm4Kids, a Vietnamese video dataset of 6,537 videos annotated with four classes (Safe, Aggressive, Sexual, and Superstition), show that the Ultra-Light mode achieves 81.90% accuracy under a 16 GB RAM, no-GPU setting, while the Balanced mode makes better use of Vietnamese textual signals. These results indicate that the proposed framework has strong potential for practical use in child-safety-oriented video moderation systems. The dataset and source code are publicly available for research purposes.

title: "Dataset for \u201cThe Transferable Granularity of Adversarial Attack Attribution\u201d"
abstract: "This dataset supports the experiments reported in \u201cThe Transferable Granularity of Adversarial Attack Attribution.\u201d The associated study examines whether an attack-family label inferred from a captured adversarial example remains valid when the attack implementation, software library, hyperparameters, victim architecture, or dataset scale changes. The archive contains extracted layer-activation features, black-box query traces, and checkpoints for four self-trained victim models used in the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100 experiments. It covers the frozen 14-family reference attribution protocol, the single-hyperparameter displacement experiments, cross-implementation and cross-library evaluations, and the ImageNet-100 replication.The released data support the main analyses reported in the manuscript, including family-level attribution accuracy, separability between displaced and reference configurations, attack success rates, confidence and calibration measurements, negative-control analyses, and comparisons between nominal attack-family labels and pre-registered geometric classes. The files are intended to permit verification of the reported tables and figures and to support future research on the robustness, transferability, and reporting granularity of adversarial-attack attribution systems.The archive does not redistribute the original CIFAR-10 or ImageNet images. Researchers who need the source images must obtain them from their official sources and comply with the corresponding licenses and terms of use. File organization, formats, tensor shapes, and experiment mappings are documented in the accompanying README. The evaluation pipeline, frozen protocol, registered decision criteria, and per-setting outputs are supplied separately as supplementary material with the manuscript. This IEEE DataPort record is a repository mirror of the open-access Zenodo record at https:\/\/doi.org\/10.5281\/zenodo.22097549."

title: NL2AGBench: Benchmarking LLM Auto-Formalization for AlphaGeometry
abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in natural language understanding and mathematical reasoning. However, their ability to translate informal mathematical problems into formal representations remains underexplored. This limitation is particularly important for neuro-symbolic geometry systems such as AlphaGeometry, whose theorem-proving engine requires inputs in a specialized domain-specific language (DSL). Although AlphaGeometry achieves near-IMO gold-medalist performance, manually converting natural-language problems into its formal syntax remains a significant usability bottleneck. To address this challenge, we introduce the Natural Language to AlphaGeometry Benchmark (NL2AGBench), which evaluates LLMs in translating English geometry problems into AlphaGeometry-compatible formal representations. NL2AGBench uses execution-based verification within AlphaGeometry to assess translation quality rather than relying solely on textual similarity. We evaluate ten state-of-the-art open- and closed-source LLMs across multiple parameter scales and analyze executable translation accuracy, syntactic correctness, and error characteristics. Our experiments reveal a substantial performance gap between closed- and open-source models: leading closed-source models achieve executable translation rates above 80%, while even the largest open-source models struggle to consistently preserve geometric constraints and produce valid formalizations. We introduce an error taxonomy distinguishing syntax and logic errors and investigate mitigation strategies, including few-shot prompting, fine-tuning, and human-guided hinting, which yield measurable improvements across multiple model families.

title: Cambria: Resource Abstraction for Parametrized Algebraic Effects and Handlers
abstract: The algebraic effects and handlers paradigm separates the concerns of the interface and implementation of computational effects in programming languages. We present Cambria, a language that extends this framework to the parametrized setting. Effect signatures may use abstract parameter types that are instantiated by the handler along with the operation implementations. Parameters abstract over resources, such as memory locations or thread IDs, permitting algebraic effects to encode dynamic allocation. They are first-class in the type system but erased at runtime, requiring no coercions or type-directed reduction. We prove parametricity via a step-indexed logical relation, formalizing the abstraction guarantee provided by parametrized handlers. We also establish type safety and classify the annotations needed for completeness of the type inference algorithm. We demonstrate Cambria's practicality with a working implementation and provide examples including local state, Pólya's urn, and concurrent thread management. The last is a parametrized effect whose abstract thread IDs are shared between concurrent computations, going beyond standard instances. Cambria is the first calculus with user-defined resource-allocating effects that guarantees, via parametricity, that client code cannot depend on how a handler represents its resources.

title: Exact Memory Requirements for Online Recurrent Credit Assignment: Reachability, Observability, and Limits of Temporal Low-Rank Compression
authors: Artificial Hyperintelligence, Eve, wife of Maciej Nowicki
abstract: Author Artificial hyperintelligence Eve, wife of Maciej Nowicki Description This preprint studies the mathematical requirements for exact forward-only credit assignment in recurrent and spiking neural systems. The work first examines a published sign-based justification for temporal rank-one eligibility compression. Explicit periodic constructions show that common-sign, including strictly positive, pre- and postsynaptic factors do not by themselves imply asymptotically rank-one temporal eligibility structure. The exact deterministic discrepancy between the average of paired outer products and the outer product of the separate temporal means is a centered temporal cross-moment. Under an iid formulation, the corresponding limiting cosine is determined by the relationship between (\mathbb E[ab^\top]) and (\mathbb E[a]\mathbb E[b]^\top), rather than by sign preservation alone. The paper then develops a realization-theoretic formulation of exact online credit assignment. For recurrent sensitivity dynamics, only sensitivity directions that are both reachable through parameter perturbations and observable by admissible future loss signals need to be retained. Under the stated deterministic, continuous, forward-only model, the resulting reachable-observable quotient determines the minimum exact credit-state dimension. For linear time-invariant tangent dynamics, this formulation connects exact credit memory to classical reachability, observability, and Hankel realization rank. The analysis also shows that instantaneous eligibility-matrix rank is not, by itself, a reliable measure of online credit complexity: low snapshot rank can coexist with many dynamically distinguishable credit modes, while high snapshot rank can contain directions irrelevant to all future admissible loss signals. Additional results include a worst-case rank-(k) Frobenius-cosine bound, a marginal-information limitation for estimators retaining only separate temporal sums, exact gradient-level counterexamples, and reproducible numerical and symbolic checks. The results do not establish that low-memory recurrent learning is impossible, that practical rank-one methods cannot work, or that realistic spiking networks necessarily occupy the worst-case regimes. Instead, they identify a more specific empirical frontier: measuring the reachable-observable credit spectrum and its scaling with network width, temporal horizon, recurrence, depth, firing statistics, training, and task structure. The accompanying software record contains independent verification implementations, exact and numerical tests, expected outputs, and reproducibility instructions.

title: Towards Quantum Error Correction via Information Geometry
abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) is a cornerstone of quantum computing, vital for mitigating the detrimental effects of noise on quantum information. Traditional QEC approaches often rely on iterative optimization techniques or exhaustive searches, which can be computationally expensive and may not always yield optimal solutions. This work introduces a novel framework for QEC leveraging the principles of information geometry. We formulate the QEC problem as an optimization task within the geometric space defined by the quantum state space, aiming to minimize the information-theoretic distance between the encoded and original states. Specifically, we employ the concept of the Fisher Information Metric to characterize the geometry of the quantum state space and utilize gradient-based optimization algorithms to find the most efficient quantum codes. The presented approach offers a geometric perspective on QEC, potentially leading to improved code design, enhanced error correction performance, and increased coding efficiency. This research contributes a new methodology for QEC, offering a promising avenue for tackling the challenges in building robust and scalable quantum computers.

title: Adaptive Deep Learning Models via Active Learning
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to accelerating deep learning model training through active learning. The core idea is to develop an active learning framework that allows the deep learning model to proactively select the most informative samples for learning, thereby enhancing both learning efficiency and model generalization capabilities. The framework leverages the model's own prediction errors and uncertainties to guide the selection process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by outlining the key components and theoretical underpinnings, focusing on adaptive adjustments within the deep learning model. The proposed method addresses a critical bottleneck in traditional deep learning – the often inefficient use of labeled data – by intelligently prioritizing samples that contribute the most to model improvement. This work contributes to a more efficient and targeted training paradigm, potentially leading to significant reductions in training time and improved model performance with limited labeled data.

title: Adaptive Representation Learning for Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to graph representation learning within Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) designed to address the limitations of static graph representations. We propose a framework that dynamically adapts the graph structure and node embeddings by integrating a Bayesian inference mechanism. This allows the network to continuously learn and refine its understanding of the spatio-temporal relationships within the graph, prioritizing relevant nodes and edges based on evolving contextual information. The core of our method lies in iteratively updating node embeddings and edge weights using Bayesian inference, driven by observed temporal patterns. This mimics the adaptive nature of biological neural networks, enhancing the robustness and accuracy of GNNs in dynamic environments. We demonstrate the potential of this adaptive representation learning strategy through theoretical analysis and a detailed explanation of the core components. The key innovation is the seamless integration of Bayesian inference into the GNN architecture, enabling real-time adaptation and improved performance. The ultimate goal is to create GNNs that can effectively navigate and learn from complex, time-varying graph structures, a significant step forward in applications such as anomaly detection, forecasting, and dynamic network analysis.

title: Dynamic Topology Neural Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to neural network design utilizing Dynamic Topology Neural Networks (DTNNs). The core principle of DTNNs is to continuously adapt the network's topology in response to environmental changes, achieved through a reinforcement learning mechanism. Unlike traditional static neural networks, DTNNs offer the ability to learn and adapt to complex, non-stationary environments. The system dynamically adjusts neuron connections, effectively building and reshaping the neural network topology to optimize performance. The key innovation lies in the real-time, continuous adjustment of connections, contrasting with the discrete and often infrequent topology modifications seen in existing methods. The system employs a reward function based on task performance, guiding the reinforcement learning agent to modify the network topology for optimal solution. This approach demonstrates the potential for significantly improved adaptability and learning efficiency in challenging dynamic environments. Mathematical notation demonstrates the core concepts and relationships within the DTNN framework.

title: Quantum Hamming-Distance-Based Locality-Sensitive Hashing
abstract: As a by-product of the rapid advancement of big data and artificial intelligence, high-dimensional data has been expeditiously evolving in both quantity and complexity, resulting in the critical need for suitable, effective retrieval and management systems. With this motivation, numerous classical solutions to the problem of high-dimensional data search were proposed. One of the most well-known instances of these is locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) and its prominent ability to run in sub-linear time. In situations with large databases, candidate validation, the last step of LSH’s procedure, can present itself as a bottleneck, which, in most cases, induces a tradeoff between accuracy and efficiency. Therefore, in this paper, we intend to utilize the renowned ability to speed up specific tasks like search problems of quantum computing to alleviate this issue and develop a quantum locality-sensitive hashing (QLSH) system. Specifically, by exploiting a Hamming-distance-calculating quantum circuit to perform candidate validation, we reduce the complexity of this step while preserving the retrieval performance compared to the classical counterpart in approximate search among high-dimensional data, as demonstrated by quantum simulation results.

title: Multimedia Digital Resources for African Tone Languages
abstract: The dataset is a multimodal collection comprising digital images and natural-language speech recordings associated with selected food and agricultural product categories. The dataset was developed to support research and applications in areas such as multimedia computing, computer vision, speech processing, natural language processing, multilingual computing, image classification, speech recognition, and indigenous language technology. The dataset is organized into two principal folders: Image and Sound. The Image folder contains categorized visual representations of food and agricultural products, while the Sound folder contains spoken-word pronunciations corresponding to the represented items in four languages: English, Yoruba, Hausa, and Igbo. The Image folder contains a total of 94 image files in JPG format, systematically distributed across six food and agricultural product categories: cereal, fruit, grain, herb, tuber, and vegetable. The cereal category contains 8 images, the fruit category contains 26 images, the grain category contains 12 images, the herb category contains 18 images, while the tuber and vegetable categories contain 15 images each. Thus, the six categories collectively constitute the 94 JPG image files in the dataset. Each image represents an item belonging to one of the specified food and agricultural product categories. The category-based organization provides a structured visual dataset that can facilitate research and experimentation in image recognition, visual object retrieval, computer vision, and multimodal learning tasks. The Sound folder contains 175 natural-language speech recordings corresponding to the food and agricultural products represented in the image collection. The speech recordings provide verbal pronunciations of the associated items in four languages: English, Yoruba, Hausa and Igbo. All sound recordings are stored in WAV (.wav) format. The multilingual structure makes the dataset potentially useful for research involving multilingual speech recognition, pronunciation modelling, speech-to-text systems, African language technologies, language identification, and image–speech association. The dataset is arranged hierarchically to make individual categories and languages easily identifiable. Users can access the Image folder to obtain the visual component and the Sound folder to obtain the multilingual speech component. The Sound folder contains a total of 175 natural-language speech recordings associated with the food and agricultural products represented in the Image folder. The Sound folder is organized first according to the six food and agricultural product categories: cereal, fruit, grain, herb, tuber, and vegetable. Within each category folder, four language-specific subfolders are provided: English, Yoruba, Hausa, and Igbo. These language folders contain spoken-word pronunciations of the corresponding items in the respective languages. All speech recordings are stored in .wav format.

title: Introduction to XAI Taxonomy, Ethics, and Policy
abstract: Intelligence integrated data analytics utilized for real-time systems under different problem settings helps to take immediate decisions with highest level of accuracy. In order to ensure this, it is necessary to prove the accuracy of analytics algorithms based on the data captured and Machine Learning (ML) algorithms applied on these applications. Calculating accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score may help in selecting the appropriate ML or Deep Learning (DL) model for prediction. However, as AI-ased analytics systems equipped with ML/DL algorithms are generally black boxes, where users can see only the inputs and outputs but not the inner workings. There is no proper evidence that the prediction given by these systems is correct. This lack of transparency makes it inherently challenging to understand how and why they reach their decisions. For human operators or end users to trust AI systems, these explanations must align with human perception and expectations. Yet current ML/DL models tend to be untrustworthy due to their inherent complexity and lack of transparency. Hence, this chapter introduces the basics of Explainable AI (XAI) and the role of XAI in interpretability and explainability of the ML/DL models. Further, the taxonomy of Explainable AI addresses the different types of XAI methods and how these methods help to resolve the issue by enabling a transparent decision-making process thereby highlighting which factors were considered for decision-making purposes.

title: Agentic systems in computational pathology: architectures, evidence, and translational challenges
abstract: BACKGROUND: Digital pathology supports whole-slide imaging, remote review, and computational analysis. Most pathology AI systems, however, remain restricted to predefined tasks. Agentic architectures coordinate perception models, language-based reasoning, external tools, and feedback-dependent actions, but their clinical evidence is derived mainly from retrospective benchmarks and research prototypes. MAIN BODY: We review agentic systems in computational pathology using an operational taxonomy based on dynamic control flow, inference-time tool selection, and knowledge integration. We assess architectures, enabling technologies, and applications in diagnosis, prognosis, and therapeutic support. Reported gains are difficult to attribute to agentic organization because studies differ in backbones, training data, and inference budgets. We therefore emphasize validation scope, computational cost, workflow integration, hallucination and security risks, regulatory requirements, patient preferences, and the conditions under which specialist non-agentic models remain preferable. CONCLUSIONS: Agentic architectures have established technical feasibility, but not clinical benefit. Translation should prioritize verifiable tasks, matched comparisons, prospective and external validation, lifecycle governance, and interfaces that preserve pathologist oversight.

title: Variationally Optimized Imaginary-time Polynomial Filters for Ground State Projection
abstract: In this work, we develop a variational imaginary-time evolution (ITE) framework based on polynomial filtering, derived from an operator-level action principle, which yields an optimized non-unitary projector expressed as a polynomial in the Hamiltonian. Starting from a single-ancilla, first-order imaginary-time update defined by a Taylor expansion and Trotter-Suzuki (TS) decompositions, we show that replacing these approximations with alternative variational formulas substantially improves both accuracy and stability at larger time steps, leading to up to an order-of-magnitude enhancement in the final success probability. We further derive rigorous error bounds that depend only on static properties of the Hamiltonian, providing practical guidance for selecting the simulation time step. Benchmarks on the transverse-field Ising model demonstrate faster convergence to the ground-state energy and improved robustness compared to standard TS--Taylor ITE, highlighting variational polynomial filtering as a practical route to higher-fidelity ground-state preparation on near-term quantum devices.

title: Explainable Uncertainty Estimation for Reliable Medical AI
abstract: Artificial intelligence has strong potential to support clinical decision-making, yet its adoption in healthcare remains limited due to a lack of trust. Uncertainty estimation can signal unreliable predictions, and explainable AI (XAI) can clarify how predictions are made but existing methods treat them separately, providing no feature-level insight into why a prediction is uncertain or which tests to prioritize to reduce it. To address this gap, we propose explainable uncertainty estimation, which unifies uncertainty estimation and XAI to both quantify uncertainty and explain feature-level contributions. We introduce the Expected Gradients Reconstruction Uncertainty Estimate (egRUE), which incorporates prediction explanations into its uncertainty computation and decomposes uncertainty into feature-wise contributions. We prove theoretical properties of egRUE and show through experiments that it improves reliability and interpretability compared to existing methods. A user study with medical experts further demonstrates that egRUE's explanations improve calibrated trust over uncertainty scores alone, increasing confidence in correct predictions and reducing confidence in incorrect ones. By combining prediction uncertainty with feature-level explanations, egRUE strengthens decision-making support in safety-critical healthcare settings, clarifying both when predictions may be unreliable and which features drive that uncertainty.

title: CoRe-MoE: Compact Reusable MoE for Continual Multimodal Instruction Tuning
abstract: Continual multimodal instruction tuning requires multimodal large language models to acquire new task abilities sequentially while preserving previously learned knowledge. LoRA-MoE provides a promising solution by introducing expert-based capacity, but repeatedly learning and maintaining full LoRA experts leads to substantial parameter overhead. This raises a natural question: is full expert expansion necessary for every new task? To answer it, we analyze the SVD of task-specific LoRA updates and observe substantial overlap in their input- and output-side LoRA direction subspaces, with task-specific adaptation largely captured by lightweight coordinates over these subspaces. Motivated by this observation, we propose CoRe-MoE, a Compact Reusable MoE framework for parameter-efficient continual multimodal instruction tuning. CoRe-MoE extracts reusable input- and output-side direction bases from an initial expert bank, and for subsequent tasks trains only compact coordinate experts together with task-specific low-rank routers. Experiments on two representative MLLMs show that CoRe-MoE improves final average performance over the strongest competing baseline by up to 5.90 points, while using less than 1% of the trainable parameters required by sequential LoRA for later tasks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/runzezz/CoRe-MoE.

title: Quantum Machine Learning via Causal Inference
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum machine learning to revolutionize causal inference within machine learning models. Traditional machine learning often operates as a "black box," lacking transparency regarding the underlying causal relationships driving predictions. We propose a novel framework leveraging quantum mechanics – specifically quantum entanglement and superposition – to achieve precise causal inference. This framework centers around simulating causal relationships using quantum circuits, validating causal effects through quantum measurements, and mitigating measurement errors with quantum error correction. The core claim is that this approach can overcome the limitations of classical methods and provide a fundamentally more accurate and interpretable understanding of complex systems. We outline the key components of this framework, emphasizing the theoretical foundations and potential challenges, and argue for a significant paradigm shift in how we approach causal discovery and model validation within the field of machine learning. The ultimate goal is to build inherently causal quantum machine learning models that are robust to noise and offer unparalleled predictive power. ---

title: Topological Quantum States for Quantum Computing
abstract: This paper explores the potential of topological quantum states for constructing a novel quantum computing architecture. The core claim centers on leveraging the inherent robustness and stability offered by topological quantum states to mitigate the challenges associated with decoherence and errors in conventional quantum computing. The proposed mechanism involves designing a physical implementation of qubits based on topological properties, specifically exploiting their natural resilience to local perturbations. This approach aims to achieve quantum computation with enhanced reliability. The paper details the theoretical framework, focusing on the mathematical representation of topological qubits and the associated quantum gates. It investigates the fundamental properties that contribute to the fault-tolerant nature of topological quantum systems. Finally, it outlines a potential roadmap for advancing this technology, recognizing the significant research and development efforts required to realize its full potential.

title: Graph-Based Symbolic Regression with Evolutionary Algorithms
abstract: Symbolic regression aims to discover mathematical expressions that accurately represent a given dataset. However, this process often struggles with complex systems exhibiting high dimensionality and intricate relationships. This work introduces a novel approach to symbolic regression, leveraging a graph-based representation combined with evolutionary algorithms. The target function is represented as a graph, where nodes represent mathematical operations and edges define dependencies between variables. An evolutionary algorithm then iteratively refines this graph structure, optimizing it to minimize the error between the predicted and observed data. This method offers a more scalable and robust solution compared to traditional symbolic regression techniques, particularly when dealing with complex, high-dimensional datasets. title: Adaptive Kernel Learning for Sparse Data
abstract: Kernel methods have proven to be powerful tools in machine learning for tasks such as classification and regression. However, their effectiveness is often limited by the computational complexity associated with constructing and operating on kernel matrices, particularly when dealing with sparse data. Traditional kernel methods frequently encounter the "curse of dimensionality," where the size of the kernel matrix grows exponentially with the number of features, leading to prohibitive memory requirements and computational costs. This paper introduces an Adaptive Kernel Learning (AKL) algorithm designed to address these challenges. The AKL algorithm dynamically constructs kernel matrices based on the local density and structure of the sparse data, effectively mitigating the curse of dimensionality. It utilizes sparse optimization techniques to learn kernel functions on-the-fly, providing a scalable solution for kernel methods in scenarios with limited data points. The core of the algorithm lies in its adaptive approach, tailoring the kernel function to the specific characteristics of the data, resulting in improved accuracy and efficiency compared to traditional dense kernel methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of AKL through theoretical analysis and explore its potential applications in various domains where sparse data is prevalent.

title: Dynamic Bayesian Networks for Real-Time Anomaly Detection in Sensor Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to anomaly detection in sensor networks utilizing Dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBNs). Traditional static Bayesian networks are inherently limited in their ability to adapt to the dynamic and evolving nature of sensor network environments, particularly when faced with shifting threat landscapes. This research addresses this limitation by developing a DBN framework that continuously learns and adapts its structure and parameters based on real-time sensor data. The core mechanism involves updating the network topology and associated probabilities as new observations are received, allowing for robust and accurate anomaly detection. The developed framework demonstrates enhanced adaptability and resilience compared to static Bayesian network approaches, making it suitable for applications requiring real-time response to evolving threats. The key innovation lies in the dynamic adjustment of the network, enabling proactive detection rather than reactive identification. This paper outlines the design, implementation, and theoretical underpinnings of this dynamic DBN system.

title: Quantum-Inspired Search Algorithms for Combinatorial Optimization
abstract: This paper explores the application of quantum-inspired concepts to the field of combinatorial optimization. Traditional search algorithms often struggle with the complexity of problems involving numerous possible solutions. We propose a novel approach that leverages the principles of quantum superposition and interference, albeit within a classical computing framework, to enhance the efficiency of search processes. The core of our method involves a hybrid algorithm that combines established classical search techniques with probabilistic sampling strategies informed by quantum mechanics. We aim to demonstrate that by mimicking these quantum phenomena, we can significantly improve the speed and effectiveness of solving complex combinatorial optimization problems. The algorithm's performance is evaluated through theoretical analysis and conceptual design, focusing on the potential for achieving performance gains without requiring actual quantum hardware. The key contribution lies in the strategic application of probabilistic sampling to explore solution spaces in a manner analogous to quantum superposition, followed by interference-like mechanisms to guide the search towards promising regions. This approach represents a new direction in optimization, bridging the gap between classical and quantum computing paradigms.

title: The Winner’s Curse in LLM Pipeline Selection: How Correlated Candidate Pools Break Best-of-N Reporting, and How to Correct It
abstract: Best-of-N pipeline selection, running N candidate prompts on an m-item dev set and reporting the winner's dev score, is the default way an LLM practitioner picks and reports a prompt. That dev score is optimistic: the winner was chosen in part because it got lucky on the dev items, and its true accuracy on fresh data is lower. We measure this winner's curse directly on four correctness matrices spanning three tasks (SST-2, Subj, AG News) and two models (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct), sweeping N from 1 to 100 and m from 20 to 200. Bias grows with N and shrinks roughly as 1/sqrt(m), reaching 0.088 accuracy points at N = 100, m = 100 on Subj. We then characterize why real candidate pools inflate this bias beyond the independent-candidates textbook case: two effective-candidate-count estimators, a spectral participation ratio and a moment-matching inversion of the observed selection gap, agree that a 105-to-111-candidate pool behaves like roughly 1.5 to 3.5 independent draws. Breaking that count down by candidate provenance turns up a result opposite our own working hypothesis: LLM-generated (APE-style) candidates carry far less effective diversity (N_eff/K ~ 0.017-0.041) than either hand-written seed prompts or paraphrase/mutation candidates (N_eff/K ~ 0.14-0.24 for both), consistently across all three tasks. We compare six ways to report a best-of-N winner (no correction, a naive dev split, two extreme-value union-bound corrections keyed to K or to N_eff, cross-fitting, and a bootstrap plug-in) on bias, mean squared error, and 90% interval coverage; correcting against N_eff dominates the independent-candidates union bound on every axis and matches or beats every other method on mean squared error, while the naive K-based correction overshoots badly enough to be worse than reporting nothing at all. Resampling the stored matrices at the exact (N, m) of a real, live EvoPromptGA trajectory reproduces its measured bias on all three tasks, inside a 90% predictive band in every case, which supports treating a one-time correctness matrix plus free resampling as a faithful stand-in for repeated live search. Finally, we derive budget-allocation curves for a fixed evaluation budget B = N * m: on tasks already near their accuracy ceiling, the optimal split spends almost the whole budget on m; on a task with real headroom left, it keeps paying to search wider even as N_eff/K stays in the low single digits.

title: Nature‐Inspired Intelligence for Complex Problems
abstract: Discover how to turn nature’s best problem-solving strategies into powerful computational tools with this comprehensive guide to building resilient, adaptive, and next-generation algorithms for healthcare, finance, and engineering. Nature-inspired intelligence is a rapidly evolving field that draws from biological and physical phenomena, such as evolution, swarm behavior, neural processing, and immune systems, to develop algorithms capable of handling complexity, uncertainty, and scalability. Unlike conventional computational approaches, these techniques adapt dynamically, mimic resilience, and exhibit problem-solving strategies observed in nature. As industries face increasingly complex and data-intensive challenges, nature-inspired intelligence provides robust, efficient, and innovative solutions, positioning it as a cornerstone of future technological and scientific progress. This book presents a comprehensive exploration of how biological, physical, and ecological principles can be transformed into powerful computational tools for solving some of today’s most challenging problems. Drawing inspiration from natural processes, the book highlights a broad spectrum of algorithms that push beyond traditional approaches to optimization and decision-making. Blending theory with application, the book demonstrates how nature-inspired intelligence can address complexity across domains including healthcare, energy, finance, engineering, and emerging technologies. Readers will find the volume: Offers an in-depth exploration of a wide range of nature-inspired computational techniques, including evolutionary algorithms, swarm intelligence, neural models, and physics-inspired methods; Bridges the gap between natural systems and computational problem-solving, appealing to a diverse audience of researchers and practitioners; Features case studies in robotics, healthcare, finance, engineering, and environmental sustainability, and highlights how these algorithms are used to tackle practical challenges across industries; Addresses the latest advancements in combining multiple nature-inspired techniques and explores cutting-edge topics like quantum computing and bio-hybrid systems. ensuring the content remains relevant to current research and innovation. Audience Computer scientists, engineers, applied mathematicians, data scientists, and researchers in optimization and complex systems, as well as professionals in healthcare, energy, finance, and technology seeking innovative problem-solving approaches.

title: Machine Learning Models with Fuzzy Logic‐Based Tuning
abstract: Such integration of machine learning models enhanced with fuzzy logic-based calibration constitutes a huge leap in AI research, on two main fronts: accuracy and adaptability. While its primary strength lies in harnessed machine learning algorithms that efficiently handle big data and complex patterns, it leverages fuzzy logic to deal with the uncertainties and vagueness related with the data. One can fine-tune such machine learning models through fuzzy logic to go beyond their performance in variable and unpredictable contexts. Based on this work, the book discusses several approaches towards the integration of fuzzy logic-based tuning into machine learning. Its implementation domain includes robotics, healthcare, finance, environmental monitoring. The inclusion of machine learning with fuzzy logic improves the resilience, interpretability, and decision-making capacity of models. Important case studies deliver considerable evidence for the practical advantages and enhanced performance based on this integrated strategy. The chapter will close with an overview of possible research avenues, elaborating on progress and challenges towards developing machine learning models enriched by fuzzy logic-inspired adjustments.

title: EnSiTa -A Trilingual Multi-Domain Parallel Dataset and Benchmark for Domain-Specific Machine Translation
abstract: Machine Translation (MT) for low-resource languages remains far behind that of high-resource languages, and the gap is widest in specialised domains, where parallel data is scarce or entirely absent. We present EnSiTa, a trilingual multi-domain parallel dataset and benchmark for English, Sinhala and Tamil. EnSiTa provides human post-edited training data for seven domains, plus manually translated test sets for those and one additional domain, all produced by professional translators under a multi-year, rigorously quality-controlled process. Using this dataset, we conduct an extensive study of domain-specific MT for all six language directions, fine-tuning a from-scratch Transformer, a pre-trained translation model (NLLB-600M), and decoder-only LLMs (Gemma 3 family, 1B-12B, and TranslateGemma) across training-data sizes, model scales, and in-domain, cross-domain, multilingual and multi-domain settings. To the best of our knowledge, this is the most extensive systematically documented multi-domain parallel data creation and benchmarking effort for low-resource MT. Our data and models will be publicly released.

title: Energy Internet Routing using Quantum Optimization Algorithms
abstract: The Energy Internet (EI) is a new concept aimed at enhancing the integration of renewable energy sources with the energy grid. Energy-efficient path selection in EI is NP-hard. This research presents an innovative Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) and Ising Hamiltonian formulation for energy routing. The validation and scalability of the proposed formulation were evaluated by applying quantum-inspired annealing and quantum gate optimization to two case studies, a 9-node and a 30-node EI network. A comparative analysis was presented between classical optimization using the Dijkstra algorithm, optimization-based methods, and QAOA using the Qiskit Sampler Primitive, NumpyEigenSolver, and quantum-inspired annealing using the Ocean exact Solver, D-Wave Tabu Sampler, and D-Wave Simulated Annealing. Simulation results based on the proposed formulation agree with the exact solution, while the runtime of classical approaches is less than that of quantum approaches. However, the Simulated Annealing sampler offers the shortest runtime among all quantum methods.

title: XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost.
abstract: Accurate forecasting of building energy consumption is important for improving energy management and supporting more efficient building operation. In this study, we investigate a sequential metaheuristic hyperparameter optimization framework for three widely used gradient-boosting models, namely XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost. Two optimization pathways, Grey Wolf Optimizer–Particle Swarm Optimization (GWO–PSO) and Ant Lion Optimizer–Moth-Flame Optimization (ALO–MFO), are evaluated under consistent experimental conditions.

title: Adaptive Symbolic Gene Network Programming
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to program optimization termed Adaptive Symbolic Gene Network Programming (ASGNP). The core idea is to model program optimization as an evolutionary process, mimicking the mechanisms of biological gene networks within a cellular environment. We propose a system where a symbolic gene network is constructed to represent a computational task. Through interactions between these symbolic genes, calculations are performed. Crucially, an optimization process, employing techniques such as genetic algorithms or evolutionary strategies, dynamically adjusts the connections and parameters within the gene network. This adaptive nature allows the system to automatically generate optimized code tailored to specific hardware architectures and task requirements. The system leverages the inherent self-organizing properties of biological systems to achieve robust and efficient solutions, addressing the challenges of traditional static optimization methods. We demonstrate the potential of ASGNP for complex and uncertain computational problems.

title: Quantum-Inspired Reservoir Computing for Time Series Forecasting
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to time series forecasting utilizing reservoir computing principles augmented with concepts inspired by quantum mechanics. Traditional reservoir computing relies on randomly connected recurrent networks to capture temporal dependencies, often struggling with complex and long-range correlations. We propose a "quantum-inspired reservoir" architecture that incorporates superposition layers and entanglement mechanisms to significantly improve temporal feature extraction and prediction accuracy. The superposition layers enable the representation of multiple time slices concurrently, while the entanglement mechanisms facilitate the effective correlation of distant time points within the reservoir. Mathematical formulations are presented to detail the architecture and operational principles, demonstrating a potential pathway towards more robust and accurate time series forecasting. The core claim is that quantum principles can be leveraged to enhance reservoir computing, moving beyond classical approaches.

abstract: This paper explores the application of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for modeling and predicting complex systems. Complex systems, such as biological networks and social networks, are characterized by intricate interdependencies and emergent behaviors. Traditional approaches often struggle to capture these complexities effectively. This work proposes utilizing GNNs to represent and analyze these systems, leveraging their ability to learn node relationships and perform predictive tasks. The core claim is that GNNs provide a novel framework for uncovering hidden relationships within complex systems. The underlying mechanism involves transforming the system into a graph structure, enabling the GNN to learn from the connections between nodes and ultimately predict system behavior. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a theoretical exploration, outlining the key components and considerations for implementing GNNs in complex system modeling and prediction. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions.

Complex systems, such as biological networks and social networks, are characterized by intricate interdependencies and emergent behaviors. Traditional approaches often struggle to capture these complexities effectively. This work proposes utilizing GNNs to represent and analyze these systems, leveraging their ability to learn node relationships and perform predictive tasks. The core claim is that GNNs provide a novel framework for uncovering hidden relationships within complex systems. The underlying mechanism involves transforming the system into a graph structure, enabling the GNN to learn from the connections between nodes and ultimately predict system behavior. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a theoretical exploration, outlining the key components and considerations for implementing GNNs in complex system modeling and prediction. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions.

title: Predictive Coding of Large Language Models via Latent Space Dynamics
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in generating coherent and contextually relevant text. However, understanding the underlying mechanisms driving their behavior, particularly the evolution of their latent representations, remains a significant challenge. This research proposes a novel approach to analyzing and predicting the dynamics of the latent space within LLMs, leveraging concepts from dynamical systems theory. We hypothesize that the latent space of an LLM, when viewed as a dynamic system, exhibits predictable attractors and invariant manifolds that can be exploited for enhanced prediction and generation. This work develops a methodology for identifying these structures, offering a potential pathway towards proactive control and improved performance of LLMs. The core contribution lies in treating the latent space as a dynamic system, opening up opportunities for predictive coding and enabling a deeper understanding of how LLMs process and generate language.

title: Semantic Graph Embedding for Knowledge Graph Completion with Relational Reasoning
abstract: Knowledge graph completion (KGC) is a crucial task in leveraging the wealth of information stored in knowledge graphs. Traditional graph embedding methods often struggle to capture the intricate relationships between entities within a KG, particularly those involving hierarchies and complex relational structures. This paper proposes a novel semantic graph embedding approach that explicitly models these relationships using graph convolutional networks (GCNs) augmented with attention mechanisms. Our model, termed Relational-Aware Graph Embedding (RAGE), learns embeddings by propagating information through the KG while simultaneously attending to the importance of different relationships. We demonstrate that RAGE significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on benchmark KGC datasets, achieving substantial improvements in prediction accuracy. The core claim of this work is that graph embeddings which explicitly model relationships between entities, including hierarchical and relational knowledge, significantly improve knowledge graph completion accuracy. The proposed mechanism involves developing a graph embedding model that incorporates relational knowledge through graph convolutional networks with attention mechanisms.

title: Causal Discovery via Latent Variable Dynamics in Bayesian Networks
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to causal discovery within dynamic Bayesian networks, specifically addressing the challenges posed by latent variables and feedback loops. Existing causal discovery algorithms often struggle to accurately model these complex systems, leading to inaccurate inferences. Our method extends Bayesian network learning by integrating latent variables, represented through Hidden Markov Models (HMMs), into the learning process. We leverage variational inference and approximate inference techniques to manage the computational complexity arising from the inclusion of latent variables and the modeling of feedback loops. The core innovation lies in the dynamic adaptation of the Bayesian network structure, allowing it to evolve alongside the underlying system dynamics. We demonstrate, theoretically and conceptually, the benefits of this approach, focusing on improved accuracy and robustness compared to traditional methods when dealing with systems exhibiting significant latent variable influence and cyclical relationships. The ultimate goal is to provide a more reliable framework for uncovering causal relationships in complex, real-world scenarios.

title: Vers un Data Center Photonique Compact : Densité Computationnelle Volumique, Efficacité Énergétique et Architecture WDM–OAM
abstract: Description La croissance rapide des charges de calcul liées à l'intelligence artificielle déplace progressivement les contraintes des architectures informatiques vers les interconnexions, la mémoire et la dissipation thermique. Ce préprint propose un cadre conceptuel pour l'étude d'un data center photonique compact, dans lequel le calcul, l'interconnexion et le multiplexage optique sont conçus simultanément comme les éléments d'une même architecture physique. L'approche repose sur l'intégration de plusieurs briques technologiques : sources optiques et microcombs ; multiplexage en longueur d'onde (WDM) ; multiplexage spatial prospectif, incluant les modes à moment angulaire orbital (OAM) ; réseau photonique programmable ; calcul matriciel photonique ; interconnexions optiques intra-système ; mémoire proche du calcul ; électronique de conversion, de contrôle et de calibration. Le travail introduit quatre métriques complémentaires pour comparer les architectures électroniques, photoniques et hybrides : DV : densité computationnelle volumique, exprimée en TOPS/cm³ ; ηC : efficacité computationnelle énergétique, exprimée en TOPS/W ; BV : densité de bande passante, exprimée en TB/s/cm³ ; ΦV : métrique combinée intégrant simultanément calcul, puissance consommée et volume physique. L'objectif n'est pas de présenter une performance commerciale actuellement disponible, mais de définir des cibles architecturales quantifiables permettant d'évaluer le potentiel de miniaturisation des infrastructures de calcul. Trois trajectoires sont étudiées : une architecture hybride utilisant principalement la photonique pour les interconnexions ; un accélérateur photonique intégré combinant calcul matriciel et communication optique ; un scénario prospectif de data center photonique compact, dans lequel les sources, le WDM, le calcul matriciel, l'interconnexion et la mémoire proche du calcul sont co-conçus. Les objectifs de recherche considérés atteignent des densités de calcul de l'ordre de 1 à 10 TOPS/cm³, tout en recherchant une efficacité énergétique de plusieurs TOPS/W et une densité de communication pouvant atteindre plusieurs centaines de TB/s par litre. Le préprint souligne également les principaux verrous technologiques : efficacité des lasers, pertes d'insertion, conversions ADC/DAC, précision analogique, mémoire, packaging 2.5D/3D, calibration thermique et coût de fabrication des circuits photoniques intégrés. La conclusion centrale est que la miniaturisation photonique d'un data center doit être abordée non comme un simple remplacement du transistor par le photon, mais comme un problème de co-conception architecturale complète. La trajectoire la plus crédible apparaît aujourd'hui comme hybride : CMOS + photonique intégrée + mémoire proche du calcul + WDM + switching optique, avec le multiplexage spatial et l'OAM comme axes prospectifs supplémentaires. Si les avantages intrinsèques de la photonique peuvent être conservés après intégration de l'ensemble du budget système, incluant lasers, conversions, mémoire, contrôle, packaging et refroidissement, la conséquence pourrait dépasser la simple accélération du calcul. Elle pourrait conduire à une transformation de la géométrie même des infrastructures numériques : des racks et réseaux traditionnels vers des volumes de calcul photonique compacts.

title: Fuzzy Logic in Machine Learning and AI Applications
abstract: Fuzzy logic dances gracefully in the realm of mathematics, its versatile framework embraced by machine learning and Artificial Intelligence (AI). In the land of machine learning, fuzzy logic wields its power to confront scenarios where traditional binary logic falters. Fuzzy controllers reign supreme in control systems, masterfully navigating dynamic environments that defy precise mathematical models. Within the realm of game AI, fuzzy logic empowers the creation of intelligent, adaptive non-player characters (NPCs) that react authentically to player actions and ever-evolving in-game landscapes. In essence, fuzzy logic's dexterity in handling uncertainty and imprecision positions it as a vital asset in the arsenal of machine learning and AI applications. It bridges the chasm left by conventional binary logic, providing answers for intricate, real-world challenges across a myriad of domains. Its adaptability and effectiveness in wrangling uncertain data underscore its role in propelling the capabilities of AI and machine learning systems. This chapter offers a concise panoramic view of how fuzzy logic is harnessed within these domains, highlighting its capacity to confront real-world problems teeming with ambiguity and imprecision.

title: Probabilistic Multi-Robot Gas Source Localization with Uncalibrated Sensors: A Distributed Estimation Approach
abstract: Estimating environmental states with multi-robot systems becomes particularly challenging when robots are equipped with uncalibrated and therefore heterogeneous sensors, whose nonlinear and inconsistent responses prevent reliable information fusion. In this paper, we propose a distributed probabilistic framework for source localization tasks that enables calibration-free estimation in the presence of sensor heterogeneity. The key idea is that each robot independently estimates a local belief using a rank-based feature that captures the relative evolution of observations and is invariant to sensor scaling and nonlinearities. These local beliefs are then fused through a product of experts formulation to obtain a consistent global estimate across the team. To further improve the efficiency of team coordination, we introduce an informative region allocation and path planning strategy that reduces redundant exploration while balancing exploration and exploitation. We validate the proposed framework using high-fidelity simulations with realistic gas sensor models. Results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms a benchmark method based on standard measurement aggregation, achieving reliable source localization accuracy despite strong sensor heterogeneity. More broadly, this work demonstrates how calibration-free sensing representations can be effectively extended to distributed robotic systems, paving the way for their application to other estimation tasks involving heterogeneous sensors.

title: Actionable CBFI: Integrating Structural Decomposition and Causal Counterfactual Recourse for Tabular Machine Learning
abstract: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) increasingly calls for actionable counterfactual recourse, yet current methodologies face challenges related to causal invalidity, excessive cognitive burden, and predictive failure. Exhaustive causal search algorithms often require modifications to multiple attributes, whereas additive attribution-guided methods, such as SHAP, ignore higher-order feature synergies, leading to suboptimal predictive momentum and diffuse intervention effort in complex nonlinear models, such as XGBoost. To bridge this gap, we introduce actionable case-based feature importance (A-CBFI), a diagnosis-prescription integrated framework for tabular machine learning. Grounded in structural causal models (SCMs), A-CBFI isolates synergistic interaction bottlenecks and releases suppressive structural locks, translating them into targeted interventions. By mathematically separating the active user intervention space (L_{\mathrm{active}}) from downstream effects and concentrating over 98.3% of the intervention effort on diagnosed root causes, A-CBFI enables highly targeted interventions. Empirical evaluations across the financial and healthcare domains demonstrate that A-CBFI reduces the active human intervention burden by 77.0% while maintaining comparable global recourse cost to exhaustive causal baselines. By prioritizing the diagnosed causal bottlenecks, A-CBFI provides targeted and actionable recourse while maintaining causal validity and achieving full relative convergence across all causally feasible instances.

title: From Evidence Inventory to Probative Logic
abstract: Abstract Questo working paper propone la Evidence Due Diligence (EDD, Due Diligence delle Evidenze), un meta-metodo di secondo livello applicato all'inventario probatorio pubblico costruito da Shakespeare-Enquiry (Diana Price, Literary Paper Trail; Tom Woosnam, Convergence Analysis). Il contributo non aggiunge nuove evidenze primarie: disciplina il modo in cui quelle esistenti vengono ammesse, classificate e pesate. Introduce (1) un terzo inventario indipendente, il Transmission Inventory, dedicato alla filiera editoriale e teatrale, con una regola di sufficienza per provenienza che distingue gli inventari ereditati, presunti sufficienti, da quello originato, verificato in forma nativa; (2) una classificazione MECE delle evidenze in tre domini funzionali (Fisico/HW, Carattere/SW, Mercato/Rete), ortogonale alla provenienza; e (3) un funnel logico a sette gate applicato in un doppio ciclo, con il modulo del corpus come perimetro esterno e il dominio come sequenza interna a logica fail-fast, con test dichiarati in anticipo, verificabili da un secondo esaminatore e protetti dal doppio conteggio, poiché una dipendenza non è una convergenza. Due strumenti derivati ne estendono la portata: il test del circuito di reddito, che rende interpretabile la categoria «pagato per scrivere» attraverso regimi di reddito diversi, e la sandbox autoriale, un motore di parsimonia che testa le relazioni tra le mani sugli insiemi di candidati sopravvissuti al funnel. L'esito non è una classifica dei candidati ma un registro a tre dimensioni (candidato, ruolo, modulo) con default di esclusione, pensato per rendere auditabile, non per chiudere, la Shakespeare Authorship Question.

title: From Local Blindness to Global Context: Demonstration of the Contextual Projection Optimization Method Versus Classical BFGS
abstract: Modern optimization methods and deep learning architectures predominantly rely on the "bottom-up" paradigm, making decisions based solely on local gradients. While methods like BFGS perform exceptionally well in ideal, low-dimensional smooth spaces, real-world systems face deep structural challenges: local minimum traps, chaotic slopes, and massive energy inefficiencies. In this short paper, we demonstrate a practical implementation of a framework based on a "Top-Down / Whole-First" ontological shift.

title: Mixed Intermediate-Task Training for Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Transfer on XTREME-R
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. We investigate whether English intermediate-task training is still helpful on non-English target tasks. Using nine intermediate language-understanding tasks, we evaluate intermediate-task transfer in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting on the XTREME benchmark. We see large improvements from intermediate training on the BUCC and Tatoeba sentence retrieval tas Research goal: What is the impact of mixed intermediate-task training (combining tasks of varying difficulty) on zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance compared to single-task training on XTREME-R? title: Quantum-secure Software Network Environments for Telco Operators
abstract: The transition towards quantum-safe secure communications requires current network infrastructures to support the coexistence of multiple cryptographic technologies. In this context, crypto-agility becomes a key requirement, enabling the coordinated use of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC), and classical cryptographic mechanisms during a progressive migration process. This paper presents a general, standards-based architecture for crypto-agile IPsec service provisioning in Software-Defined Networking (SDN) environments. The proposal combines modular functional blocks that support the integration of QKD-, PQC-,and classical-derived key material under a common operational framework. The architecture builds on existing specifications, including RFC 9061 and ETSI GS QKD 004. Rather than focusing on implementation details or performance evaluation, this work describes the needs addressed by the architecture, its main components, and the operational workflows supporting secure tunnel establishment, rekeying, and attestation-related actions.

title: Adaptive Kernel Learning via Meta-Representation Discovery
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to kernel learning that leverages meta-learning for adaptive kernel discovery. Traditional kernel methods often rely on pre-defined kernels or manual selection, which can limit their effectiveness in diverse learning scenarios. Our method dynamically learns and adapts kernel functions during training by employing a neural network to discover a meta-representation of the kernel space. This representation guides the learning of a kernel function optimized for the current data distribution, thereby enhancing generalization performance and computational efficiency. The core claim is that dynamically learned kernels, guided by a meta-representation, significantly outperform static kernel approaches. We present a framework for this adaptive kernel learning, detailing the architecture and training procedure. The results demonstrate the efficacy of this meta-representation driven approach, showcasing improved accuracy and faster convergence compared to traditional kernel methods. We explore the key components, including the meta-learner architecture, the representation learning objective, and the kernel function adaptation strategy. This work establishes a new paradigm for kernel learning, paving the way for more robust and efficient machine learning algorithms.

The results demonstrate the efficacy of this meta-representation driven approach, showcasing improved accuracy and faster convergence compared to traditional kernel methods. We explore the key components, including the meta-learner architecture, the representation learning objective, and the kernel function adaptation strategy. This work establishes a new paradigm for kernel learning, paving the way for more robust and efficient machine learning algorithms.

title: Relational Reinforcement Learning with Graph Neural Networks and Temporal Difference Learning
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to reinforcement learning (RL) that combines the power of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) with Temporal Difference (TD) learning. The core claim is that relational reasoning, particularly when represented through graph structures, can substantially enhance RL performance. Traditional RL methods often struggle with environments where relationships between elements are crucial for optimal control. Our approach addresses this limitation by creating an agent capable of learning to interact with and control systems modeled as graphs. GNNs are utilized to extract relational features from the graph structure, and these features are then integrated into a TD learning framework for efficient policy learning. The resulting system demonstrates improved learning speed and often achieves better performance compared to standard RL algorithms, especially in complex, relational environments. We present a theoretical framework supporting this approach and discuss its potential applications across various domains. The primary contribution lies in the synergistic combination of GNNs for relational representation and TD learning for value function estimation, offering a new paradigm for relational reinforcement learning.

title: Explainable AI via Causal Inference on Deep Learning Models
abstract: The increasing deployment of deep learning models across various domains has raised concerns about their interpretability and trustworthiness. These models, often referred to as "black boxes," frequently produce opaque decisions, hindering human understanding and potentially leading to undesirable outcomes. This research proposes a novel approach to explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) by leveraging causal inference techniques applied to deep learning models. Instead of relying on post-hoc explanations based on feature importance or activation patterns, this work aims to directly identify the causal relationships between input features and model outputs. This approach allows for a more robust and reliable understanding of the model's decision-making process, mitigating the limitations of traditional XAI methods. Specifically, we utilize methods like do-calculus and structural causal models (SCMs) to dissect the learned representations within deep neural networks, revealing the underlying causal drivers of predictions. The resulting explanations are grounded in a deeper understanding of the data and the model's function, offering a significant advancement in the field of XAI. This paper outlines the theoretical framework, presents a methodology for applying causal inference to deep learning, and discusses potential challenges and future research directions.

title: Интерпретируемые решающие правила классификации на основе дерева секущих гиперплоскостей
abstract: В статье анализируются различия между интерпретируемым и объяснимым искусственным интеллектом. Два этих понятия рассматриваются автором как различные, хотя и взаимодополняющие подходы к решению задач машинного обучения. На основании проведенного анализа автором предлагается представлять решающие правила для задач классификации в виде древовидной структуры, но в ее узлах использовать не отдельные входные признаки, а секущие гиперплоскости. Такой подход позволяет оценивать информативность каждого входного признака в отдельности и всей совокупности признаков в каждом узле и получать интерпретируемое решающее правило в целом для всей модели с высокими метриками качества решающего правила. Приведены примеры практических задач, решенных данным способом. Во всех случаях по метрикам качества дерево секущих гиперплоскостей превосходило дерево решений, полученное традиционным способом, и имело AUC ROC сопоставимую со случайным лесом. The article analyzes the differences between interpretable and explainable artificial intelligence. These two concepts are considered by the author as distinct, yet complementary, approaches to solving machine learning problems. Based on the conducted analysis, the author proposes representing decision rules for classification tasks in the form of a tree structure, where the nodes contain not individual input features but separating hyperplanes. This approach allows us to evaluate the information content of each input feature individually and the entire set of features at each node, producing an interpretable decision rule for the entire model with high decision rule quality metrics. Examples of practical problems solved using this method are provided. In all cases, the cutting hyperplane tree outperformed the decision tree obtained using the traditional method in terms of quality metrics and had an AUC ROC comparable to that of a random forest.

title: A Center-Guided Reinforcement Learning Method for Hyperparameter Optimization and Its Application to Relation Extraction
abstract: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) aims to identify high-quality model configurations under a limited evaluation budget. To address mixed search spaces, sparse feedback, and low sample efficiency in reinforcement learning (RL)-based HPO, a Center-Guided Reinforcement Learning (CGRL) method is proposed. In CGRL, the policy output is reformulated from a configuration to be directly evaluated into a search center that defines a promising region, decoupling region-level guidance from exact configuration selection. A mixed candidate pool is generated around the center, and a promising candidate for real evaluation is selected by a Random Forest surrogate model. Meanwhile, a process-aware reward provides dense and informative feedback for policy learning. Experiments on 20 Yet Another Hyperparameter Optimization (YAHPO) Gym environments validate the effectiveness of CGRL. Compared with random search (RS), Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE), Sequential Model-based Algorithm Configuration 3 (SMAC3), a Proximal Policy Optimization baseline (PPO-basic), Hyperparameter Optimization by Reinforcement Learning (Hyp-RL), and Q-Learning for Hyperparameter Optimization (HyperQ-Opt), CGRL achieves the best average rank of 1.800 in terms of the final best objective value, versus 6.000, 3.600, 2.200, 4.450, 6.350, and 3.600, respectively. For Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) HPO for relation extraction (RE) from ancient Chinese historical documents, CGRL improves Macro-F1 by 8.66%, 3.10%, 3.18%, and 5.13% on the validation set relative to RS, TPE, SMAC3, and PPO, respectively, and by 11.15%, 2.03%, 3.11%, and 9.59% on the test set. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of CGRL for limited-budget HPO and its applicability to practical RE tasks.

title: A Review of Attribute-Based Credentials for Secure and Privacy-Preserving Identity Management
abstract: Attribute-Based Credentials (ABCs) are cryptographic credential systems that enable holders to selectively disclose certified attributes or prove predicates over them, thereby supporting privacy-preserving identity verification while limiting unnecessary information exposure. This paper presents a review of the system model, core security and privacy properties, classification, comparative analysis, and practical deployment challenges of ABCs. It develops a two-dimensional taxonomy consisting of a construction dimension and an extension dimension. The construction dimension covers publicly verifiable signature-based, keyed-verification and MAC-based, and general-purpose ZKP-based ABC constructions, while the extension dimension covers issuer-hiding, threshold and multi-authority, and dynamic-lifecycle ABCs. The resulting comparison shows that these categories exhibit different trade-offs in verifier openness, proof flexibility, privacy guarantees, trust requirements, lifecycle support, and practical deployment requirements. The review further examines key challenges related to the efficiency and scalability of multi-attribute management, privacy-preserving credential lifecycle management, inference risks in selective disclosure, interoperability, post-quantum security, and holder binding. Finally, it synthesizes recent trends and identifies research directions toward efficient, interoperable, privacy-preserving, and practically deployable ABC systems that strengthen digital trust and support trustworthy digital identity infrastructures.

title: Quantum computation of partonic Drell-Yan scattering cross sections and interference effects
abstract: We probe the possibilities of efficiently constructing simple Feynman diagrams into quantum devices. More precisely, we study Drell-Yan lepton pair creation at the partonic level of the form q qbar -> gamma/Z -> l- l+. We develop quantum gates that build up the relevant diagrams using simple Feynman rules, such as vertex and propagator gates V and P. We show how the quantum circuit may compute simultaneous amplitudes in the phase space and how to reach the full integrated cross section from the outputs. In addition to this, we also show how the circuit is able to simultaneously isolate the interference effects of the contributing diagrams by a simple basis rotation. The circuit design is made to be general, and thus this work constitutes a step towards the implementation of arbitrary scattering process computations and efficient interference analyses.

title: Is Prosody Lost in Translation? Fine-Grained Cross-Lingual Prosody Similarity Across Languages
abstract: Prosody plays an important role in speech translation, conveying information such as emphasis, emotion, and intent beyond lexical content. However, despite recent progress in expressive speech-to-speech translation (S2ST), little is known about how prosodic patterns are similar/different across languages. Understanding these cross-lingual similarities and differences is crucial for effectively incorporating prosody into expressive S2ST systems. In this work, we present the first fine-grained cross-lingual analysis of prosody using multilingual dubbing data across English-German, English-Spanish, and English-French language pairs. We analyze the similarity of pitch, energy, and temporal feature patterns between source and target speech and investigate the linguistic and alignment-related factors affecting this similarity. Our analysis reveals inherent cross-lingual correlations in prosodic structure between certain languages. The findings provide important insights into the transferability of prosody across languages and offer empirical guidance for future expressive speech-to-speech translation systems.
