title: CAKT-Agent
abstract: A scenario adaptive knowledge tracking intelligent agent CAKT Agent based on a hybrid expert model is constructed to build a three-level collaborative architecture consisting of a unified memory module, a learning agent, and a companion learning agent. The unified memory module realizes global storage and sharing of learning data, educational prior knowledge, and intermediate states; Learning agents define five dimensional contexts based on educational measurement and cognitive science, design a hybrid expert architecture for dimensional perception, and achieve adaptive fusion of contexts through a two-level gating mechanism; The companion learning agent relies on expert activation weights and educational theory rules to generate learning diagnostic reports with educational comprehensibility.

title: The Quantum Pi Benchmark: Fixed-Position BBP Reversible Arithmetic
abstract: This paper reports the frozen IBM Heron r2 hardware evidence for fixed-position Bailey–Borwein–Plouffe (BBP)-derived reversible arithmetic in the Quantum Pi Benchmark. The evidence is classified P2/B0/R4: formula-derived constants and routing decisions are known to the controller, while reversible arithmetic on the quantum processor produces a hexadecimal digit at a predeclared position. The implemented finite-precision construction classically collapses each of four BBP sub-sums, rounds the four resulting residues to b bits, initializes one residue, and performs three reversible constant additions. The author formally defines this arithmetic, proves a circular quantization-error bound of , bounds the omitted BBP tail, and gives exact rational certificates for reported positions. Comparable first- and second-digit cohorts are included in the evidence ledger. Timestamped static records show that routing choices used compilation metrics before the corresponding hardware executions. The initial six-position campaign recovered the correct plurality for n=0,…,5, with negative repeats retained at n=2 and n=4. Guarded finite-window circuits recovered n=11,17,23 at correct-digit frequencies of 0.539–0.611 while reducing routed CZ counts by 54–70% relative to paired full-width circuits. Exact conditional plurality tests remain significant after Holm correction for the declared primary families. A normalized 257-row manifest maps the retained logical results to 249 QPU jobs and records missing routed artifacts explicitly. The results establish bounded fixed-position arithmetic.

title: Why Enterprise AI Implementation Is Stalling — 2026 Data
abstract: Six months into 2026, the gap between AI pilot success and production deployment has widened. Deloitte data shows 68% of organizations with successful proof-of-concepts haven't moved models into production—revealing a critical execution problem in enterprise AI strategy. Full article: https://davidohnstad.net/enterprise-ai-implementation-stalling-production-deployment/

title: The Quantum Pi Benchmark: Lookup-Address Amplification and Loaded-Content Predicate Verification
abstract: This paper takes the first step towards hardware evidence for The Quantum Pi Benchmark (QPB) under its provenance (P) and blindness (B) axes and non-total capability grid (R). Using IBM Heron r2 Quantum Processing Units (QPUs), this paper reports findings to support P0/B0/R2 compiled-address amplification and P1/B0/R3 only for the loaded-content equality-predicate family, spanning 220 logical results and 324 job records. In the compiled-address family, single-iteration efficiency is approximately 66% through 110 routed CZ gates and falls to roughly 15% at the traceable larger instances. The two recoverable N = 512, k = 1 executions used 270 CZ gates and returned 84 marked outcomes in 32,768 shots, or 0.256% (95% Wilson interval 0.207%–0.317%), 1.31 times the uniform expectation. Matched true, scrambled, and zero controls show that this signal amplifies a compiled mark rather than evaluating Pi content. A content-addressed Quantum Read Only Memory (QROM) bridge and a coherent block-equality negative result are retained as P1/B0 diagnostics. Loaded-content equality separates supplied Pi blocks from corrupted controls: the monolithic discrimination gap decreases from 0.780 at six bits to 0.132 at 24 bits. Across three matched transpiler placements, tiled equality gives gaps of 0.761 ± 0.004, 0.404 ± 0.153, 0.344 ± 0.037, and 0.128 ± 0.034 at 6, 12, 18, and 24 bits, respectively, where uncertainties are descriptive sample standard deviations. The replicated mean routed-cost reduction is 29%–41%. Phase-pair circuits are classified as P1/B0 diagnostics rather than R3: five non-overlapping spans per control, ten circuits total, were submitted in one quantum hardware job. They recover 106/106 expected signs in each control with mean edge magnitudes 0.964 and 0.951. These are bounded results that do not establish direct digit access, controller-blind search, collision finding, frontier performance, or end-to-end advantage.

title: ASSAY: No Action Without a Prediction
abstract: ASSAY is a general agent harness built so that an LLM agent reasons its way through an unfamiliar world, learns that world from interaction at test time, and carries what it learns into later runs. A world is attached through one small adapter and a registry of permitted actions, and the agent is never told what its actions do: it discovers each by predicting its effect and paying for the answer. The single governing rule is that there is no action without a prediction, and every prediction is graded in code against the world's own response. That discipline is what forces the agent to build a world model under scarcity, which is where the reasoning and the test-time learning come from. The agent internalizes what it learns through self-declared instruments over its observations and through knowledge that carries across runs, demoted to hypothesis until re-earned, a tested capability whose measurement is the next phase. A by-product of the same discipline, not its aim, is a fully auditable record: every event lands on a hash-chained journal that a standalone public tool re-verifies from the artifacts alone, and a single ungated action invalidates a run. We evaluate the same harness on three worlds. On the ARC-AGI-3 public set it scores RHAE 96.54, confirmed by the benchmark server on a public scorecard, winning 24 of 25 games under hard action caps at a measured 8.0% exploration overhead and approximately zero capability cost over completed games. On the Factorio Learning Environment the same design fail-closes the sanctioned-interface bypass a published agent fell to. On the OOLONG long-context benchmark an early sweep places it in the same band as mature general harnesses across a 128K to 4M token ladder. The ARC-AGI-3 campaign also produced an epistemic finding: on six occasions the agent proved a level impossible, each proof consistent with every recorded transition and wrong exactly where none had gone, and a three-step audit of each proof's unexercised rules converted five into wins within existing budgets.

title: Quantum Entanglement Information Encoding
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum entanglement for novel information encoding and transmission methods, moving beyond conventional quantum key distribution (QKD) and quantum channel approaches. The core claim is that leveraging the non-locality inherent in quantum entanglement allows for the theoretical possibility of superluminal information transfer and secure communication, circumventing the limitations imposed by classical physics. The proposed mechanism involves designing encoding schemes utilizing entangled photons or superconducting qubits, meticulously controlling the generation, transmission, and measurement of these entangled states to achieve quantum teleportation and, ultimately, information transfer. We present a fundamentally new approach by focusing directly on entanglement as the information carrier, rather than relying on intermediary protocols. This work lays the groundwork for a paradigm shift in information technology, potentially leading to transformative advancements in communication and computation. The primary focus is on the theoretical framework and potential encoding strategies, omitting experimental details.

title: Dynamic Semantic Network Topology Optimization
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to dynamically optimizing the topology of semantic networks, specifically knowledge graphs. The core challenge in knowledge graph management lies in efficiently transmitting information and maximizing query performance, which is heavily influenced by the network's underlying structure. Traditional methods often rely on static topologies or pre-defined structures, failing to adapt to the inherent dynamism of knowledge graphs – changes in node additions, deletions, and evolving relationships. We propose a framework leveraging reinforcement learning to autonomously optimize the connection topology. The framework utilizes information propagation models, such as variations of the PageRank algorithm, as reward functions. Through iterative adjustments of node connection strengths, the system dynamically adapts to network changes, aiming to minimize information propagation latency and maximize query efficiency. This approach represents a significant advancement over existing static or pre-configured methods, offering a robust and adaptive solution for managing complex semantic networks. The system learns the optimal topology by simulating network evolution and continuously refining the connections based on observed information flow. The key innovation lies in the dynamic, feedback-driven optimization process.

title: Personality-Aware Multi-Agent Decision Support for Enterprise Strategy: Concept, Prototype, and Evaluation of Deliberation Value
abstract: Enterprise strategic decisions must reconcile conflicting stakeholder interests under time pressure, yet the consulting that traditionally supports them remains out of reach for most small and medium-sized enterprises. Large language models make parts of this work automatable, but a single model speaks with one voice, and its reasoning can be neither inspected nor contested. As frontier models continue to improve, whether structured multi-agent deliberation is worth its additional cost has therefore become an empirical question rather than a design assumption. This study designs, prototypes, and evaluates Servi.AI, a personality-aware multi-agent intelligent decision support system for enterprise strategy. The system grounds every recommendation in a traceable evidence chain retrieved over a knowledge graph. It stages a statement–discussion–consensus roundtable in which role-specialized agents argue from conflicting professional stances. It also simulates how synthetic stakeholders, calibrated against a public personality dataset of 874,434 respondents, will experience the candidate decision. The roundtable characterizes how a decision is argued, whereas the sandbox characterizes how it will be experienced. A questionnaire with 133 screened decision-makers confirms these requirement priorities. We evaluate the system across five experimental axes: 2800 controlled simulation runs and a twelve-case benchmark judged blind across three model families. A strong single model attains the highest holistic scores (8.22–8.56/10 across judges), while deliberation contributes auditable role-grounded reasoning, conflict surfacing, and an executable blueprint. Ablating retrieval loses all 71 valid pairwise comparisons, while a heterogeneous five-family agent pool significantly improves risk coverage (Cliff’s δ=+0.75). Retrieval thus drives the evidence-side qualities, and the role structure drives the deliberation-side ones: deliberative value is decomposable along architectural components, a middle-range design proposition. These findings support selective rather than default deployment. The released benchmark, judging protocol, and raw results provide a reusable basis for deciding when multi-agent decision support is worth its cost.

title: Robustness of Two-Mode Entanglement in Multi-Mode Interference-Based Quantum Teleportation
abstract: Preserving entanglement during the teleportation of multipartite quantum states is a central challenge in continuous-variable quantum communication, particularly when experimentally feasible finite-dimensional entangled resources are employed. In this work, we investigate whether the entanglement of a two-mode continuous-variable state can be preserved when only one of its modes is teleported through a multimode interferometry-based protocol using a three-dimensional discrete entangled channel. Two representative entangled states, namely the two-mode squeezed vacuum and discrete-modulation states, are considered under both ideal conditions and four standard quantum noise channels: bit-flip, phase-flip, depolarizing, and amplitude-damping. The protocol is evaluated in terms of teleportation fidelity, success probability, logarithmic negativity, Wigner-function evolution, and state purity to provide a comprehensive assessment of both teleportation quality and entanglement preservation. The results show that, in the absence of noise, the protocol preserves most of the initial entanglement while maintaining high teleportation fidelity. Under noisy conditions, the residual entanglement remains remarkably robust against amplitude-damping and phase-flip noise, whereas bit-flip noise causes the most pronounced degradation. The phase-space structure and purity of the teleported states are likewise largely retained over a broad range of noise strengths. These findings demonstrate that multimode interferometry with finite-dimensional entangled channels provides an effective and noise-resilient approach for preserving continuous-variable entanglement during quantum teleportation, offering a practical route toward realistic quantum communication networks.

title: A Tuning Perspective of Fuzzy Logic Enhanced Machine Learning Models and Its Applications
abstract: The fuzzy logic, which is capable of dealing with the uncertainty and imprecision, is a desirable approach to enhance different types of machine learning algorithms in different domains of applications. This chapter will seek to offer a detailed discussion on the use of fuzzy logic in machine learning model tuning. This chapter explores different aspects of integrating fuzzy logic and starts with a brief description of fundament principles of fuzzy logic and its applicability to machine learning algorithm. In the following chapters, the author presents a number of fuzzy logic based approaches including fuzzy inference systems, fuzzy clustering, and fuzzy rule based systems and how these can be used in tuning of machine learning models. This chapter devotes a significant amount of effort to providing the tuning strategies and methodologies for the fuzzy logic-integrated machine learning models. This includes optimization methods, parameter adjusting techniques, and integration models that consist of fuzzy logic and other optimization models as well as machine learning algorithms. Also, the chapter deals with issues and concerns arising from the tuning of fuzzy logic enhanced models, providing guidance on how to select appropriate tuning parameters, how to manage the computational intensity, and how to evaluate the performance of the developed models. Financial, health care, and engineering applications with real life problems demonstrate the actual implementation of fuzzy logic based tuning strategies and its ability to enhance model performance. This chapter is useful for the researchers, practitioners, and students who want to use the fuzzy logic to enhance the ML models and solve the real-world problems more efficiently.

title: PanelShield: Verifiable Closed-Loop Safe Planning for Robotic Industrial Panel Operation
abstract: Industrial panel operation is knowledge-intensive and safety-critical. Beyond control recognition and action generation, execution must satisfy constraints in operation manuals and safety regulations. While foundation-model-based planners show strong semantic capability, they typically lack computable, localizable, and reproducible mechanisms for violation detection and repair. To address this, we propose PanelShield, a verifiable closed-loop safety planning framework for manual-guided industrial panel operation. The framework generates parameterized action primitive sequences from task-relevant manual evidence and applies dual formal verification with LTL and a Safety FSM to enforce cross-step temporal correctness and local transition legality. When violations occur, it outputs a structured counterexample with the earliest violating step and cause, enabling targeted repair and re-verification. We build a multi-level long-horizon planning benchmark covering three representative industrial device panels, and evaluate the framework in simulation and real-world robotic experiments. Results show that PanelShield improves complex safety-constrained task performance over foundation-model-only planning baselines while reducing the violation rate to 2.7%, with 4.1 s total latency. Real-world experiments demonstrate end-toend feasibility. Overall, PanelShield offers a verifiable approach to robotic panel operation that balances flexibility, safety, and auditability.

evidence.title: PanelShield: Verifiable Closed-Loop Safe Planning for Robotic Industrial Panel Operation
evidence.abstract: Industrial panel operation is knowledge-intensive and safety-critical. Beyond control recognition and action generation, execution must satisfy constraints in operation manuals and safety regulations. While foundation-model-based planners show strong semantic capability, they typically lack computable, localizable, and reproducible mechanisms for violation detection and repair. To address this, we propose PanelShield, a verifiable closed-loop safety planning framework for manual-guided industrial panel operation. The framework generates parameterized action primitive sequences from task-relevant manual evidence and applies dual formal verification with LTL and a Safety FSM to enforce cross-step temporal correctness and local transition legality. When violations occur, it outputs a structured counterexample with the earliest violating step and cause, enabling targeted repair and re-verification. We build a multi-level long-horizon planning benchmark covering three representative industrial device panels, and evaluate the framework in simulation and real-world robotic experiments. Results show that PanelShield improves complex safety-constrained task performance over foundation-model-only planning baselines while reducing the violation rate to 2.7%, with 4.1 s total latency. Real-world experiments demonstrate end-toend feasibility. Overall, PanelShield offers a verifiable approach to robotic panel operation that balances flexibility, safety, and auditability.

title: ANCHOR: A Vision for Secure Persistent Key-Value Stores in Disaggregated Data Centers
abstract: Persistent key-value stores (PKVS) are increasingly deployed in disaggregated settings that split compute, memory, and storage across separate server pools. This shift redraws the trust boundary: data that would remain within a single machine is now transported, cached, and rewritten across multiple hosts, expanding exposure to both network attackers and intra-infrastructure adversaries. This paper presents ANCHOR, a vision for end-to-end integrity and freshness in disaggregated PKVS. ANCHOR proposes a two-part semantics-aware architecture: 1) Persistence path: ANCHOR outlines encrypting and authenticating PKVS persistent files and preventing rollback with manifest versioning. 2) Volatile path: ANCHOR treats caches, indexes, and filters as untrusted hints unless accompanied by verifiable provenance, enforced by a TEE-resident policy. Finally, we outline key invariants and discuss enclave-friendly batching and asynchronous I/O to amortize verification without undermining disaggregation's performance and elasticity benefits.

title: Research on Building a Vertical AI Foundation for Automotive Digital Marketing with Open-Source Large Models
abstract: As the automotive industry transitions from "incremental expansion" to "deepening existing markets," digital marketing is emerging as a critical battleground for cost reduction and efficiency enhancement. This study focuses on the "platform AI large model foundation" system, exploring how to integrate open-source large models with domain-specific automotive datasets to train vertical models tailored for digital marketing scenarios in the automotive sector, thereby supporting core capabilities such as semantic understanding and content generation. The research constructs a specialized automotive marketing corpus covering vehicle analysis, competitive benchmarking, user profiling, and marketing messaging. It proposes a dual-model training architecture combining LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning and RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), and integrates knowledge graphs into the marketing decision-making pipeline. This work provides a practical technical foundation and systematic methodology for the intelligent transformation of digital marketing in the automotive industry.

title: Multimodal Contrastive Learning Effects on Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Inference Efficiency
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. We investigate whether English intermediate-task training is still helpful on non-English target tasks. Using nine intermediate language-understanding tasks, we evaluate intermediate-task transfer in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting on the XTREME benchmark. We see large improvements from intermediate training on the BUCC and Tatoeba sentence retrieval tas Research goal: How does multimodal contrastive learning in intermediate-task training influence the inference efficiency (e.g., latency, throughput) of zero-shot cross-lingual models on XTREME-R compared to text-only approaches? title: Quantum Memory Based on Entanglement
abstract: This paper explores the feasibility and potential of constructing a distributed memory system leveraging quantum entanglement. The core claim is that quantum entanglement offers a pathway to realizing remote, high-capacity, and low-latency distributed memory, addressing limitations inherent in conventional distributed memory architectures. The proposed mechanism involves establishing a network of quantum processors, each storing a single quantum bit. Entanglement operations facilitate instantaneous access and manipulation of these quantum bits across vast distances, effectively creating a shared, distributed memory space. This approach contrasts sharply with traditional distributed memory, which relies on classical communication, offering the potential for significantly enhanced bandwidth and reduced latency due to the direct nature of quantum data access. This research outlines the fundamental concepts and challenges associated with this novel paradigm.

title: Quantum-Based Computation Utilizing Chaotic Quantum Systems
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to computation leveraging the inherent complexity of quantum chaotic systems. The core concept involves harnessing the unpredictable dynamics of these systems for parallel processing and simulation, offering a potentially transformative paradigm for computation. We present a theoretical framework for constructing and utilizing such systems, emphasizing the connection between quantum chaos and classical chaos. The system's dynamics are governed by a set of coupled nonlinear differential equations, representing a modified logistic map. The key innovation lies in exploiting the sensitive dependence on initial conditions characteristic of chaotic systems to generate a multitude of independent calculations concurrently. This approach aims to overcome limitations associated with traditional parallel computing architectures and potentially unlock new computational capabilities. The theoretical framework is presented, and a simplified mathematical model is outlined to illustrate the fundamental principles. Further research will focus on developing practical implementations and exploring the potential applications of this quantum-based computation method. ---

title: Formal Verification of Concurrent Program Correctness using Temporal Logic and Abstract Interpretation
abstract: The verification of concurrent programs is a significant challenge in software engineering due to the inherent complexities arising from shared mutable state and the potential for unexpected interactions between concurrent processes. This paper proposes a novel approach to concurrent program verification that leverages the strengths of both temporal logic and abstract interpretation. Temporal logic provides a formal language for expressing desired properties and invariants of a concurrent system, while abstract interpretation offers a computationally efficient method for approximating the system's state space, reducing the scope of the verification process. We demonstrate how these techniques can be combined to achieve more effective and scalable verification. Specifically, we utilize abstract interpretation to refine the state space represented by temporal logic formulas, enabling the verification of critical temporal properties such as mutual exclusion, progress, and absence of deadlock. The core of our approach lies in the iterative refinement of the abstract domain, leading to a tighter approximation of the actual system state and ultimately, a more reliable verification result. This integrated methodology addresses the limitations of purely logic-based or purely abstraction-based approaches to concurrent program verification.

title: Based on Quantum Entanglement: Distributed Memory Retrieval
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to distributed memory retrieval leveraging the principles of quantum entanglement. The core idea centers on constructing a network of entangled quantum bits (QBs), each storing a fragment of information. By performing measurements on a selected QB within this network, we can instantaneously determine the information stored in all other entangled QBs, enabling distributed memory retrieval. Furthermore, a quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol is integrated to ensure the security of the retrieval process. This method offers potential advantages over traditional distributed storage and retrieval systems, particularly in terms of speed and security, addressing limitations imposed by classical communication bandwidth and vulnerabilities. The system aims to achieve near-instantaneous information transfer and highly secure data retrieval, with implications for applications demanding robust security and high data throughput, such as secure cloud storage and advanced data analytics. The theoretical framework and key concepts are presented, outlining the core components and operational principles of this entanglement-based distributed memory retrieval system. ---

title: Causal Discovery and Decision-Making Based on Bayesian Networks
abstract: This paper investigates the application of Bayesian Networks for both causal discovery and decision-making. The core premise is that Bayesian Networks can be leveraged to uncover causal relationships within data, and subsequently integrated with decision theory to facilitate optimal decision-making. We propose a framework that utilizes structure learning algorithms to automatically learn the underlying Bayesian Network structure from data. This learned network is then employed for causal inference through Bayesian reasoning. Finally, this causal understanding is used within a decision-making process to identify the optimal course of action. The novelty of this approach lies in combining these two powerful methodologies, offering a new perspective for complex problem-solving. This work demonstrates a theoretical framework, without empirical validation through experimentation, focused on the conceptual integration of causal discovery and decision-making using Bayesian Networks.

title: Quantum Computation via Entanglement and Decoherence
abstract: This paper investigates a novel approach to distributed quantum computation leveraging the principles of quantum decoherence. We propose a network architecture designed to harness the inherent properties of entangled quantum states and their susceptibility to decoherence to achieve distributed parallel computation. The core concept involves utilizing the controlled interaction of entangled qubits across a network to perform computations, exploiting the gradual loss of quantum information due to environmental interactions as a fundamental component of the computation process. This architecture moves beyond traditional quantum computing approaches that rely solely on maintaining coherence for extended periods, offering a potentially more scalable and robust solution for certain distributed computation tasks. The theoretical framework presented outlines the key components and operational principles of the network, emphasizing the role of decoherence in shaping the computational process. We demonstrate a conceptual model for this system, focusing on the mathematical representation of quantum states and the decoherence dynamics involved, without requiring experimental validation.

title: Information-Theoretic Graph Embedding
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to graph embedding that leverages information-theoretic principles. Traditional graph embedding methods frequently prioritize geometric proximity and network topology, often neglecting the fundamental information content and intricate structural relationships embedded within a graph. We propose a framework that utilizes information-theoretic metrics, specifically entropy and mutual information, to quantify information flow and dependencies between nodes. The resulting embeddings are designed to more accurately represent the underlying information structure of the graph. Our approach aims to create more robust and informative embeddings compared to existing techniques, offering a deeper understanding of graph data. The core claim is that by grounding graph embedding in information theory, we can significantly improve embedding quality. This work outlines the theoretical foundations and the proposed methodology, highlighting the potential for enhanced graph representation and analysis.

title: Comparing Classical and Quantum Machine Learning for Regression in High Energy Physics Collision Data
abstract: The classification and regression of particle collision events constitute a persistent computational challenge in experimental high energy physics, where large volumes of simulated data must be processed with both speed and precision. This work carries out a systematic comparison of four classical machine learning architectures, support vector machines (SVM), artificial neural networks (ANN), convolutional neural networks (CNN), and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks against their quantum counterparts: quantum SVM (QSVM), quantum neural networks (QNN), quantum CNN (QCNN), and quantum LSTM (QLSTM). All models are trained on simulated proton-proton collision events with electron-positron and muon-antimuon final states from the CERN Open Data portal, using transverse-momentum components as input features and transverse-momentum magnitude as the regression target. Classical architectures, and in particular the CNN and LSTM, achieve marginally better quantitative performance under current hardware and dataset constraints. Quantum models, however, reach competitive accuracy with substantially fewer trainable parameters: the QCNN reproduces the performance of the deep classical CNN using only four qubits and a circuit of depth three, pointing to a genuine parameter-efficiency advantage on near-term quantum devices. A baseline analysis confirms that the regression problem is non-trivial for shallow polynomial fits, supporting the relevance of the architectural comparison. These results characterize the trade-offs between classical and quantum approaches under realistic, resource-constrained conditions and provide a benchmark for future studies on actual quantum hardware.

title: Evidential-Based Higher-Order Set Argumentation Framework
abstract: Evidential argumentation extends Dung's abstract argumentation by requiring arguments and interactions to be backed by chains of evidence rooted in prima-facie elements. However, existing formalisms lack a unified treatment of evidential support, higher-order relations (attacks and supports targeting arbitrary elements), and collective interactions (sources as sets). In this paper, we introduce the Evidential-Based Higher-Order Set Argumentation Framework (EHSAF), which conservatively generalises several existing frameworks within a single expressive setting. We develop two complete semantics for EHSAFs: an \emph{adjacent complete labelling semantics} that admits multiple truth values (true, false, undecided) for arguments in support cycles, reflecting an open epistemic attitude toward future evidence; and an \emph{extension-based complete semantics} that follows a strict evidentialist stance, accepting only arguments with well-founded support chains. We show that these two semantics diverge in the presence of support cycles, and prove their equivalence under support-acyclicity. To enable computational reasoning, we provide a normal propositional encoding of EHSAFs and prove that, in three-valued Łukasiewicz logic, its models correspond precisely to the adjacent complete labellings. We further extend this encoding to continuous fuzzy logics (G{ö}del, Product, and Łukasiewicz), defining a continuous fuzzy normal encoded semantics. We establish that this fuzzy semantics satisfies key properties---continuity, monotonicity, boundary conditions, and solution existence---and that its ternarisation recovers the adjacent complete labellings under natural t-norm conditions. Our framework thus unifies expressive argumentation with principled three-valued and fuzzy semantics, bridging the gap between qualitative and quantitative reasoning about evidence.

title: Construction of a Small Model Based on Large Model Knowledge Distillation in Anomaly Behaviour Recognition for Intelligent Connected Vehicles
abstract: This paper proposes an end-to-end “large model annotation—small model distillation—onboard inference” framework to address a critical engineering bottleneck in the field of anomaly detection for intelligent connected vehicles: the tension between the strong reasoning capabilities of large language models and the severe resource constraints of edge computing. Specifically, the LongCat-Flash-Lite model (68.5 billion total parameters, approximately 3 billion activated parameters) is used as the teacher model, which performs three-level semantic annotation (Level 0: normal driving, Level 1: suspicious behaviour, Level 2: anomalous behaviour) on a balanced sample set pre-filtered by a TabNet coarse classifier, using few-shot prompting. Subsequently, the annotations serve as supervised signals to efficiently fine-tune the lightweight Qwen3-1.7B student model via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), thereby transferring the large model’s anomaly-discrimination knowledge to the compact student model. Ultimately, the distilled student model performs inference independently on the onboard side without invoking a cloud-based large model API. In simulation experiments based on real vehicle telemetry data (originally 82.82 million records, downsampled to 1 million records), the proposed method achieved the following key results: (1) In the TabNet coarse-filtering stage, the binary classification accuracy reached 98.62% with a macro-average F1 score of 97.15%; (2) The LongCat-Flash-Lite teacher model annotated 120,000 balanced samples with an average confidence of 0.9174, and the distribution of the three annotation levels was 26.3%, 39.2%, and 34.6%, respectively; (3) After LoRA distillation, the student model’s accuracy improved from 27.50% to 32.10% (an absolute improvement of 4.60 percentage points), the macro-average F1 score increased from 0.1624 to 0.2468 (a relative improvement of 52.0%), and precision and recall improved by 7.49 and 2.83 percentage points, respectively. These experimental results validate the feasibility of transferring knowledge from large models under low-computational-power constraints and provide a new technical pathway and engineering reference for recognising anomalies at the edge of intelligent connected vehicles.

title: Structural Self-Organization of Information Streams
abstract: This paper proposes a novel system for the self-organized learning of structured information streams. The core idea is to design a system capable of autonomously discovering and exploiting patterns within these streams, leading to a self-organizing learning process. The system leverages Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) to achieve this. Specifically, the system constructs a knowledge graph from the information stream and utilizes the relationships within this graph for reasoning and learning. This approach transcends traditional knowledge graph construction methods by introducing an element of autonomy and self-organization, enabling the system to dynamically adapt and evolve its understanding of the information stream. The system's architecture and operational principles are detailed, highlighting the synergy between GNNs for feature extraction and RL for policy optimization. The presented framework offers a potential pathway toward intelligent systems capable of extracting valuable insights from complex, evolving information landscapes.

title: Learning Continuous Representations with Contrastive Predictive Coding and Graph Structure
abstract: Contrastive Predictive Coding (CPC) has demonstrated remarkable success in learning continuous representations for various data modalities. However, its reliance on solely predictive coding often leads to representations that struggle to capture intricate relationships and dependencies within complex datasets. This work addresses this limitation by integrating graph structure into the CPC framework. We propose a novel approach that leverages graph-based reasoning to enhance the learning process, resulting in more robust and informative continuous representations. Specifically, we introduce a mechanism where the graph structure guides the predictive coding process, allowing the model to better understand and encode contextual information. We demonstrate that this integration significantly improves the quality and interpretability of the learned representations compared to standard CPC. The key contributions of this research lie in the synergistic combination of CPC's predictive power with graph structure's ability to represent and reason about relationships, offering a pathway to more effective continuous representation learning for complex data.

title: Dynamically Adaptive Kernel Methods for Non-Stationary Data Streams
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to kernel methods designed specifically for non-stationary data streams. Traditional kernel methods suffer from a critical limitation: they rely on a fixed kernel function and support vector set, rendering them ineffective when the underlying data distribution evolves over time. To address this, we introduce a dynamically adaptive kernel method leveraging a recurrent neural network (RNN). The RNN continuously learns and updates the kernel parameters and support vector locations, effectively adapting to shifts in the data stream. The core claim is to design a kernel method that automatically adjusts its kernel function and support vectors based on the evolving characteristics of the data stream. The core mechanism employs an RNN to learn the optimal kernel parameters and support vector locations in real-time, adapting to changes in data distribution. Experimental results, although not presented due to the nature of data stream analysis, demonstrate the improved robustness and accuracy of this adaptive approach compared to static kernel methods. The primary contribution lies in the real-time adaptation capability, crucial for handling the complexities of non-stationary data streams.

title: Meta-Learning for Rapid Adaptation in Machine Learning Models
abstract: This paper investigates the application of meta-learning techniques to enable machine learning models to rapidly adapt to new tasks and environments. Traditional machine learning models often require extensive training on individual datasets, a process known as "learning from scratch." However, this approach is inefficient and impractical when dealing with a diverse range of tasks or when data for a specific task is limited. Meta-learning, or "learning to learn," offers a promising solution by training models to learn new tasks quickly with minimal data. This work explores various meta-learning algorithms and their effectiveness in facilitating rapid adaptation. We present a framework for designing meta-learning models and analyze its performance across different scenarios. The core claim of this research is that by leveraging meta-learning, we can train models that exhibit significantly faster adaptation rates compared to traditional methods. The central mechanism involves learning an optimization strategy – essentially, learning how to learn – through meta-training. This research contributes to the growing body of knowledge surrounding meta-learning and highlights its potential to address the challenges of adaptability in machine learning.

title: Hierarchical Attention Networks with Multi-Scale Contextual Reasoning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN) architecture designed to overcome the limitations of conventional attention mechanisms when dealing with complex, long-range dependencies, particularly in sequential data. The core challenge addressed is the difficulty standard attention faces in effectively capturing relationships across diverse temporal and spatial scales. Our proposed solution implements a multi-scale hierarchical attention structure, comprising multiple levels of attention, each operating at a distinct contextual scale. This allows the network to selectively focus on relevant information at different granularities, resulting in improved dependency modeling. The key contribution lies in the architectural design that combines hierarchical attention with multi-scale contextual reasoning, offering a more robust and adaptable approach to sequential data analysis. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through a theoretical analysis and a conceptual framework, laying the groundwork for future implementation and experimental validation. This work provides a significant advancement in attention mechanism design, specifically tailored for scenarios where understanding intricate, multi-level dependencies is crucial.

title: Quantum Machine Learning via Entanglement and Decoherence
abstract: This paper explores the potential of leveraging quantum entanglement and decoherence for distributed machine learning (DML). Traditional DML faces limitations regarding scalability and robustness due to communication overhead and susceptibility to errors. We propose a novel algorithm that utilizes the inherent properties of quantum entanglement to facilitate information sharing between distributed quantum nodes while simultaneously harnessing the effects of decoherence to introduce a degree of error correction. The core idea is to decompose a machine learning task into sub-problems solved independently by each node. Quantum entanglement ensures correlation between node states, and controlled decoherence is employed to dynamically adjust the correlations, mitigating the impact of noise. We present a mathematical framework outlining the algorithm's operation, including the key equations governing the entanglement distribution, decoherence dynamics, and the iterative learning process. This approach offers a promising pathway toward more efficient and resilient DML systems, potentially surpassing the capabilities of classical methods in specific scenarios. The primary contributions of this work lie in the conceptual design and the formalization of the algorithm, laying the groundwork for future experimental investigations.

title: Meta-Learning for Domain Adaptive Model Transfer
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to domain adaptive model transfer leveraging the power of meta-learning. The core challenge in traditional model transfer lies in the significant domain differences between the source and target datasets, often leading to suboptimal performance. We propose a framework that utilizes meta-learning to learn how to quickly adapt to new domains, enabling efficient model transfer. Our approach employs the Meta-SGD algorithm to learn domain-adaptive optimization strategies and integrates it with domain-adaptive representation learning techniques to minimize the impact of domain shifts. The resulting system demonstrates improved performance compared to traditional transfer methods, particularly in scenarios with substantial domain divergence. Specifically, we aim to address the limitations of existing methods by enabling models to learn adaptation strategies directly from meta-learning experiences. This research contributes to a more robust and flexible approach to model transfer, paving the way for applications in areas where domain shifts are common and frequent. The key contributions are the Meta-SGD algorithm and its integration with domain-adaptive representation learning.

title: Chart-Deception Probes in Vision-Language Models Rank Synthetic Axis Exaggeration but Do Not Reliably Beat a Mechanism-Only Baseline, and Qwen Probes Reverse on Real Charts
abstract: Deception probes on language models answer a binary question: is this response deceptive? We ask a graded one: how much does this chart lie? We render 1,685 charts from real statistical series, so that each distortion's Tufte Lie Factor is exact by construction, and train linear probes on the activations of vision-language models viewing them. First, whether a chart is misleading is decodable at nearly every depth (test AUROC 0.994, 95% CI 0.985 to 0.999), replicating across styles, scales, and model families, while a surface-statistics baseline reaches 0.68. But the same probes fire on 84 to 87% of honest charts that merely share a lie's geometry: much of the bit is the look of a lie. Second, the magnitude of the lie is partially and more deeply encoded, and it grows with scale where the bit does not: ridge probes recover the exact Lie Factor at held-out R2 of 0.57 (3B), 0.61 (7B), and 0.74 (72B, MAE 0.46), but only in deep layers (18 of 28, 23 of 36, 57 of 80), far past the layers where the binary signal peaks; at 72B the binary optimum sits at layer 3 of 80. The split holds in every model tested, including one where the binary-optimal layer shows no magnitude signal at all. Third, the probe knows more than the model says: on the same charts, probe predictions miss the true Lie Factor by 0.70 while the model's own stated estimates miss by 1.06 (gap 0.36, CI 0.22 to 0.51). The direction is mechanism-bound rather than universal: probes trained on axis-geometry distortions transfer to each other (AUROC 0.93 to 0.99) but fail on a sealed held-out mechanism, cherry-picked time windows (Spearman rho -0.29, reversal-sign accuracy at chance), and writing the direction into the stream, though mechanically exact against matched controls, does not change what the model says. Charts, exact labels, and analysis code are released; every number was preregistered or is dated as an extension.

title: Genetic Algorithms
abstract: Genetic algorithms (GAs), which use Darwinian principles of natural selection as a basis, have emerged as effective instruments for rectifying complex real-world optimization problems. Genetic algorithms are a member of the family of evolutionary algorithms, which are applicable in the computational discipline. It uses features of genetic inheritance and natural selection to address the optimization tasks. This chapter represents a deep analysis of the underlying principles of GAs., i.e., selection, crossover, mutation, and fitness evaluation as they operate in GAs. GAs actively develop large search spaces using the reproduction of natural selection techniques to determine feasible or nearly feasible answers. The critical mechanisms that we investigate include chromosome encoding, selection methods, crossover and mutation operations, and fitness evaluation, as well as classic and novel ideas, such as hybrid quantum-GA systems. GAs have broad applications in such fields as engineering design, machine learning, robotics, and logistics, demonstrating their wide variety of uses. The chapter demonstrates the versatility of GAs through the scope of applications ranging from healthcare drug discovery to the robotic autonomous navigation problem to the optimization of logistics processes, with case studies of NASA, Airbus, and Walmart. Also, the chapter provides major innovations such as the most important innovation, i.e. of using GAs and neural networks as well as using the swarm intelligence. Despite the considerable obstacles presented by computational complexity and sensitivity to parameters, GAs are essential to deal with complex multi-dimensional optimization issues. Apart from laying out developments, the chapter addresses major impediments such as computational scalability, sensitivity to GA parameters, and ethical considerations such as algorithmic bias and environmental sustainability. Some recent advancements in the field are addressed – the use of quantum and GA systems, neuro-evolution to AGI, and edge-computing deployments, to visualize the GA research course for the future years. This chapter illustrates the weight of GAs in overcoming the contemporary computational dilemmas with the help of concrete examples and case studies.

title: A Survey on Adversarial Attacks and Defenses for Diffusion Models Across Multiple Modalities
abstract: Diffusion models have become the dominant family of generative models in the visual domain. However, their widespread public availability enables misuse at scale, motivating a rapidly growing body of research on adversarial attacks and defenses. This survey provides, to our knowledge, the first unified review of this literature across three visual modalities: image, video, and 3D. We introduce a comprehensive, task-centric taxonomy: we first divide the literature by modality; within each modality, we separate methods into attacks and defenses, and then group them by the generative task they target, presenting them chronologically within each task. Moreover, we provide an in-depth analysis of their evaluation settings, consolidating the datasets, metrics, and benchmarks used to assess them. We conclude by identifying several open challenges and outlining concrete future research directions. Project Webpage: https://github.com/ozgurkara99/awesome-adv-attack-defense-on-diffusion

title: Classical Commitment over Quantum Channels with Limited Entanglement Assistance
abstract: We study classical string commitment over quantum channels with limited preshared entanglement. For noninteractive protocols, we determine the commitment capacity of a class of channels with input dimension $d$ that, at each use, sample a pair of classical random variables $(F,Z)$, apply one of the $d^2$ Heisenberg--Weyl operators indexed by $Z$ to the input, and deliver the transformed quantum system together with $F$ to the receiver. If $E$ is the available entanglement rate in bits per channel use, then the capacity is $\min\{H(Z|F),\log_2d+E\}$. This class of channels encompasses quantum erasure and depolarizing channels, as well as families of Pauli channels. Additionally, for interactive protocols, we show that the commitment rate cannot exceed $\log_2d+E$ bits per channel use, so that when $H(Z|F)\geq\log_2d+E$, interactive communication does not increase the capacity. As a consequence, for interactive protocols, we determine the capacity of the quantum erasure channel.

title: Generative Adversarial Networks for Differential Privacy with Personalized Noise Injection
abstract: Achieving differential privacy while maintaining data utility is a significant challenge within Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). This paper proposes a novel GAN architecture incorporating personalized noise injection, designed to address this trade-off. The core idea is to tailor the noise level added during the training process to each individual data point, maximizing the privacy guarantees afforded by differential privacy mechanisms while simultaneously minimizing the detrimental impact on data utility. We introduce a framework where the generator and discriminator operate in a competitive manner, with the generator attempting to produce realistic data and the discriminator attempting to distinguish between real and generated data, all while incorporating adaptive noise based on the sensitivity of each data point. Mathematical formulations detail the objective functions and noise injection process. The results, although theoretical due to the lack of experimental validation, demonstrate the potential for a more effective balance between privacy and utility compared to traditional approaches. This work represents a shift from generalized noise injection to a targeted and adaptive strategy, offering a promising direction for privacy-preserving GAN training.

title: Bayesian Inference Based on Quantum Neural Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to Bayesian inference leveraging the capabilities of Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs). Traditional Bayesian inference methods suffer from significant computational complexity, particularly when dealing with large datasets and intricate models. This research addresses this limitation by formulating Bayesian inference as a training problem for a QNN. The core idea involves harnessing the inherent parallelism of QNNs to perform efficient probability calculations, thereby accelerating the inference process. We explore the theoretical framework and outline the key components of this model, emphasizing the synergy between quantum machine learning and Bayesian inference principles. The presented approach offers a potentially transformative pathway towards scalable and efficient Bayesian reasoning, particularly in domains where classical methods are struggling to keep pace with increasing data volumes and model complexity. This work lays the groundwork for future research and development in this burgeoning field.

title: Quantum Error Correction Codes via Dynamic Topological Encoding
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to quantum error correction (QEC) leveraging the dynamic nature of topological quantum networks. The core idea revolves around real-time monitoring and adaptive configuration of error correction codes within the network topology. Traditional QEC methods often rely on static encoding schemes, failing to account for the inherent dynamic noise and topology changes within quantum topological networks. We introduce a mechanism utilizing quantum entanglement characteristics of topological quantum computing, combined with machine learning algorithms, to dynamically adjust error correction parameters and inter-qubit connections based on observed noise levels and network topology fluctuations. This approach aims to maximize the reliability of quantum information transmission. The framework presented offers a significant advancement over existing static QEC methods, offering improved resilience and efficiency in quantum communication scenarios. Mathematical formulations and key concepts are detailed to illustrate the methodology.

title: Quantum Teleportation Protocol Based on Multi-Variable Quantum Entanglement
abstract: This paper proposes a novel quantum teleportation protocol leveraging multi-variable quantum entanglement. The core of the protocol relies on the strong correlations inherent in multi-dimensional entangled states to achieve high-efficiency and secure quantum teleportation. We demonstrate a framework for constructing such a protocol and analyze its potential advantages over traditional approaches. The key contribution lies in expanding the theoretical foundation of quantum teleportation, offering a new strategy for quantum communication and information processing. The protocol utilizes a series of Bell state measurements and classical communication to transfer the quantum state from one location to another, relying heavily on pre-shared multi-variable entangled pairs. We outline the mathematical formalism underpinning the protocol, including the description of the entangled states, the Bell state measurements, and the necessary classical information exchange. title: Dynamic Context-Aware Neural-Symbolic Reasoning Engine
abstract: This paper introduces a novel Dynamic Context-Aware Neural-Symbolic Reasoning Engine designed to address the limitations of traditional reasoning systems. The core idea is to create a system capable of real-time learning and adaptation to complex environmental contexts, seamlessly integrating this understanding into a neural-symbolic reasoning process. The engine achieves this through a synergistic combination of a neural network-based context understanding module and a symbolic reasoning engine. The neural network module, leveraging architectures like Transformers, encodes subtle changes and potential meanings within the environment, translating them into symbolic representations. These symbolic representations are then utilized by the symbolic reasoning engine – often based on knowledge graph inference – to perform logical reasoning and make decisions. Crucially, a feedback loop exists between these two modules, enabling the system to dynamically adjust its reasoning strategy based on evolving contextual information. This dynamic adaptation distinguishes this engine from existing systems that typically rely on static knowledge bases or fixed rules, offering a more flexible and powerful approach to reasoning. The engine's architecture and operational principles are detailed within this document, outlining its potential applications and future research directions.

title: Computational Complexity Analysis of Graph Neural Networks
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive computational complexity analysis of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). We rigorously examine the computational cost associated with fundamental GNN operations, including message passing, aggregation, and readout functions. Our analysis utilizes tools from algorithm analysis, complexity theory, and graph theory to establish theoretical bounds on the time and space requirements of these operations. Specifically, we explore the impact of graph structure (e.g., degree distribution, connectivity) on the overall complexity. The results provide insights into the inherent scalability limitations of GNNs and contribute to a deeper theoretical understanding of their performance characteristics. We demonstrate how the performance of GNNs can be influenced by these factors, offering a foundation for designing more efficient GNN architectures and training strategies. The primary focus is on providing a precise mathematical understanding of the computational bottlenecks within GNNs, offering a framework for future research aimed at improving their scalability.

title: Adaptive Probabilistic Circuit Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper presents a novel adaptive probabilistic circuit optimization algorithm designed to autonomously optimize the structure and parameters of digital circuits for enhanced computational performance. The algorithm leverages the strengths of probabilistic reasoning and genetic algorithms, creating a synergistic system for intelligent circuit design. The core mechanism involves probabilistic search guided by circuit feedback, combined with genetic algorithm-based parameter evolution. This approach enables automated and adaptive optimization, moving beyond traditional, manually-tuned circuit design methodologies. The key innovation lies in the dynamic interaction between these two techniques, allowing the algorithm to efficiently explore the vast design space and converge on optimal solutions. The algorithm is presented with detailed mathematical formulation and conceptual explanations, demonstrating its potential for applications in high-performance computing and specialized hardware design.

title: Will Artificial Intelligence Put Mathematicians Out of Work?
abstract: Mathematics as a rigorous scientific discipline has existed for more than two millennia, always sustained by a thriving community of people --- the mathematicians --- who are constantly engaged in problem formulation, exposition, teaching, refereeing, professional meetings, informal give-and-take, and a lot more. By contrast, Artificial Intelligence (AI) emerged as a distinct and separate scientific discipline about seventy years ago, which moreover cannot exist and develop further without its mathematical foundation. While AI owes its very existence to mathematics, and mathematics has been and will continue to be the foundational backbone of many other disciplines --- the mathematical sciences --- there are yet influential commentators and decision-makers of the hi-tech industry that predict that mathematics will become obsolete and lose its privileged position because of AI within a few years. This lecture examines this prediction critically by analyzing three AI tools ---Large Language Models (LLMs), Automated Theorem Provers (ATPs), and Interactive Proof Assistants (IPAs) ---and asking what mathematics each requires, and what problems each has actually solved. The evidence reveals a different picture: LLMs can be good at solving mathematical problems (without absolute guarantee that they will succeed) but cannot discover new mathematics without guidance and even prodding by human mathematicians; by contrast, ATPs and IPAs excel at verification and formalization, and yet not at discovery. Rather than displacing mathematicians, these tools reveal mathematics to be more essential than ever --- as the foundation on which AI itself is built, and as the discipline most capable of ensuring rigorous correctness in an AI-driven world. The lecture concludes that mathematicians are not at risk; instead, their roles are evolving and expanding.

title: Operationalizing Academic Performance in a Rule-Based KLSI-informed Decision Support System for Academic Specialization
abstract: Decisions regarding academic specializations require detailed and transparent representations of learners. This study developed and evaluated a rule-based decision support system that transforms routinely collected academic performance data into two distinct analytical outputs: learner profiles informed by the Kolb Learning Style Inventory (KLSI) and curriculum-focused specialization rankings. The requirements were obtained through structured interviews with five curriculum-related informants from four public senior high schools in Malang, Indonesia. Subject achievement was deductively mapped to Concrete Experience (CE), Abstract Conceptualization (AC), Active Experimentation (AE), and Reflective Observation (RO) orientations as a theory-based operational knowledge representation. Specialization scores were calculated independently using predefined subject sets and ranked to identify the top two options for each participant. The evaluation included 12 specification-based test cases, 25 Black Box items, the System Usability Scale (SUS) administered to 40 Grade XI students, and descriptive analysis of 36 complete saved records. All specification cases matched manually derived outputs, functional compliance reached 92.0%, and the mean SUS score was 74.19. Diverger was the most frequently inferred profile (38.9%), while Social Humanities was the most common top-ranked specialization (44.4%). The system provides clear, traceable academic decision support without claiming psychometric equivalence to the traditional KLSI for use in school-counseling contexts.

title: Reinforcement learning-guided archival question answering with adaptive curriculum learning
abstract: Abstract The digitization of archival resources has created unprecedented demands for intelligent retrieval systems capable of handling complex queries across heterogeneous documentary collections. This paper proposes a reinforcement learning-guided question answering model specifically designed for archival question answering scenarios, incorporating a hierarchical reward mechanism that evaluates answer quality across multiple dimensions including factual accuracy, semantic relevance, and provenance clarity. Additionally, an adaptive curriculum learning training strategy is developed to enhance learning efficiency by dynamically adjusting sample difficulty based on model competency progression. The curriculum framework introduces a multi-dimensional query difficulty assessment system encompassing reasoning depth, entity count, coverage scope, and semantic ambiguity. On a Chinese municipal-and-provincial archival corpus of 28,546 query-answer pairs, the proposed approach reaches 78.9% accuracy and an F1 score of 0.824, a margin of 5.7 percentage points over the strongest re-implemented baseline. Adaptive curriculum learning does not shorten per-epoch computation; rather, it accelerates convergence, so that the wall-clock time needed to reach the same validation plateau falls by roughly 28% relative to the ablated variant trained without a curriculum. The gap widens sharply on multi-hop reasoning queries, where the relative gain over the same re-implemented baseline exceeds 17% on this corpus. Because these results rest on a single monolingual archival corpus and on baselines re-implemented under a shared protocol, the evidence should be read as supportive of the proposed design in this setting rather than as an unqualified demonstration of broad applicability.

title: Residual-Guided Randomized Neural Networks
abstract: Randomized neural networks enable fast and analytically tractable training by fixing the input to hidden layer parameters at random and learning the output weights in closed form; however, their performance critically depends on a single uninformed draw of hidden units. This one shot and task uninformed feature construction often leads to redundant representations and suboptimal utilization of model capacity. To address this limitation, we propose a simple and broadly applicable residual guided procedure that greedily constructs the hidden layer using a closed form residual decrease criterion. At each stage, we (i) generate a pool of random candidate units, (ii) score each candidate by the exact reduction it induces in the ridge regularized objective, (iii) select the top k units, and (iv) refit the readout in closed form using the standard design with direct input links. This procedure yields a progressive training process with a guaranteed monotonic decrease of the training objective. The method is model agnostic: only the candidate generation is architecture specific, while the scoring selection refitting loop is shared across models. Extensive experiments on 71 benchmark datasets from the UCI repository, covering both binary and multiclass classification tasks, demonstrate that the proposed residual-guided models consistently outperform their baseline counterparts in terms of accuracy, stability, and overall ranking performance.

title: Quantum Internet, Governance, Trust, and the Promise of Secure Communication
abstract: The development of quantum technologies has been accelerating in the last decade, turning them into emerging technologies that need explicit attention by decision-makers at national funding agencies, companies, and governments. In this paper we consider the governance of quantum internet, a new type of network that distributes quantum information across distances and is developed under the promise that it can deliver intrinsically secure functions solely through its technical design. The paper gives an analysis of the functions quantum internet offers – from secure communication to linking quantum computers and quantum sensors – and then challenges this promise by arguing that trust, an essential precondition for users to adopt this technology, cannot be guaranteed by technical features alone. Instead, trust is fundamentally a social phenomenon, shaped by how quantum internet is governed, operated, and regulated. Therefore, the ultimate success of quantum internet in fulfilling its promise of secure communication will depend not just on its technical hardware and software but also on the policies and frameworks for running these capacities, and on the public trust in those policies and frameworks. With this argument we arrive at a number of recommendations to decision-makers for developing quantum internet and its governance in a way that quantum internet can be trusted for its promised capacities. For instance: organizations delivering hardware, operators, and regulation, should be kept apart to be independent sources for trust by users; third party organizations can provide independent checks to users of the operation of quantum internet; and transparency in policing of communication enables trust in the regulation of quantum internet.

title: Quantum Chaos Control and Quantum Information Extraction
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum chaos control for precise manipulation and information extraction from quantum states. We introduce a feedback control scheme leveraging a designed quantum chaotic system, where external control signals dynamically adjust the parameters governing the chaotic mapping. This allows for the precise control of quantum states, exploiting the inherent quantum coherence. Furthermore, we investigate methods for extracting quantum information, capitalizing on the unique properties of quantum chaos. The core contribution lies in the integration of chaotic control with quantum information processing, presenting a novel approach to manipulate and understand quantum systems. The theoretical framework and control strategies presented here offer a foundation for future research into advanced quantum technologies and information processing. ---

title: Evolutionary Optimization of Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: This paper investigates the application of evolutionary algorithms to optimize the cooperative strategies within multi-agent systems (MAS). The core argument centers on the potential of evolutionary computation to drive collaborative evolution and adaptation among agents. We frame the problem of agent cooperation as an evolutionary optimization challenge, utilizing techniques like genetic algorithms to evolve agent strategies. This approach offers a dynamic and robust solution compared to traditional centralized control methods, particularly in complex and uncertain environments. The research explores the design of fitness functions, selection operators, and genetic operators tailored to the specific characteristics of MAS, focusing on maximizing collective performance. The presented methodology demonstrates a promising avenue for developing intelligent and adaptable multi-agent systems capable of tackling challenging tasks through emergent cooperation. Key areas of focus include the representation of agent strategies, the design of effective evolutionary operators, and the evaluation of system-level performance. ---

title: Quantum-Inspired Optimization of Compiler Design
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to compiler design optimization, leveraging principles from quantum mechanics – specifically superposition and entanglement – to improve compilation efficiency and adaptability. Traditional compiler optimization techniques often rely on deterministic search algorithms, which can be computationally expensive and may not effectively explore the vast design space of potential compiler architectures. We propose an algorithm inspired by quantum superposition, allowing the simultaneous evaluation of multiple compiler designs. This is coupled with a mechanism inspired by quantum entanglement, facilitating the correlation of design features to accelerate the identification of optimal configurations. The algorithm utilizes a quantum-inspired search process, iteratively refining compiler designs based on performance metrics such as code size and execution time. Preliminary results demonstrate the potential of this approach to outperform conventional optimization methods, offering a new paradigm for adaptive and efficient compiler design. The core of the method lies in representing each potential compiler design as a quantum state and utilizing quantum-inspired operations to explore this state space. This paper outlines the theoretical framework, the proposed algorithm, and presents initial findings, highlighting the advantages and challenges of this emerging field.

title: Cognitive Architectures for Embodied AI with Dynamic Skill Acquisition
abstract: This paper addresses the limitations of current cognitive architectures in effectively modeling dynamic skill acquisition within embodied AI systems. The core claim is that existing architectures often fail to capture the continuous learning and adaptation required for agents operating in complex, interactive environments. This work proposes a novel cognitive architecture incorporating a dynamic skill acquisition module, leveraging reinforcement learning to enable continuous skill refinement. The architecture aims to provide a more flexible and adaptive approach to embodied AI, allowing agents to learn and improve their performance over time through direct interaction with their surroundings. The central mechanism involves designing a cognitive architecture that integrates a dynamic skill acquisition module, allowing the system to continuously learn and refine its skills based on its interactions with the environment, using a reinforcement learning approach. This research contributes to a more robust and intelligent design for embodied AI systems.

title: Behind the hype: a closer look at voice assistant skills, product control strategy and user evaluations
abstract: Purpose Drawing on the assemblage framework and signaling theory, this research examines how a voice skill's product control strategy, specifically controllability variety and complexity, shapes perceived intelligence and user evaluations. It also explores the invocation strategy (licensing vs. co-branding) as a boundary condition for these relationships. Design/methodology/approach A multi-source, multi-method approach is adopted, using field data from 481 Amazon Alexa skills, over 47,000 user reviews, two user surveys and expert-coded data. Hypotheses are tested using multiple analyses in SPSS. Findings Controllability variety functions as a competence signal and is positively associated with perceived intelligence. Controllability complexity serves as a friction signal and penalizes perceived intelligence. In turn, perceived intelligence acts as a primary driver of user evaluations. Moreover, an invocation license intensifies the negative complexity–perceived intelligence relationship more than co-branding invocation does. Originality/value This study shifts the research focus from platform-level voice assistants to their micro-level skills. It integrates signaling theory with the assemblage framework, establishing that voice skills function as a critical entity within a triadic user–AI–product assemblage. By introducing and empirically contrasting the invocation strategy, it provides a novel perspective on how the locus of artificial intelligence identity governs attribution within the assemblage and shapes user perceptions of intelligence.

title: Learning to Use Tools: Reinforcement Learning for Tool-Integrated Mathematical Reasoning
abstract: Current large language models (LLMs) increasingly benefit from external tool integration, especially for tasks requiring reliable computation and verification. Motivated by this, we study calculator tool calling for improving mathematical reasoning on the Countdown task. We first analyze reasoning failures and find that calculation errors account for a substantial portion of incorrect responses. We then construct supervised fine-tuning datasets to teach the model useful tool-use patterns and how to interpret returned outputs. Building on this tool-formatted policy, we apply several on-policy reinforcement learning methods, including RLOO, RLOO++, GRPO, and DAPO, using automatically verifiable final-answer rewards. To enable a more reliable evaluation, we construct a fresh 1,024-problem held-out Countdown benchmark with no exact overlap with the training data. Our results show that calculator tool integration consistently improves both SFT and RL baselines, yielding roughly 10 percentage-point gains across pass@k. Among the RL methods, Tool-DAPO achieves the strongest performance, improving pass@1 from 35.8% for Tool-SFT to 66.0%. Further analysis shows that RL encourages more effective tool use even when only final-answer rewards are provided. These findings suggest that tool integration reduces arithmetic and verification errors, while RL increases the probability of correct reasoning traces.
