title: Cognitive Architectures for Robotic Learning via Simulation
abstract: This paper explores the application of cognitive architectures to robotic learning within simulated environments. The core idea is to replicate fundamental aspects of human cognition within a robotic system, facilitating learning through interactive trial and error. We propose a framework integrating perception, memory, planning, and action, modeled after human cognitive processes. This architecture allows robots to learn complex tasks effectively within simulation, potentially resulting in more robust and adaptable robotic agents compared to traditional, purely reactive approaches. The presented architecture aims to bridge the gap between theoretical cognitive science and practical robotics, offering a pathway to building intelligent robots capable of learning in dynamic and unpredictable environments. The key contribution lies in the systematic integration of cognitive components into a learning loop, enabling robots to develop strategies and adapt to novel situations. Further research will focus on scaling this architecture to more complex tasks and exploring its performance in real-world robotic systems.

title: Dynamic Programming for Quantum Circuit Optimization
abstract: Quantum circuit optimization is a critical challenge in the development and execution of quantum algorithms. The exponential growth in the complexity of quantum circuits necessitates efficient optimization techniques. This paper proposes a novel approach utilizing dynamic programming to systematically explore and minimize the resources (gate count and circuit depth) required for a given quantum circuit transformation. The core mechanism involves constructing a dynamic programming table to store the optimal solutions for subproblems, leveraging the overlapping subproblems inherent in the circuit transformation process. The algorithm systematically builds solutions from smaller circuit fragments, ultimately arriving at the globally optimal transformation. The potential scalability of this approach, combined with its ability to directly address the combinatorial nature of circuit optimization, offers a promising avenue for advancing quantum computing. This work provides a theoretical framework and outlines a detailed algorithm for dynamic programming-based quantum circuit optimization.

title: Latent Brittleness: Failure Heterogeneity Under Matched Specification, and the Perturbation-Measure Dependence of Robustness Conclusions
abstract: Version 0.5.0 — Cohort E has run. Its preregistration was deposited in v0.4.0 before execution, which makes the central result confirmatory rather than post-hoc. Design. Two arms, one protocol: MNIST+MLP and CIFAR-10+CNN, 72 models each, 100% retained. A fixed 25-epoch budget identical for every model removes the epoch confound. No baseline band — nothing is selected, and baseline accuracy is residualised instead. A three-way disjoint split (30,000 train / 2,000 match / 2,000 stress) removes the test-set reuse disclosed in the manuscript. Models are competent: 95–98% on MNIST, up to 72% on CIFAR. Result: 3 of 5 preregistered questions pass. Partial generalisation. Seed-level failure heterogeneity holds in both regimes (p = 6.0e-4 and 2.0e-4). Networks identical in architecture and training specification, trained under an identical fixed budget, converge to parameter states with measurably and consistently different failure behaviour. Previously a corrected post-hoc analysis under a flawed design; now confirmatory. The perturbation-measure reversal is bounded. MNIST reverses more strongly than the earlier cohort (-0.866 fractional vs +0.797 absolute). CIFAR does not — the absolute per-layer cap exceeds a small CNN convolutional layer's total weight count, so the two parameterisations stop being distinct interventions. A stated scope condition with a mechanism. Two prior claims are withdrawn or downgraded. Family organisation of stressors falls from +0.464 under the flawed design to +0.173 (MNIST) and -0.011 (CIFAR): regime-specific and less than half the reported size. The magnitude-plus-tilt curve representation is withdrawn — the tilt mode carries less variance than a matched monotone null in both arms. Disclosure. The Q4 pass/fail criterion as coded did not implement what the preregistration described in prose: it tested the tautological quantity rather than the tilt mode against the null, and passed one arm on that basis. We report Q4 as failing in both arms, following the prose, and disclose the mismatch rather than take the favourable reading. External validity — the largest open weakness in the manuscript — is now closed as partial, with the boundaries named. Code: MIT. Text, data and logs: CC BY 4.0.

title: Trustworthy AI at the air quality-health nexus: a systematic review of federated learning, distributed ledger technologies, and explainable AI
abstract: Abstract Air quality (AQ) related health risks are increasing globally, creating urgent demand for artificial intelligence (AI) systems that are privacy-preserving, transparent, and auditable. Although Federated Learning (FL), Distributed Ledger Technologies (DLT), and Explainable AI (XAI) are widely recognized as core components of trustworthy AI, existing research remains divided across technical and application domains. This study conducts a computational, multistage systematic review (SR) of scholarly literature records published between 2011 and 2025 using the Semantic Scholar Graph API with intersection and union search strategies. A total of 13 458 records were retrieved and refined into a research-grade corpus of 7 215 publications through DOI-based deduplication, abstract quality diagnostics, venue and publication type screening, and exclusion of non-research artifacts. We used synergy detection, bibliometric analysis, and semantic clustering to study how these technologies are combined and distributed across research domains. The semantic clustering was performed using Sentence-BERT embeddings and UMAP. The results reveal a major structural gap. Among the 6 942 technology-tagged publications in the final 7 215-paper corpus, only 25 studies were identified as triple-synergy candidates that jointly mention or report the combined use of FL, DLT, and XAI, accounting for approximately 0.4%. Among these 25 triple-synergy publications, only two studies (8%) addressed climate or environmental applications, whereas 23 studies (92%) focused on healthcare or general AI. Semantic analysis further categorizes the studies into four areas: environmental sensing, provenance, governance, and clinical risk modeling. This division creates a critical challenge for scalable deployment, cross-domain interoperability, and policy-ready AI systems for AQ-health decision-making. To address this gap, we propose the Green-AI-Trust Stack, a layered architectural framework that integrates three complementary pillars (FL for privacy-preserving distributed learning, DLT for verifiable data and model provenance, and XAI for interpretable inference and decision support within a unified AQI-health pipeline). The findings provide practical direction for researchers, policymakers, and practitioners by identifying key research gaps, methodological needs, and future opportunities for reliable, auditable, and explainable AQI-health AI systems.

title: On Left Adjoints Preserving Colimits in Homotopy Type Theory
abstract: We examine how the standard proof that left adjoints preserve colimits behaves in the setting of wild categories, a natural setting for synthetic homotopy theory inside homotopy type theory. We show that the proof may fail for adjunctions between wild categories and even produce a wild left adjoint that fails to preserve colimits. Our core contribution, however, is a sufficient condition on the left adjoint for the proof to go through. The condition, which we call 2-coherence, expresses that the naturality structure of the hom-isomorphism commutes with composition of morphisms. We present two useful examples of this condition in action. First, we use it, along with a new version of a known trick for homogeneous types, to show that the suspension functor, as well as a generalization thereof, preserves graph-indexed colimits. Second, we show that every modality, viewed as a functor on coslices of a type universe, is 2-coherent as a left adjoint to the forgetful functor from the subcategory of modal types, thereby proving this subcategory is cocomplete. We have formalized our main results in Agda.

evidence.title: On Left Adjoints Preserving Colimits in Homotopy Type Theory
evidence.abstract: We examine how the standard proof that left adjoints preserve colimits behaves in the setting of wild categories, a natural setting for synthetic homotopy theory inside homotopy type theory. We show that the proof may fail for adjunctions between wild categories and even produce a wild left adjoint that fails to preserve colimits. Our core contribution, however, is a sufficient condition on the left adjoint for the proof to go through. The condition, which we call 2-coherence, expresses that the naturality structure of the hom-isomorphism commutes with composition of morphisms. We present two useful examples of this condition in action. First, we use it, along with a new version of a known trick for homogeneous types, to show that the suspension functor, as well as a generalization thereof, preserves graph-indexed colimits. Second, we show that every modality, viewed as a functor on coslices of a type universe, is 2-coherent as a left adjoint to the forgetful functor from the subcategory of modal types, thereby proving this subcategory is cocomplete. We have formalized our main results in Agda.

title: Temporal Memory-Aware Online Test-Time Adaptation on Dynamic Graphs
abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) on graphs aims to adapt a graph neural network (GNN) that is well-trained on the training graph to the test graph, which involves potential distribution shifts that may harm model generalization and test-time inference. While recent efforts have investigated TTA on static graphs, there is still a research gap on dynamic graphs learned with dynamic GNN (DGNN) models, where both structural connectivity and node semantics evolve continuously over time. This makes adapting a DGNN model for reliable test-time performance substantially challenging. To fill this gap, in this work, we propose a novel framework of temporal memory-aware Online Test-Time Adaptation on Dynamic Graphs, named DGOTTA, to effectively adapt well-trained DGNNs during test time. Specifically, the proposed DGOTTA contains three modules: (1) temporal-aware augmentation, to extend the diversity of test dynamic graphs for addressing complex temporal and spatial shifts; (2) memory-aware model prediction, to alleviate catastrophic forgetting; (3) consistency-guided online adaptation, to enforce temporal alignment and memory smoothness. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets and four DGNN backbones demonstrate that DGOTTA significantly improves generalization under diverse distribution shifts and multiple model architectures.

title: Feasibility Assessment of Solar and Wind Energy Development in Taif, Saudi Arabia
abstract: This study assessed the feasibility of solar and wind energy development in Taif, Saudi Arabia, by evaluating renewable resource availability, technical performance, and economic feasibility to support sustainable energy planning under Saudi Vision 2030. An embedded mixed-methods descriptive–exploratory research design was employed, utilizing secondary data from reputable national and international renewable energy databases complemented by expert validation from ten renewable energy specialists. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, weighted mean, ranking, and composite mean, while qualitative responses were used to support the interpretation of the findings. The results indicated that Taif possesses considerable potential for renewable energy development, with solar energy demonstrating greater reliability and feasibility than wind energy because of its high solar irradiance and more stable resource availability. Although wind energy was also found to be feasible, its performance was more dependent on local terrain and site-specific environmental conditions. The findings further showed that renewable energy projects in Taif are economically viable based on favorable economic feasibility indicators and supportive national energy policies. In addition, rooftop photovoltaic systems were identified as an effective approach for reducing electricity demand and enhancing energy sustainability. The study recommends prioritizing solar energy development in high-resource areas, promoting hybrid renewable energy systems where appropriate, expanding rooftop photovoltaic applications, and conducting more localized assessments to support evidence-based renewable energy planning and investment decisions in Saudi Arabia.

title: Quantum Entanglement Entropy-Driven Distributed Memory Access
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to distributed memory access leveraging the principles of quantum entanglement entropy. The core idea is to utilize entanglement entropy to efficiently coordinate and route memory access requests, mitigating the latency and bandwidth bottlenecks associated with traditional global consistency models. We construct a quantum entanglement network connecting multiple computing nodes, enabling them to share entangled states. The entropy of these entangled states serves as a metric for determining which nodes possess the desired data. This allows for a fundamentally different, quantum-physical based coordination mechanism, moving beyond the complexity of conventional routing algorithms and consistency protocols. The proposed system aims to achieve significantly reduced access times and improved network utilization by exploiting the inherent correlations provided by quantum entanglement. The theoretical framework and key concepts are presented, outlining the potential for a substantial improvement in distributed memory system performance. The central equation describing the entanglement entropy-based routing is: $E = \sum_{i=1}^{K} |s_i|^2$, where $E$ is the entanglement entropy, and $s_i$ represents the state of the $i$-th entangled qubit. This equation defines the entropy value as the sum of the squared magnitudes of the states of the entangled qubits. Furthermore, the probability of a node possessing the required data is proportional to the entanglement entropy: $P(node_i) = \frac{E_i}{\sum_{j=1}^{K} E_j}$. The system's performance is analyzed considering the number of entangled qubits ($K$), the entanglement fidelity, and the access latency. We explore potential optimizations and scaling strategies for large-scale distributed systems.

title: Quantum-Inspired Probabilistic Programming for Complex Systems
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to probabilistic programming that draws inspiration from the principles of quantum mechanics. Traditional probabilistic programming methods struggle to efficiently represent and reason about complex systems characterized by inherent uncertainty, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional state spaces and intricate dependencies. Our proposed framework, termed "Quantum-Inspired Probabilistic Programming" (QIPP), addresses these limitations by incorporating concepts such as superposition and measurement. This allows for the simultaneous evaluation of multiple potential states, which are then probabilistically collapsed during inference, mirroring the process of quantum measurement. The core of QIPP lies in a redesigned syntax and runtime environment that natively supports these 'quantum-inspired' probabilistic representations. We demonstrate, theoretically, how this approach can enhance the simulation and reasoning capabilities for systems where classical probabilistic methods fall short, offering a fundamentally different paradigm for managing uncertainty. The presented methodology offers a path towards more robust and accurate modeling of complex systems across various domains.

title: Dynamic Contextual Cognitive Neural Symbolic Reasoning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for dynamic contextual cognitive neural symbolic reasoning, aiming to bridge the gap between the contextual understanding capabilities of deep learning and the precise reasoning capabilities of symbolic systems. The core idea is to develop a system that dynamically learns and adapts its understanding of complex problems by integrating neural networks for contextual feature extraction with a symbolic reasoning engine for logical inference. The system achieves this through a feedback loop: the neural network automatically learns to represent key concepts and relationships within a problem, while the symbolic engine utilizes these representations to perform logical reasoning and decision-making. Crucially, the system dynamically adjusts the neural network's weights based on the evolving input data, optimizing the neural symbolic representation, and consequently, the symbolic engine's strategy. This dynamic interplay constitutes a significant advancement over existing approaches, which often treat neural symbolic reasoning as a static or weakly integrated process. The proposed framework offers a pathway to systems capable of truly understanding and solving complex problems in a context-aware and adaptive manner. ---

title: Adaptive Neural Architecture Search via Evolutionary Strategies Guided by Information Theory
abstract: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has emerged as a powerful technique for automating the design of neural networks, but its computational cost remains a significant barrier to widespread adoption. This work proposes a novel approach to accelerate and improve NAS by leveraging evolutionary strategies guided by information theory. Specifically, we minimize prediction entropy as a key objective function, using mutual information to guide the search towards architectures that effectively reduce uncertainty in the output. Our method provides a principled way to prioritize architectures, moving beyond traditional trial-and-error approaches. The core claim is that by incorporating information-theoretic principles, NAS can be significantly more efficient and effective. The proposed framework demonstrates the potential for substantial improvements in both the speed and accuracy of NAS.

title: Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning with Intrinsic Motivation and Reward Shaping
abstract: This paper investigates the challenges of learning complex tasks within Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (HRL) frameworks, specifically addressing the issues of instability and difficulty in achieving long-horizon goals. We propose a novel HRL system that integrates intrinsic motivation, such as curiosity-driven exploration, with reward shaping techniques. The core idea is to leverage internal, self-generated rewards alongside task-specific rewards to guide the learning process, effectively mitigating the problems associated with sparse or delayed extrinsic rewards. The system utilizes a multi-level hierarchy, with lower-level policies focused on immediate exploration and higher-level policies learning to achieve long-term objectives. We demonstrate through theoretical analysis and a conceptual design that this combined approach can significantly improve learning stability and accelerate the discovery of robust policies. The proposed architecture provides a framework for tackling complex, sequential decision-making problems where traditional RL methods often struggle. This work lays the groundwork for more efficient and reliable HRL systems capable of mastering challenging environments.

title: Multi-CAST Kamang (audio recordings)
abstract: This archive contains audio recordings for the Multi-CAST Kamang corpus (Walker et al. 2026), originally published in August 2026 with version 2608 of the Multi-CAST collection (Haig & Schnell 2015). The annotation and documentation files accompanying these files have been archived separately. The recordings are available as WAV and MP3 files. Kamang [kama1365], spoken on Alor Island, Indonesia, belongs to the westernmost Papuan (non-Austronesian) language family, the Alor-Pantar languages, which are separated from the New Guinea mainland by around 1000 kilometres. Today, Kamang is spoken by approximately 6000 people, but is severely endangered: (older) adults are generally bilingual with the local variety of Malay, while younger generations tend to speak Malay only. Of the ten texts in the corpus, six were recorded in 2010, one in 2015, and three in 2020. The earlier texts (2010, 2015) were originally recorded, transcribed, translated, and glossed by Antoinette Schapper; the texts from 2020 by George Saad. Citation Walker, Katherine & Saad, George & Schapper, Antoinette & Mayer, Clemens. 2026. Multi-CAST Kamang. In Haig, Geoffrey & Schnell, Stefan (eds.), Multi-CAST: Multilingual corpus of annotated spoken texts. [version of the annotations used]. Bamberg: University of Bamberg. title: Differential Privacy-Based Location and Trajectory Data Protection for Utility-Preserving Location-Based Services
abstract: The widespread use of location-based services (LBSs) has led to the continuous collection of user location and trajectory data, increasing the risk of privacy leakage and creating a persistent tradeoff between privacy protection and data utility. To address this problem in discrete location query scenarios, this paper proposes a single-point location privacy protection method based on Q-R tree retrieval and differential privacy, termed QRDPP. QRDPP combines the adaptive spatial partitioning capability of a Q-tree with the minimum bounding rectangle (MBR)-based indexing capability of an R-tree. It applies an improved geometric privacy budget allocation strategy to leaf nodes and an arithmetic allocation strategy to non-leaf nodes, followed by Laplace perturbation of the corresponding location data and node information. For continuous trajectory query scenarios, this paper proposes a spatiotemporal generalization and differential privacy method, termed STG-DPTP, to address inadequate temporal protection, inappropriate generalization, and trajectory distortion. STG-DPTP performs hierarchical spatiotemporal clustering, separately models temporal and spatial distributions using Gaussian kernel density estimation, dynamically optimizes bandwidth parameters through Bayesian optimization, selects representative candidate subsets using the exponential mechanism, and generates protected trajectories through constrained sampling. Experiments on the GeoLife dataset evaluate the proposed methods in terms of query accuracy, computational efficiency, spatial trajectory similarity, reconstruction error, adversarial uncertainty, and temporal preservation. The results show that QRDPP improves the utility and efficiency of privacy-preserving spatial queries, while STG-DPTP better preserves the spatial distribution, trajectory structure, and temporal characteristics of the original data under the adopted differential privacy framework.

title: CLE-DTSNet: a hybrid dynamic CNN-transformer network for precise gland segmentation in confocal laser endomicroscopy
abstract: Automated segmentation of gastrointestinal (GI) glands in Confocal Laser Endomicroscopy (CLE) images plays a vital role in the early diagnosis and treatment planning of GI diseases. However, accurate segmentation is challenging due to the irregular morphology, blurred boundaries, and multi-scale distribution of glands. In this work, we proposed an efficient hybrid dynamic CNN-transformer segmentation framework, CLE-DTSNet specifically tailored for CLE gland images. Specifically, CLE-DTSNet incorporated a dynamic multi-scale transformer (DMST) block, which combined deformable convolutions, cross-scale feature fusion, and a multi-head self-attention mechanism to capture irregular morphologies, enrich feature representations, and model global context, thereby enhancing semantic understanding and addressing the morphological diversity of glands. We further introduced an adaptive feature calibration (AFC) block that employed a unique dual-calibration mechanism to suppress noise and enhance feature representations in low-contrast regions. These modules were integrated into an encoder-decoder architecture, supplemented by a dynamic multi-scale fusion (DMSF) block that achieved intelligent fusion of multi-scale segmentation results through adaptive weight learning to address multi-scale distribution. Furthermore, the joint optimization of main and auxiliary edge losses with a small-object weighting scheme ensured the precise segmentation and boundary localization of complex glandular structures. Experimental results demonstrated that the method achieved excellent and robust segmentation performance for multiple gland types on both the CLE and GlaS datasets. The method shows potential to assist clinicians in precise lesion localization and regional analysis, promising to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of GI disease diagnosis.

title: CohortContrast: Enrichment-based methodology for identification of clinically relevant concepts in real-world data
abstract: Objective: Selecting cohort-relevant clinical concepts from high-dimensional observational health data remains a persistent bottleneck in trajectory analysis, phenotyping, and real-world evidence studies. We developed an OMOP-compatible workflow for deriving compact, clinically interpretable concept sets from broad real-world data concept spaces. Methods: We applied the workflow to OMOP-mapped observational data from the Estonian nationwide OPTIMA database using lung cancer and prostate cancer cohorts. Candidate concepts observed during cohort-specific windows were contrasted against control periods or cohorts using statistical enrichment tests, filtered against time-matched background populations, aggregated through OMOP vocabulary hierarchies, and merged using correlation-based redundancy reduction. We evaluated the resulting concept sets by quantifying dimensionality reduction, examining downstream exploratory patient clustering, and conducting clinician-based relevance assessment of extracted diagnosis-concept pairs. Results: The study included 7579 patients with lung cancer and 11,547 patients with prostate cancer. The workflow reduced the concept space from 5793 to 296 concepts in lung cancer and from 5759 to 170 concepts in prostate cancer, corresponding to 94.9% and 97.0% reductions, respectively. Retained concepts spanned diagnostic, treatment, monitoring, supportive-care, and outcome domains. Exploratory clustering identified three clinically interpretable pathway-pattern groupings in each cohort. Across two clinician raters, 85.4–88.0% of the 466 extracted diagnosis–concept pairs were assessed as directly or indirectly related to the target condition. Conclusion: Enrichment-based cohort contrast can transform broad OMOP concept spaces into compact, clinically interpretable, cohort-specific representations for exploratory trajectory analysis and real-world evidence research. The workflow provides a reproducible concept-prioritization step for OMOP-based cohort characterization, with an open-source implementation available for reuse.

evidence.title: High-Resolution Dynamical Eigenspectroscopy via Variational Trotter Compression on a Superconducting Qubit Processor
evidence.abstract: The pursuit of high-resolution eigenspectroscopy on noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices is often hindered by the trade-off between circuit depth and coherence time. In this work, we introduce and experimentally demonstrate a dynamical eigenspectroscopy protocol that extracts fine-grained energy structures from time-dependent survival amplitudes. To overcome the finite coherence window of current superconducting processors, we employ Variational Trotter Compression (VTC) as a practical means to extend the duration of high-fidelity unitary evolution. Using a multi-connected 9-qubit superconducting processor, we reconstruct the time-domain autocorrelation signal via quantum state tomography for the H2 molecule at different bond lengths and for the Fermi-Hubbard model across different correlation regimes. Through multi-frequency fitting and Fourier analysis, the extracted eigenenergies agree with the exact-diagonalization values to within 2x10^-3, including the near-degenerate levels in the strongly interacting regime. Our results establish experimental dynamical spectroscopy as a robust and generalizable framework for simulating both quantum chemistry and strongly correlated lattice systems, bridging weak- and strong-coupling regimes on near-term quantum hardware.

title: DARTS: Decoder-Aware Representation Tuning via Surgery for Model Merging
abstract: Model merging combines multiple task-specific fine-tuned LLMs into a single multi-task model without additional training. However, merged models are known to suffer from representation bias: systematic drift between the merged model's hidden states and those of each individual source model. Prior work (Yang et al., 2024a) study and mitigate this bias for encoder-based vision models using a lightweight correction module trained with L1 loss. However, such bias is not studied for decoder models due to their autoregressive nature. We analyze the problem of representation bias in decoder models, and show two challenges absent in encoders: (1) the causal attention mask causes bias to accumulate across token positions, requiring position-dependent correction; and (2) not all token positions are equally important, i.e., high-entropy (decision-critical) positions matter far more than low-entropy ones. To address these challenges, we propose Decoder-Aware Representation Tuning via Surgery (DARTS). DARTS employs a novel entropy-weighted L1 loss to upweight correction at high-entropy positions where errors most affect generation quality, and a per-position additive bias that captures position-dependent error without overparameterization. We perform extensive evaluation on three domains: code generation (HumanEval), mathematical reasoning (GSM8K), and instruction following (AlpacaEval) on Llama-2-7B models, and show DARTS achieves significant improvement over the standard surgery approach while adding negligible parameters ($0.1\%$ of total parameters).

title: Temporal Graph Embeddings with Causality Inference
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to graph embedding that integrates temporal dynamics and causal inference. Traditional graph embeddings often treat graphs as static structures, failing to capture the evolving nature of relationships and the underlying causal dependencies within the network. Our method, Temporal Graph Embeddings with Causality Inference (TGECI), combines Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) with a causal Bayesian network representation. The GNN learns node embeddings, while the Bayesian network models the temporal evolution of relationships using learned Markovian transition probabilities, explicitly capturing the directionality and strength of these dependencies. We demonstrate that this approach significantly improves graph embedding quality, enabling more accurate node representations and facilitating temporal reasoning within the graph structure. The core claim of this work is that incorporating temporal dynamics and causal relationships can dramatically enhance graph embeddings. The proposed mechanism involves a novel embedding technique utilizing GNNs and a causal Bayesian network. This addresses the limitations of existing static graph embeddings by allowing for the capture of evolving relationships and reasoning about their influence.

title: Hyperdimensional Bayesian Networks for Causal Inference with High-Dimensional Data
abstract: This paper investigates the application of hyperdimensional Bayesian networks (HBNs) to address the challenges of causal inference within high-dimensional datasets. Traditional Bayesian networks suffer from the "curse of dimensionality," rendering accurate inference and structure learning increasingly difficult as the number of variables grows. HBNs offer a potentially scalable solution by representing variables using high-dimensional binary strings, facilitating efficient probabilistic inference and learning causal relationships. This work proposes a framework for adapting Bayesian structure learning algorithms to hyperdimensional spaces, leveraging the inherent properties of HBNs for robust causal discovery. The core innovation lies in the utilization of hyperdimensional data structures to overcome computational limitations and provide a viable approach to modeling complex, high-dimensional causal networks. We explore the theoretical foundations and demonstrate the potential of HBNs for tackling real-world causal inference problems.

title: Quantum Chaos and Control in Quantum Computing
abstract: This paper investigates the intersection of quantum chaos and quantum computing control. It explores the potential influence of chaotic behavior within quantum systems on computational processes and proposes control strategies to mitigate these effects. The core argument centers on the recognition of quantum chaos as a crucial, yet often overlooked, element in the precise control required for reliable quantum computation. Through the application of chaos theory, this work analyzes the manifestation of chaotic dynamics in quantum systems, detailing the implications for qubit stability and gate fidelity. Specific control techniques, including feedback mechanisms and tailored Hamiltonian designs, are examined and discussed, ultimately aiming to harness, rather than suppress, chaotic behavior to potentially enhance certain quantum algorithms. The research contributes to a deeper understanding of the complex relationship between quantum systems and chaos, providing a foundation for the development of more robust and adaptable quantum control protocols. The study utilizes mathematical formalism to rigorously define and analyze the concepts explored, focusing on key equations governing quantum dynamics and chaotic systems.

title: Quantum Computing Resource Allocation Optimization Problem
abstract: Quantum computing holds immense promise for solving complex problems intractable for classical computers. However, realizing this potential hinges critically on efficient resource allocation. This paper addresses the optimization of resource allocation in quantum computing, specifically focusing on problems like quantum circuit design and qubit allocation. We propose a methodology leveraging optimization techniques, primarily linear and integer programming, to determine optimal resource configurations. The core claim is the development of an effective method for this type of optimization. The mechanism involves formulating the resource allocation problem as a mathematical optimization problem and utilizing established techniques to find the optimal solution. This research contributes to the burgeoning field by providing a structured approach to tackling the fundamental challenge of resource allocation, aiming for efficiency and optimality in quantum computational tasks. The primary objective is to present a framework for systematically addressing resource allocation, a critical factor in the successful deployment of quantum computing technologies.

title: Quantum Entanglement Communication Architecture Optimization
abstract: This paper investigates the optimization of quantum entanglement communication architectures with the primary goal of achieving ultra-long-distance, high-fidelity quantum information transmission. The core strategy involves precise modeling and control of noise and environmental interference within the entanglement communication framework. A novel architecture is proposed, leveraging quantum feedback control and high-precision environmental isolation to monitor and compensate for decoherence and noise affecting entangled states. Employing multi-layered entanglement nodes and quantum channels, the architecture optimizes the transmission path of entangled states, thereby enhancing the reliability and rate of information transfer. The research addresses the limitations of existing architectures, which primarily focus on entanglement generation and transmission while neglecting detailed environmental control. The proposed approach represents a significant advancement in mitigating practical environmental challenges and realizing robust quantum communication systems. The key elements of this approach are a refined noise model, active feedback control, and optimized channel design. The effectiveness of this strategy is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and modeling, paving the way for future experimental validation.

title: Artificial Ecologies as an Object of Engineering Design: A Logical Core and Research Program for the Collective Evolution of LLM Populations
abstract: Abstract Multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) today predominantly scale a fixed agentic architecture: increasing the number of instances improves parallelism and search coverage, but does not by itself constitute an evolving population in the biological or cultural sense of the term. This paper introduces a formal distinction between replication, variation, and evolution as a logical core, refined by a four-level hierarchy of stringency - behavioral diversity, functional variation, heritable functional variation, and cumulative evolution - from which a research program is deductively unfolded: the design space therefore expands beyond the individual agent and fixed inter-agent coordination protocols to include the design of the environment in which population-level adaptation takes place - an environment that generates ecological pressure, heritable organizational variables, and selection. The paper's central thesis can be stated compactly: within the proposed framework, the primary object of evolutionary analysis is not the individual agent but the organization of the population. From this core, the following are successively derived: the concept of artificial ecological attractors, a hierarchy of heritable variables, a distinction between levels of collective emergence, an explicit inventory of sources of false-positive emergence, and an operational indicator that is consistent with a culturally inherited convention and inconsistent with a transient coordination artifact when control conditions are satisfied. The paper does not claim empirical validation of the full program: its aim is to fix the logical structure and to delineate a space of testable consequences. As an illustration of the core's applicability, one minimal and cheaply implementable experimental protocol is presented - a turnover persistence test for the stability of a convention under complete population replacement - whose status is explicitly limited to demonstrating operationalizability rather than confirming the program as a whole. The described protocol was not run by the authors; no empirical results from its application are claimed in the present work.

abstract: Background: Service-wide toxicity figures circulate in regulatory debate as though they described a platform.Whether such a figure is stable, or an average over communities that differ, is untested.Objective: To estimate the difference in discourse hostility between a strongly and a minimally moderated platform in matched communities, and to test whether it changes over time, varies across communities, and rests on equivalent measurement.Methods: A matched observational panel of 914 community-platform-month cells, of which 820 formed 410 matched pairs across six identically named communities on Reddit and Voat over 71 overlapping months to December 2020, was analysed.Hostility was modelled as a latent construct with three indicators and tested for cross-platform invariance.Month-clustered regressions, random-effects pooling, Newey-West trends, and bias-corrected bootstraps were estimated with Holm adjustment across nine directional tests.Results: Matched cells on the minimally moderated platform were more hostile (+0.066 in toxicity, 95% CI 0.053 to 0.078; p < 0.001) and more negative in valence (-0.064, 95% CI -0.076 to -0.053).The difference widened by +0.002898 units per month (p < 0.001), reversing sign at month 10.2, and was null only between months 9.1 and 13.6.Between communities, I-squared reached 96.5% and Hedges g ranged from 0.36 to 1.70, so the prediction interval for an unmeasured community (-0.0363 to 0.1676) included zero.Metric invariance held (p = 0.174); scalar invariance did not (p < 0.001). Conclusion:The platform difference is real, widening, and community-conditional rather than constant, and raw levels are not comparable across services.Comparative metrics need a heterogeneity statistic, a prediction interval, and an observation window.

title: Optical processing units vs. GPUs and TPUs: conditions for performance and energy advantage
abstract: The conditions under which optical processing units (OPUs) can outperform conventional electronic accelerators, such as graphics processing units (GPUs) and tensor processing units (TPUs), are investigated. Because integrated system-level implementations remain unavailable, experimental validation is infeasible; a modeling-driven approach is therefore adopted to identify favorable configurations prior to fabrication. An analytical design space exploration framework is developed that extends roofline-based latency modeling to photonic cores and identifies total computational parallelism—core size squared times core count—as the governing parameter of OPU competitiveness. The latency model, validated against representative GPU and TPU measurements, enables efficient exploration of key variables, including core dimensionality, modulation frequency, and numerical precision. Optical loss, modulation bandwidth, and signal-to-noise limitations of integrated photonic platforms constrain the accessible design space. Physically realizable parameter regimes are identified in which OPUs achieve performance and energy-efficiency parity with, or advantage over, their electronic counterparts. These results establish the conditions under which photonic computing can provide a quantifiable benefit, clarify the corresponding architectural constraints, and yield concrete specifications for subsequent high-fidelity simulation and prototyping.

title: EXPOSE: Explainable and Domain-Robust Embeddings from Pathology Vision Foundation Models using Sparse Autoencoders
abstract: Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) are widely used in computational pathology but remain sensitive to domain shifts arising from variations in staining, tissue preparation, and scanner hardware. A key limitation is that VFM embeddings entangle biological with domain-specific information, hindering cross-domain generalization. We propose Explainable Probing of Cross-Domain Sparse Embeddings (EXPOSE), a framework that uses Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) as an explainable bottleneck to identify and suppress domain-specific components in VFM embeddings. We train a sparse representation of VFM features, use a linear classifier to identify domain-specific latent dimensions, and mask these features prior to downstream relapse prediction without retraining the backbone model. Experiments on a large prostate cancer dataset with multiple acquisition domains show that SAE features capture both domain- and task-specific information, which are partially disentangled in the latent space. Removing domain-specific features improves cross-domain performance and increases embedding robustness as measured by the Domain Robustness Index (DoRI). Code is available at https://github.com/imsb-uke/expose .

title: A Framework for a Mobile-Enabled Earthquake Early Warning System (EEWS) for Notre Dame of University
abstract: This study developed a proposed Mobile-Enabled Earthquake Early Warning System (EEWS) framework for Notre Dame of Dadiangas University to strengthen campus earthquake preparedness, awareness, and readiness. Further, the study, recognizing that even short warning windows can reduce injuries and improve response coordination, the study aimed to assess the institutional practices and perceptions related to earthquake impacts and drills, and design a layered, feedback-driven EEWS framework that connects official seismic sources to rapid mobile alerts and measurable response actions. A descriptive correlation approach was used, utilizing multiple instruments such as a structured survey questionnaire to gather baseline information on earthquake drill frequency and perceived earthquake impact indicators. A total of 100 respondents participated across the departments of the university. The results show that earthquake drills are usually done. Most of the respondents who answered said they were done once a year or twice a year, while twelve (12) said they were done more than twice a year, and one (1) said they weren't done at all. The survey revealed that the magnitude of the earthquake had the biggest impact followed by other impacts of the earthquake and injuries caused by the earthquake Potential loss of life or death and physical or structural damage were rated as moderate. Based on these results and how EEWS is currently used, the study suggested a five-layer framework: (1) a detection layer that uses external seismic data providers like PHIVOLCS and the Japan Meteorological Agency; (2) a data processing layer with an eventprocessing and decision engine supported by a database and analytics module; (3) an alert dissemination layer that sends push and SMS notifications to mobile phones; (4) a response layer that combines campus protocols and user actions through the NDDU mobile EEWS app; and (5) a monitoring and evaluation layer that collects metrics and user feedback to keep the system tuned and better. Overall, the study gives a useful, campus-specific EEWS framework that connects detection to decision to action and makes sure that it is always getting better through tracking and user feedback. This helps universities be safer and more coordinated when they prepare for and respond to earthquakes.

title: Inteligencia artificial para diseñar proyectos de investigación
abstract: Este libro analiza el uso de la inteligencia artificial como herramienta de apoyo para diseñar proyectos de investigación de manera más estructurada, crítica y metodológicamente coherente. La obra examina cómo estas tecnologías pueden intervenir desde la identificación y delimitación de problemas científicos hasta la formulación de preguntas, la comparación de alternativas metodológicas, el diseño de instrumentos y la evaluación de riesgos asociados con el proceso investigativo. A lo largo de cinco capítulos se estudian aplicaciones concretas de la inteligencia artificial para buscar y organizar antecedentes, detectar vacíos de conocimiento, analizar tendencias, generar y refinar preguntas científicas, simular decisiones sobre enfoque, diseño, población, muestra, técnicas de recolección y análisis de datos, así como revisar cuestionarios, escalas, entrevistas y protocolos de observación. También se abordan problemas relacionados con sesgos, errores, viabilidad, trazabilidad y confiabilidad de las decisiones asistidas. La obra sostiene que la inteligencia artificial puede ampliar la capacidad de exploración, comparación y revisión del investigador, pero no sustituye el juicio científico, la validación metodológica ni la comprobación de las fuentes. Su uso exige supervisión humana, criterios explícitos y una evaluación constante de la calidad de la información empleada.

También se abordan problemas relacionados con sesgos, errores, viabilidad, trazabilidad y confiabilidad de las decisiones asistidas. La obra sostiene que la inteligencia artificial puede ampliar la capacidad de exploración, comparación y revisión del investigador, pero no sustituye el juicio científico, la validación metodológica ni la comprobación de las fuentes. Su uso exige supervisión humana, criterios explícitos y una evaluación constante de la calidad de la información empleada.

title: Long-term climatological analysis of solar radiation and sky conditions in Salvador, Brazil, using the daily clearness index
abstract: Long-term climatological analysis of solar radiation and sky conditions is essential for energy planning and solar resource assessment, particularly in tropical coastal regions. This study presents a computational methodology for characterizing solar radiation and sky conditions in Salvador, Bahia, Brazil, using the daily clearness index proposed by Liu and Jordan. Experimental measurements of global solar irradiance were subjected to quality control, temporal aggregation, and climatological statistical analysis to characterize global irradiation, the clearness index, and sky condition classes. The results showed an annual mean clearness index of 0.56, with predominantly partly cloudy skies (60.69%). Cloud cover variability was found to have a greater influence on solar radiation availability than astronomical seasonality. The proposed methodology proved suitable for the climatological characterization of solar radiation in a tropical coastal environment, providing a reproducible computational workflow for comparative climatological studies and energy planning.

title: Quantum-Inspired Stochastic Differential Equations for Reinforcement Learning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to reinforcement learning (RL) utilizing stochastic differential equations (SDEs) inspired by quantum mechanics. Traditional SDEs employed in RL frequently suffer from computational complexity and reliance on approximation techniques. This work proposes a framework that directly incorporates principles of quantum measurement and superposition to generate SDEs characterized by intrinsic stochasticity. The underlying mechanism leverages the inherent uncertainty present in quantum measurements to drive policy optimization, potentially leading to more efficient and accurate learning. We formulate the SDEs using a representation that mimics quantum state evolution, introducing a novel operator that allows for controlled stochastic noise generation. The theoretical framework is presented, outlining the key equations and their implications for policy learning. The approach demonstrates the potential to bypass classical approximations inherent in existing SDE-based RL methods, offering a promising direction for enhanced performance and scalability. The core of the work lies in the reformulation of the stochastic differential equation, shifting from a purely deterministic approach to one that reflects the probabilistic nature of quantum systems. This results in an SDE that is fundamentally more amenable to efficient sampling and optimization.

title: Privacy-Preserving Communication Based on Asymmetric Information Theory
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to privacy-preserving communication utilizing the principles of asymmetric information theory. Traditional cryptographic methods often struggle with the evolving threat landscape and the increasing computational power available to adversaries. Our proposed framework leverages the inherent properties of asymmetric information theory – specifically, the ability to establish secure channels with minimal prior knowledge – to provide a fundamentally different solution. We detail a protocol where communication information is both encrypted and pseudonymized, significantly reducing the risk of information leakage. The core claim driving this research is the effective utilization of asymmetric information theory for secure communication. We establish this through a detailed explanation of the underlying mechanisms, focusing on the manipulation of information entropy and the creation of robust, statistically indistinguishable communication channels. This work contributes to a new paradigm in secure communication, offering a potentially more resilient and adaptable solution compared to conventional cryptographic approaches. ---

title: Quantum State Compression and Information Extraction via Quantum Decoherence
abstract: This paper investigates a novel approach to quantum state compression and information extraction leveraging the inherent properties of quantum decoherence. The core concept involves utilizing the decoherence process itself as a tool for compressing quantum states while simultaneously extracting information preserved during this process. We demonstrate a theoretical framework wherein controlled decoherence can be harnessed to reduce the dimensionality of a quantum state, effectively compressing it, and simultaneously identify and isolate the information content that survives the decoherence. This work establishes a new perspective on quantum information processing, viewing decoherence not merely as a detrimental effect but as a potentially valuable resource for information manipulation. The proposed method offers a fundamentally different strategy for quantum state manipulation compared to traditional approaches, presenting a promising avenue for enhanced quantum state compression and information retrieval. The framework includes key mathematical formulations describing the decoherence process, state compression, and information extraction.

title: Distributed Differential Privacy with Byzantine Fault Tolerance
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to achieving both strong differential privacy guarantees and Byzantine fault tolerance (BFT) in distributed systems. The core of the system leverages a verifiable random function (VRF) based consensus protocol built upon a Byzantine fault-tolerant distributed ledger. This architecture effectively addresses the inherent challenges of protecting sensitive data while maintaining system availability and data integrity even in the presence of malicious actors. The system utilizes VRF to mask computation results, providing differential privacy, and the distributed ledger to ensure robustness against Byzantine attacks. The key innovation lies in the verifiable and layered design, offering a rigorous framework for combining these two traditionally disparate goals. We demonstrate a theoretical framework for the system's operation, outlining the protocols involved and the mathematical properties utilized to guarantee both privacy and fault tolerance. The system achieves a privacy parameter ε and a fault tolerance threshold τ, where ε controls the privacy loss and τ represents the level of Byzantine fault tolerance. The system's architecture is designed to be adaptable to various distributed applications, offering a robust solution for sensitive data processing in challenging environments.

title: Dynamic Program Synthesis and Adaptive Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to program synthesis and optimization, termed Dynamic Program Synthesis and Adaptive Optimization (DyPSA). The core claim is to design a system capable of dynamically adjusting program structure and algorithms in real-time, responding to evolving runtime environments and program execution states. This is achieved through a combined mechanism of program synthesis and reinforcement learning. The system generates multiple potential program structures using synthesis techniques and then employs reinforcement learning to select the optimal structure. Furthermore, it incorporates dynamic adjustment based on the program's execution status, ultimately aiming for superior performance and adaptability. This work addresses the limitations of traditional static compilation methods by enabling intelligent self-tuning within a program. The proposed system represents a significant step toward creating truly adaptive and robust software solutions.

title: Distributed Proof Carrying with Byzantine Fault Tolerance for Machine Learning Models
abstract: This paper proposes a novel protocol for securely distributing and aggregating machine learning model parameters within a decentralized network, specifically designed to withstand Byzantine failures. The core of the system utilizes cryptographic techniques, primarily verifiable random functions (VRFs) and secret sharing schemes, in conjunction with distributed consensus algorithms to guarantee the integrity and convergence of model updates, even when a subset of nodes intentionally corrupt the data. The system achieves robustness by ensuring that any malicious alterations to model parameters are detectable and can be mitigated through the consensus process. We outline the key components of the protocol, including the parameter sharing strategy, the VRF-based update verification, and the consensus mechanism. Simulation results (presented in a theoretical context) demonstrate the protocol's ability to maintain model accuracy and integrity under various Byzantine attack scenarios, highlighting its potential for secure and reliable distributed machine learning. The system provides a foundation for building trust and collaboration in decentralized machine learning applications, particularly those involving sensitive data or critical decision-making processes.

title: Pandora’s Toolbox: A Survey of Generalist Agent Security from the Lifecycle Perspective
abstract: Generalist agents are evolving from task-oriented systems into autonomous, self-evolving systems that acquire reusable skills, maintain long-term memory, interact with external environments, and refine themselves through recursive workflows. This shift creates a lifecycle security challenge beyond conventional model-centric or component-wise perspectives: vulnerabilities may arise from acquired external capabilities, be amplified through the orchestration of skills, memory, and tools, materialize as consequential actions, and persist through feedback across future evolution. Security for generalist agents is therefore inherently a lifecycle problem rather than a collection of isolated component- level risks. Motivated by these observations, we present a lifecycle survey organized around three stages: provenance, orchestration, and execution. We trace how risks originate, propagate, accumulate over long-horizon interactions, and persist through feedback. Across this lifecycle, we map four coupled attack surfaces: skill supply chains, user inputs, long-term memory, and external environments, and organize evaluations and defenses by where safety evidence is collected and interventions occur. Evaluations span interactive execution and offline trajectory auditing, while defenses cover input and context filtering, decision and control integrity, and runtime monitoring and enforcement. Finally, motivated by the growing importance of recursive and self-evolving AI, we identify adversarial risk generation, fine-grained safety attribution, and adversarial-feedback-driven continual safety evolution as three connected directions that form a closed loop of risk discovery, diagnosis, and mitigation toward safe recursive self-improvement agents. The latest papers and repositories are maintained at Pandora-Agent.

title: XAI in Model Validation
abstract: The DL models need to be validated to ensure the trained model is trustworthy, fair, and robust before deployment in real-time environment. Generally, the DL models are validated using various performance measures such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-Score. However, using these metrics will never give us confidence in the outcome unless it has been proved that the model has taken into consideration the relevant features for its prediction results. Hence, to identify why a model has provided a particular decision/prediction, it is necessary to reveal any potential blind spots, overfitting issues, and bias leakage during model training and validation. As the traditional performance metrics cannot reveal them, it is essential to apply XAI-based metrics and measures to ensure the model’s trustworthiness. In addition, it is essential that the XAI methods’ explanations must be evaluated using metrics such as fidelity, unambiguity, and interpretability size. This chapter provides a detailed overview on the application of various metrics and measures to evaluate the fidelity and trustworthiness of the DL models using XAI and to validate the applicability of a model’s explanations.

title: Hybrid quantum–classical AI models for secure communications: a systematic review
abstract: Abstract The emerging era of quantum computing has highlighted the importance of secure communication systems that combine quantum-resistant cryptography, quantum communication, and advanced security analytics. This systematic review critically examines hybrid models of quantum and classical artificial intelligence, focusing on architectures for quantum key distribution (QKD), intrusion detection, network management, and the integration of post-quantum cryptography. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, studies from January 2020 to July 2026 were sourced from IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, Wiley Online Library, and backward citation searches. Out of these, 30 primary studies met the inclusion criteria and were evaluated using an eight-item quality rubric and a five-level evidence-maturity framework. The findings are grouped into three categories: AI-enhanced QKD and secure communication, hybrid quantum–classical learning for intrusion detection, and post-quantum or hybrid cryptographic solutions. AI-supported QKD research has shown notable reductions in parameter search time while maintaining near-optimal secret-key rates, primarily in simulation settings. Hybrid quantum machine learning models showed competitive intrusion detection accuracy and F1 scores, but improvements over classical methods were modest, dataset-dependent, and often lacked comprehensive reporting on false positives, statistical significance, or computational costs. Post-quantum cryptography approaches demonstrated greater maturity, with evaluations involving Transport Layer Security (TLS), Internet Protocol Security (IPsec), embedded devices, wireless links, and hardware accelerators, although performance varied with platform resources, cryptographic object sizes, network conditions, and side-channel protections. Among the studies, half were simulation-based, 30% involved laboratory experiments, and 20% were functional prototypes; none showed sustained operational deployment of an integrated hybrid quantum–classical AI security system. The review concludes that current evidence supports application-specific feasibility rather than universal quantum advantage. Achieving practical deployment requires standardized benchmarking, comparable classical baselines, transparent cost analysis, hardware validation, interoperable protocols, and longer-term field testing.

title: AGENT-O: A Semantic Agent Card Framework for Interoperable and Governed Healthcare AI Agents
abstract: AGENT-O is a modular ontology framework that defines a semantic Agent Card for representing health-oriented AI agent systems and supports assessment of reporting completeness in scientific publications. AGENT-O was developed as an OWL 2/RDF ontology covering runtime, models, workflow, tools, clinical use, evaluation, provenance, governance, and reporting assessment. Evaluation included ontology inventory, OWL-RL reasoning, three SHACL suites, 12 SPARQL competency queries, three cases, and model-assisted reporting-completeness assessment of 279 papers across five dimensions. The ontology contained 1,962 RDF triples and 1,922 Protege axioms, with 252 active classes, 198 active object properties, and 51 datatype properties. All SHACL suites conformed on example graphs, all competency queries returned prespecified evidence, and all 279 papers were scored. Incomplete reporting was highest for runtime/architecture (84.6%), governance/safety (82.8%), and provenance/reproducibility (78.1%), compared with evaluation (25.8%) and benchmark-process alignment (29.8%). AGENT-O supported semantic Agent Card representation and reporting assessment while revealing an evaluation-specification gap: evaluation and benchmark procedures were reported more consistently than runtime architecture, governance, and reproducibility. AGENT-O provides a reusable ontology, semantic Agent Card profile, and reporting-completeness workflow for structured reporting and gap identification, but does not assess agent quality or deployment readiness.

title: Hybrid Differentially Private Conditional Diffusion for Synthetic EHR Generation in Medical IoT Environments
abstract: Privacy-preserving synthesis of electronic health records is difficult because clinical data combine continuous measurements, categorical diagnoses, class imbalance, missingness, and multiple trust boundaries. PrivMedSynth is presented as a conditional diffusion framework for mixed type tabular health records in Medical Internet of Things edge cloud environments. The framework applies a local randomizer before transmission and trains a conditional diffusion model with differentially private stochastic gradient descent in the cloud. Continuous features are perturbed with a calibrated Gaussian mechanism, categorical variables are protected with generalized randomized response, and clinical conditions are used as explicit generation controls. Rényi differential privacy accounts for repeated cloud updates and is converted to an approximate differential privacy guarantee. The revised formulation distinguishes the formal privacy guarantee from empirical membership inference performance and makes the privacy unit, adjacency relation, modality budget, and noise parameterization explicit. The experiments report a total variation distance of 0.041, a downstream AUROC of 0.884, and a membership inference AUROC of 0.503 on MIMIC III. These utility and attack results remain conditional on the stated preprocessing and require reproduction under the corrected accounting before being interpreted as a final end to end guarantee. The framework provides a principled basis for studying the privacy and utility tradeoff in distributed synthetic clinical data generation.

title: Cognitive Robotics via Embodied Bayesian Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to cognitive robotics centered around the integration of Bayesian networks within a robotic system—a methodology termed "Embodied Bayesian Networks." The core claim is that current robotic systems struggle to effectively synthesize sensory information with action planning. This deficiency stems from a lack of a robust, probabilistic framework capable of representing and reasoning about the inherent uncertainty within the robot's operational environment. The proposed solution utilizes embodied Bayesian networks to create a dynamic, probabilistic representation of the robot's understanding of the world. This system allows for the modeling of relationships between sensory inputs, internal states, and intended actions, facilitating predictive action planning and adaptation. The system's architecture incorporates a key element: the robot's physical embodiment directly influences the structure and parameters of the Bayesian network, creating a more grounded and intuitive understanding. This approach mimics human-like embodied cognition, offering a potentially more robust and adaptable solution for complex robotic tasks. The paper details the design principles, key components, and potential applications of this system, highlighting its advantages over existing approaches.

title: Hypergraph-Based Reasoning for Causal Discovery
abstract: Causal discovery aims to infer causal relationships from observational data. Current causal discovery algorithms often struggle with complex, non-linear relationships, particularly those represented by hypergraphs, which are commonly used to model intricate interactions among variables. This paper proposes a novel algorithm, Hypergraph-Based Reasoning (HBR), that explicitly leverages the structure of hypergraphs to enhance causal discovery. HBR incorporates mechanisms for handling feedback loops and confounding variables, addressing key limitations of existing methods. The core idea is to utilize hypergraph connectivity patterns to identify potential causal links. The algorithm employs a scoring function based on hypergraph distance metrics and iteratively refines the causal graph. The effectiveness of HBR is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and a conceptual outline of its implementation. The primary contribution lies in providing a framework for directly utilizing hypergraph topology to improve the accuracy and robustness of causal inference, offering a potential solution to the challenges posed by complex, non-linear causal systems.

title: Formal Verification-Driven Adaptive System Programming
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to system programming that leverages the power of formal verification alongside adaptive optimization techniques. The core claim is that rigorous verification of system code, combined with real-time adaptation of execution paths and resource allocation, can significantly enhance system performance and reliability. The proposed methodology divides the system programming process into two distinct phases: formal verification and adaptive optimization. Formal verification, utilizing techniques like model checking and SMT solvers, guarantees code correctness by ensuring adherence to predefined specifications. Subsequently, adaptive algorithms dynamically adjust execution paths and resource allocation based on verification results and runtime data, optimizing system behavior. This approach overcomes limitations of traditional formal verification by directly informing optimization strategies, resulting in improved system performance and robustness.

title: Dynamic Quantum Degradation Model
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic quantum degradation model that shifts the perspective on quantum error correction from solely environmental noise to the inherent dynamic properties of quantum algorithms. Traditional models primarily attribute quantum degradation to external disturbances. However, this model posits that the dynamic evolution of quantum algorithms – specifically, the time-varying interactions between qubits – constitutes a significant source of error. The model mathematically formalizes this process, simulating quantum algorithm execution to identify and analyze specific dynamic patterns leading to degradation. The core claim is that these patterns are not simply noise-induced, but rather fundamentally arise from the algorithm's operation. This framework offers a new lens through which to understand and potentially mitigate errors in quantum computation.

title: Causal Discovery from Streaming Data with Bayesian Networks and Granger Causality
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to causal discovery from streaming data, addressing the limitations of traditional methods that necessitate static datasets. The core of the proposed algorithm combines Bayesian Networks with Granger causality tests to effectively learn causal relationships from dynamic data streams. The algorithm iteratively updates the Bayesian network structure based on Granger causality results, providing a robust mechanism for adapting to changing relationships within the stream. We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach through a theoretical framework and illustrate its potential applications in real-time system monitoring and dynamic decision-making. The key contribution lies in the integration of two distinct yet complementary techniques, enabling causal discovery in environments where data arrives continuously and evolves over time. The algorithm's ability to handle temporal dependencies and adapt to evolving relationships makes it particularly suitable for complex, real-world streaming data scenarios.

title: Hierarchical Symbolic Regression with Neural Symbolic Representation Learning
abstract: Symbolic regression seeks to discover mathematical expressions that accurately represent a given data set. Despite its theoretical appeal and successes in specific domains, symbolic regression often struggles with complex, high-dimensional function spaces due to the inherent challenges of exhaustive search and the difficulty in guiding the regression process effectively. This paper proposes a novel approach, Hierarchical Symbolic Regression with Neural Symbolic Representation Learning (HSR-NSRL), to address these limitations. The core idea is to leverage the strengths of both symbolic regression and neural networks. Specifically, we introduce a neural network to learn a neural symbolic representation of the function space. This representation, capturing underlying relationships and patterns, acts as a guiding framework for the symbolic regression process, substantially reducing the search space and enabling the discovery of more complex and accurate mathematical models. The hierarchical structure of the approach allows for progressively refined representations, leading to improved regression performance. We demonstrate the efficacy of HSR-NSRL through theoretical analysis and outline the key components of the architecture, highlighting its potential for tackling challenging regression problems.

title: Emoji
abstract: # README: Data Availability, De-identification, and Reproducibility This folder contains de-identified derived datasets, coding files, statistical outputs, and analysis scripts associated with the manuscript: **When Emojis Mislead Sentiment Analysis: Pragmatic Drift, Semantic Asymmetry, and Emoji Polarity in Chinese Digital Discourse** The files are provided to support analytical reproducibility while protecting questionnaire participants and reducing risks associated with user-generated social media content. ## Data Collection Period The questionnaire data were collected between October 11, 2025 and November 14, 2025. ## Included Materials ### Corpus-Derived FPEI Data - `deidentified_emoji_count_matrix_for_FPEI.xlsx` This file is the main public reproducibility dataset for the False-Positive Emoji Index (FPEI) analysis. It does not contain raw comment text. Each row represents one anonymized analytical record and includes only: - anonymous comment ID; - corpus type (`false_positive`, `model_positive`, or `model_negative`); - occurrence counts for the 20 emojis reported in Table 1. This matrix can be used to reproduce `fp_per_1000`, `pos_per_1000`, `neg_per_1000`, FPEI values, bootstrap confidence intervals, and comment-level sensitivity analyses. ### Statistical Output Files - `emoji_FPEI_bootstrap_CI_and_sensitivity.xlsx` - `emoji_FPEI_from_deidentified_matrix_check.xlsx` - `annotation_reliability_sensitivity_analysis.xlsx` - `emoji_questionnaire_blind_consistency_analysis.xlsx` - `emoji_semantic_polarity_scores_20_items_by_filename.xlsx` These files report the statistical results used in the revised manuscript, including FPEI estimates, bootstrap confidence intervals, inter-annotator reliability, questionnaire coding consistency, polarity scores, quadrant positions, and chi-square tests. ### Questionnaire Coding Files - `types-annotator 1/` - `types-annotator 2/` - `Five_Category_Semantic_Coding_Rules_EN.docx` The `types-annotator 1` folder contains the first-round five-category semantic coding for the 20 emoji questionnaire items. The `types-annotator 2` folder contains blind review samples coded by a second annotator for reliability checking. The coding rule document describes the five semantic categories used in the questionnaire analysis. ### Analysis Scripts - `analysis_scripts/` The scripts reproduce the main reported analyses from the submitted derived datasets. See `analysis_scripts/README_analysis_scripts.md` for details. For public reproducibility of the FPEI analysis, the preferred script is: - `analysis_scripts/06_FPEI_from_deidentified_matrix.py` This script reads only `deidentified_emoji_count_matrix_for_FPEI.xlsx` and does not require raw comment text. ## Materials Not Publicly Redistributed The raw social media comment corpus is not publicly redistributed because it consists of user-generated social media content that may contain identifiable or traceable textual information and may be subject to platform terms-of-service and copyright restrictions. The raw corpus files used during analysis included comments classified by the sentiment analysis API as positive, negative, or neutral, as well as the manually validated false-positive corpus. For public sharing, these raw text files have been replaced by the de-identified emoji count matrix described above. Item-level offensiveness ratings linked to the restricted raw comment corpus are not fully redistributed in text-linked form. To support transparency, the aggregated reliability results are provided in `annotation_reliability_sensitivity_analysis.xlsx`, and the script used to calculate Fleiss' kappa, Krippendorff's alpha, ICC, and sensitivity checks is provided in `analysis_scripts/02_annotation_reliability.py`. De-identified item-level rating files can be made available upon reasonable request where permitted by institutional and platform-related data restrictions. ## Privacy and De-identification Before public sharing, the datasets were processed to remove or avoid information that could directly or indirectly identify questionnaire participants or social media users. The public corpus-derived files do not include: - raw social media comment texts; - usernames; - social media profile information; - links; - timestamps; - original row numbers from the raw corpus; - account identifiers or other identifying metadata. The public questionnaire-related files do not include: - participant names; - phone numbers; - email addresses; - IP addresses; - precise questionnaire submission timestamps; - original questionnaire platform sequence numbers. Where participant-level or response-level data are included, records are organized for analysis using non-identifying item labels or anonymized analytical structure. ## Reproducibility Notes The Baidu Sentiment Analysis API screening step is not reproduced here because the API is a commercial closed-source system and may produce version-dependent results. The submitted scripts begin from saved model-classified and manually annotated derived datasets used in the revised analysis. The de-identified matrix and statistical output files are intended to reproduce the analyses reported in the manuscript, rather than to redistribute the original social media corpus. ## Terms and Reuse The shared files are intended for verification of the analyses reported in the manuscript and for non-commercial academic research. Users should not attempt to re-identify questionnaire participants, social media users, or the original comment source from the shared materials.
